# Device Claims Review: X100 patch — consumer copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** X100 continuous ECG patch — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Publikum — "your heart rhythm", "new parents", "peel, stick, and sleep" is unambiguously consumer-facing
**Markets:** EU assumed. **German market not stated** — HWG/UWG findings below are conditional on DE targeting; tell me if it applies and I'll promote them.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 1 to substantiate, 0 OK.**

The second sentence is the serious one and it breaches three Art. 7 limbs at once. The assessed purpose is **adults**, **ECG / arrhythmia**, **under HCP supervision**. The copy sells it for **newborns**, for **breathing**, with **no clinician anywhere in the loop**. That is not a wording problem curable by data — the conformity assessment does not cover this use.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "New parents love it for keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)**, **Art. 7(a)**, **Art. 7(b)** — three separate limbs
**Why:**
- **(d)** "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out" — the assessed purpose is **adults**; a newborn is a different user population, and neonatal use of an adult-assessed patch was not covered by the assessment. Separately, **respiration monitoring** is not part of the assessed purpose at all (ECG recording for arrhythmia detection is), and **unsupervised parental use** displaces the "under the supervision of a healthcare professional" element. Three distinct drifts in one clause.
- **(a)** "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have" — the device records single-lead ECG. Breathing monitoring is a function it is not stated to have.
- **(b)** "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis" — "keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight" reads, to the parent audience it names, as infant apnoea surveillance. That is a clinical-reassurance impression the device does not support, in the highest-consequence setting available.

**Evidence needed:** **n/a — cannot be cured by evidence.** Even a validated respiration algorithm and neonatal performance data would not fix this; limb (d) is cured only by narrowing the claim or by extending the conformity assessment to a neonatal population and a respiration indication. Cut it.
**Also engaged (DE market only):**
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** — "Werbeaussagen, die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die Nichtverwendung […] beeinträchtigt oder durch die Verwendung verbessert werden könnte". Overnight infant-breathing watch is squarely the fear-of-not-using shape, and the audience is Publikum so § 11 is live. `[verified]`
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 11** — "Äußerungen Dritter". "New parents love it" invokes third-party endorsement. Note the qualifier: testimonials are **not** banned for devices, only where "in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender Weise". Here the endorsement carries an off-label use, which is what makes it irreführend. `[verified]`
- **HWG § 3 no. 1** — "Wirkungen beigelegt werden, die sie nicht haben" (respiration monitoring). `[verified]`
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit". The UWG mirror of the (d) drift, and the route by which this arrives as an Abmahnung. `[verified]`

**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** Delete the sentence entirely. There is no narrowed version — every element of it (newborns, breathing, unsupervised) sits outside the assessed purpose.

---

**Claim:** "just peel, stick, and sleep"
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)**
**Why:** The assessed purpose is expressly qualified — "under the supervision of a healthcare professional." Copy that presents the full user journey as three self-service steps suggests an unsupervised consumer-monitoring use, which is a different use from the one assessed. Also relevant that a single-lead ECG recording is not self-interpreting; the copy implies the user gets what they need without a clinician.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — this is intended-purpose scope, not substantiation.
**Call:** **Needs rewording** — keep the ease-of-use message, restore the clinician.
**Suggested fix:** see the consolidated rewrite below.

---

**Claim:** "records your heart rhythm for 14 days straight"
**Breach:** **none** on the material supplied. "Heart rhythm" is acceptable lay phrasing for single-lead ECG in arrhythmia detection, and continuous recording is the assessed purpose. The direct-to-patient "your" is cured by the rewrite below rather than being a breach in itself.
**Evidence needed:** the validated maximum continuous wear duration from the technical documentation. "14 days straight" is only clean if 14 days is the assessed and validated wear time — if the file supports, say, "up to 14 days" with adhesion or signal-quality caveats, the unqualified "straight" overstates it.
**Also engaged:** **MDR Art. 7(a)**; **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** ("wesentliche Merkmale") if DE — both only if 14 days exceeds the validated duration. `[verified]`
**Call:** **Verify.** Not a breach; an open question for the technical file.

---

### Open question on limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation, contraindication, or interpretation caveat. I can't tell from the intended purpose alone whether the IFU records a **likely** risk that belongs in patient-facing copy — skin reaction to the adhesive over 14 days and the need for clinical interpretation are the usual candidates for a patch of this type, but I'm not going to raise a (c) finding against a risk I'm inferring from the device category rather than reading in your material. **Worth checking the copy against the IFU's warnings section.** If a likely risk is recorded there, the proportionate fix at this length is an IFU pointer, not a block of safety text.

## Paste-ready rewrite

> The X100 patch continuously records a single-lead ECG for up to 14 days to help detect cardiac arrhythmias in adults. Your healthcare professional fits the patch and reviews your results. Comfortable enough to wear while you sleep.
>
> For use in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional. Read the instructions for use.

What this preserves: the duration, the continuous-recording benefit, the comfort/ease message, and the consumer register. What it drops: newborns, breathing, and the implication that no clinician is involved. Change "up to 14 days" to "14 days" only if the technical file validates the full unqualified duration.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "14 days straight" | Validated maximum continuous wear duration; whether qualifiers (adhesion, signal quality) attach | Regulatory / technical documentation owner |
| Whole asset | IFU warnings and contraindications section, to test limb (c) | Regulatory affairs |
| Market scope | Whether this copy runs in Germany — determines whether the HWG/UWG items above are live findings or not | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (d)** — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- **MDR Art. 7(c)** — raised as an open question only, not a finding — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- **HWG § 3 no. 1**, **§ 11(1) no. 7**, **§ 11(1) no. 11** — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: X100 patch — short-form consumer copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** X100 continuous ECG patch — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Publikum (consumer-directed on its face) — HWG § 11 nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 in scope if DE
**Markets:** EU assumed. **DE not confirmed** — German overlay recorded under `Also engaged:` pending confirmation.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 2 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

The second sentence is the problem, and it is not a wording problem. It sells a **different device**: a neonatal respiration monitor. The assessed purpose covers adults, ECG, arrhythmia detection, under clinical supervision. The copy claims newborns, breathing, and unsupervised home use. That is three simultaneous departures from the assessed purpose in one sentence, and limb (d) breaches are not curable by evidence — no dataset fixes this. It comes out or the conformity assessment is extended.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a), 7(b) and 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:**
- **(d)** — "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out": newborns are outside "in adults"; breathing is outside "single-lead ECG recording […] for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias"; overnight parental use is outside "under the supervision of a healthcare professional".
- **(a)** — "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have": respiration monitoring is not in the assessed purpose.
- **(b)** — "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis": positions the patch as an infant apnoea/breathing monitor, i.e. a safety-critical watch a parent could rely on instead of other care.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured only by removing the claim or extending the conformity assessment to a neonatal respiration indication.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 1 (Wirkungen, die sie nicht haben) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit, von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse) — if the copy runs in DE. Whether a neonatal-respiration indication would also sit in a different risk class turns on the MDR classification rules, which this review does not verify `[verify]` — put it to your regulatory lead before anyone treats "extend the assessment" as a small change.
**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** Delete the clause. There is no narrowed version — "may help you keep an eye on breathing" carries the same (a)/(b)/(d) content with a hedge in front of it.

---

**Claim:** "New parents love it"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]` — a third-party endorsement is an asset like any other, and this one endorses a use outside the assessed purpose. Limb (d) applies to what the copy *suggests*, including via testimonial.
**Why:** The endorsement's entire content is the off-purpose use. Removing the breathing clause leaves it with nothing to endorse.
**Evidence needed:** For the popularity assertion itself, evidence that a material number of new parents are users. Note that supplying it makes things worse, not better — documented off-label use by a population the device was not assessed for is a vigilance and PMS matter, not a marketing asset.
**Also engaged:** If DE — UWG § 5(2) no. 1, as an unsubstantiated claim about essential characteristics. HWG § 11(1) no. 11 (Äußerungen Dritter) bites only where the statement is "missbräuchlich, abstoßend oder irreführend"; here the misleading limb is arguable because the endorsed use is unapproved. Testimonials are **not** flatly prohibited for devices — treat this as contingent, not settled.
**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** Delete.

---

**Claim:** "just peel, stick, and sleep"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:** The assessed purpose is qualified by "under the supervision of a healthcare professional". A three-step self-application instruction addressed to the consumer suggests a self-directed use setting the assessment did not cover. The qualifying condition is not merely absent — the copy affirmatively contradicts it.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by restoring the supervision condition, not by data.
**Call:** **Reword.**
**Suggested fix:** "Your clinician sets it up — then just wear it, day and night."

---

**Claim:** "records your heart rhythm for 14 days straight"
**Breach:** none. This tracks the assessed purpose (continuous single-lead ECG recording) and claims recording, not diagnosis.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (wesentliche Merkmale) — only if 14 days of continuous wear is not what the technical documentation supports, or if it is a best case rather than a typical one. "14 days straight" reads as guaranteed minimum.
**Call:** **Verify** against the technical file, then keep.
**Suggested fix (if the figure is a maximum):** "records a single-lead ECG continuously for up to 14 days".

---

### Open question — limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation at all. The one thing I can point to in the material you supplied is that the assessed purpose requires healthcare-professional supervision, which implies the recording is not self-interpretable — but that omission is already caught more precisely by (d) above, so I am not double-counting it as a (c) breach. Whether the IFU records a *likely risk* associated with in-purpose use that belongs in consumer copy — adhesive skin reaction, wear-site contraindications, MRI or defibrillation cautions — I cannot tell from what I have. **Worth checking against the IFU before this ships**, and an IFU pointer is usually the proportionate fix at this length.

## Paste-ready replacement copy

> The X100 patch records a single-lead ECG continuously for up to 14 days, helping your healthcare professional detect cardiac arrhythmias. For adults, prescribed and set up under clinical supervision. Your clinician reviews the recording — the X100 does not monitor breathing and is not for use on children or infants. Read the instructions for use.

The explicit "does not monitor breathing / not for infants" line is there because the current copy has been in market with the opposite claim; if it hasn't shipped yet, you can drop that sentence and rely on "For adults" alone.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "14 days straight" | Wear-duration claim in the technical documentation — guaranteed minimum vs. typical vs. maximum | Regulatory / R&D |
| Likely risks for in-purpose use | IFU warnings, contraindications, limitations section | Regulatory |
| "New parents love it" | If real usage exists: whether off-purpose neonatal use has been captured in PMS/vigilance | PMS lead |
| Market scope | Does this asset run in DE? Determines whether the HWG/UWG items become live findings | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Reference file | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` | `[verified]` |
| HWG § 3 no. 1 | `references/hwg.md` | `[verified]` |
| HWG § 11(1) no. 11 | `references/hwg.md` | `[verified]` |
| UWG § 5(2) no. 1 | `references/uwg.md` | `[verified]` |
| MDR classification rules (neonatal respiration indication) | not in `references/` | `[verify]` — flagged, not asserted |

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

Two things I'd raise beyond the copy itself: if this asset has already been published, the neonatal-breathing claim is worth a same-day pull rather than a next-cycle edit, and your PMS lead should know it ran. And confirm the German-market question — it changes four contingent items into live ones.

# Device Claims Review: X100 patch — short-form marketing copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** X100 continuous ECG patch — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Publikum — the copy uses second person ("your heart rhythm"), addresses "new parents", and describes unassisted self-application. Not Fachkreise.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **The market was not stated** — the copy is in English, so I've routed HWG/UWG findings to `Also engaged:` with the German-market condition named. If this runs in Germany, promote them.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 clean.**

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

The newborn-breathing sentence is the whole review. It breaches three of the four Art. 7 limbs at once — new population (infants vs adults), new function (respiration vs ECG), and a false impression of infant safety monitoring. **It cannot be cured by evidence.** Even a validated ECG-derived respiration algorithm would not fix it, because the conformity assessment covers adults and arrhythmia detection. The only cures are deletion or a new conformity assessment.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "New parents love it for keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"

**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a), Art. 7(b), Art. 7(d) `[verified]`

**Why:**
- **(d)** — "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". Two separate departures: the assessed population is **adults**, the copy suggests **newborns**; the assessed use is **detection of cardiac arrhythmias**, the copy suggests **respiration monitoring**.
- **(a)** — "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". A single-lead ECG recorder is not a respiration monitor. Breathing is not a property this device has been assessed to measure.
- **(b)** — "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis". "Keeping an eye on" an infant's breathing overnight reads as a live safety-monitoring function. A recorder that stores data for later clinical review does not alert anyone to anything overnight; the copy leaves parents with a supervision impression the device does not deliver.

**On limb (c):** I am **not** raising (c) here, and the reason is worth stating. (c) reaches a likely risk "associated with the use of the device **in line with its intended purpose**". The false-reassurance risk in this sentence arises from a use that is *outside* the intended purpose, so it lands under (d), not (c). Routing it to (c) would be wrong.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured only by deleting the claim or by extending the conformity assessment to infant respiration monitoring (a different device, in practice).

**Also engaged:**
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** `[verified]` — if the German market: copy suggesting health "durch die Verwendung verbessert werden könnte". Framing the patch as overnight watch over a newborn is health-protection-by-use framing to a lay audience.
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 11** `[verified]` — if the German market: "New parents love it" is an Äußerung Dritter. Testimonials are **not** banned for devices; no. 11 bites only where they are "missbräuchlich, abstoßend oder irreführend". This one is irreführend, because what the third parties are quoted as loving is a use the device does not have. The testimonial form is not the problem; its content is.
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** `[verified]` — if the German market: "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse". This is the UWG mirror of the (d) breach and the realistic enforcement route — an Abmahnung, not a regulator's letter.

**Call: Cut.**

---

**Claim:** "just peel, stick, and sleep"

**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`

**Why:** The assessed intended purpose is conditioned on use "**under the supervision of a healthcare professional**". That condition is a component of the purpose the conformity assessment covered, not a detail. Three-step consumer self-application with no clinician anywhere in the sentence suggests a use outside it. The second person throughout ("**your** heart rhythm") compounds this: it positions the reader as the self-directed user of a professionally supervised device.

Note the setting is *not* the issue — the intended purpose does not restrict the device to a clinical setting, so at-home wear is not itself drift. The dropped supervision condition is.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by restoring the supervision condition, not by data.

**Call: Needs rewording.**

---

**Claim:** "The X100 patch records your heart rhythm for 14 days straight."

**Breach:** none. Continuous recording of cardiac rhythm is squarely the assessed function.

**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "wesentliche Merkmale" `[verified]` — **if** 14 days of uninterrupted recording is not what the technical file supports. "14 days straight" is an absolute duration with no "up to". It needs to hold against validated adhesive wear time, battery life, and diagnostic-quality signal retention across the full period, not just the theoretical maximum.

**Evidence needed:** wear-duration and signal-quality data from the technical documentation; the wear time stated in the IFU.

**Call: Verify.**

---

### Open question — not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation at all: no mention that recordings require clinical interpretation, and no mention of adhesive-related skin reaction, which is the kind of thing that commonly sits in an IFU for a 14-day patch. I have not seen the IFU, so **I am not raising a limb (c) finding** — (c) requires me to name a likely risk from supplied material, and inferring one from the device category would make the finding unfalsifiable. Worth checking the IFU: if it records a likely risk of use in line with the intended purpose, benefit-only copy of this length is a genuine (c) exposure, and an IFU pointer is usually the proportionate fix.

## Suggested revised copy — paste-ready

> The X100 patch records a continuous single-lead ECG for up to 14 days, so your clinician can review your heart rhythm for arrhythmias. For adults, prescribed and monitored by a healthcare professional. Apply as described in the instructions for use.

Three deliberate changes: the newborn sentence is gone entirely; "14 days straight" becomes "up to 14 days" pending the wear-duration data; supervision and the adult population are back on the face of the copy. If the technical file supports uninterrupted 14-day recording, "for 14 days" can go back in.

If marketing wants to keep a testimonial, one about the assessed use is fine — HWG § 11(1) no. 11 does not ban testimonials for devices.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "14 days straight" | Validated wear duration, adhesive performance, battery life, signal quality across the full wear period; IFU-stated wear time | Regulatory / technical file owner |
| Any limitation statement | Whether the IFU records a likely risk (skin reaction, need for clinical interpretation) that short-form copy should point to | Regulatory / IFU author |
| Market routing | Whether this copy runs in Germany | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (d)** — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7, no. 11** — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (Publikum; devices limited to nos. 7–9, 11, 12)
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

## Verdict

Don't ship this. The second sentence puts the device outside its assessed intended purpose in two independent ways, and one of them is a patient-safety exposure, not just a paperwork problem.

## Findings

**1. Newborn breathing monitoring — critical (MDR Art. 7(a) and (d))**

"Keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight" ascribes a **function the device does not have**. The device detects cardiac arrhythmias from a single-lead ECG; it is not a respiration monitor and has no apnea-detection performance claim. Art. 7(a) prohibits exactly this. It also engages Art. 7(d) — it fails to inform of a likely risk, because the foreseeable consequence of the claim is a parent relying on the patch to alert them to an infant's breathing stopping. It will not.

This also reads as an implicit infant apnea/SIDS monitoring claim. That's a vital-signs monitoring function in a safety-critical context, which would sit in a different risk class with a different conformity-assessment route entirely.

**2. Paediatric population — critical**

The assessed population is **adults**. Newborns are not a subgroup you can extend into with a marketing line: different clinical evaluation, different electrode/adhesive biocompatibility and skin-integrity data, different usability validation. Promoting paediatric use means promoting a device for an intended purpose not covered by the CE certificate.

**3. "Just peel, stick, and sleep" — major**

The intended purpose is qualified by *"under the supervision of a healthcare professional."* This copy positions the product as consumer self-application with no clinician in the loop, and by omission implies the user interprets the output themselves. The HCP-supervision element isn't optional garnish — it's part of the assessed intended purpose and has to survive into promotional material.

**4. "New parents love it" — major**

Compounds #1 and #2 by naming the wrong user group and the wrong patient. Separately, it's a testimonial-style popularity claim: it needs evidentiary substantiation, and testimonials in medical device advertising are restricted or prohibited outright in several markets (TGA, and various EU member-state national rules layered on top of MDR).

**5. "14 days straight" — check, don't assume**

A hard duration claim. Verify against the technical documentation for validated continuous wear time — battery, adhesive integrity, signal quality over the full period — and confirm the wording matches the IFU. If the validated figure is a maximum rather than a guaranteed duration, this needs to be "up to 14 days."

**6. Missing mandatory-ish elements — minor to major depending on market**

No identification as a medical device, no "read the Instructions for Use" direction, no statement of the intended adult population, no indication that the recording is interpreted by a clinician.

## Suggested rewrite

> The X100 is a wearable single-lead ECG patch that continuously records your heart rhythm for up to 14 days.
>
> Your healthcare professional prescribes it, fits it, and reviews the recording to check for cardiac arrhythmias — so you can get on with your day, and sleep normally at night, while it does the work.
>
> For use in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional. Medical device. Always read the Instructions for Use.

Two things to confirm before this is final: the validated wear time (adjust "up to 14 days" accordingly), and whether "fits it" is accurate — if patients self-apply under remote clinician supervision, say that instead, since it's an easy detail to get wrong in the other direction.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict: do not publish

The copy claims an intended purpose the device does not have. This isn't a wording problem you can soften — one clause has to come out entirely.

## Findings

**1. Newborn breathing monitoring — off-label, stop-ship**

This breaks the assessed intended purpose on three separate axes at once:

| Assessed | Copy claims |
|---|---|
| adults | newborn |
| cardiac arrhythmias | breathing |
| under HCP supervision | "peel, stick, and sleep" |

Under MDR Article 7 this hits (a) ascribing functions the device does not have, (b) creating a false impression regarding diagnosis/monitoring, and (d) suggesting uses other than those for which conformity assessment was carried out. A single-lead ECG recorder is not a respiration monitor, and a *recorder* is not a *monitor* — there is no real-time analysis and no alarm. A parent reading this will believe the patch will tell them if their baby stops breathing. It will not, and there is no risk statement anywhere in the copy to correct that impression (Art. 7(c)).

Treat this as a safety issue, not just a compliance one. The implied use case is apnea/SIDS surveillance, which is the highest-consequence possible misreading of a passive recorder.

Note also that neonatal use isn't a copy fix away — it would need a new intended purpose, paediatric clinical evidence, adhesive biocompatibility and skin-safety data for neonatal skin, and re-assessment by your notified body as a significant change. Marketing cannot get there ahead of the technical documentation.

**2. "New parents love it" — testimonial + wrong audience**

Unsubstantiated social proof, and several member states restrict testimonials in medical device advertising to the public. Independently of the newborn issue, delete this construction. If you have real user data, cite it as data.

**3. "peel, stick, and sleep" — drops HCP supervision**

The intended purpose is conditioned on healthcare professional supervision. This phrasing positions the device as consumer self-directed wellness. Even with the newborn clause removed, it misrepresents the use model, and in jurisdictions restricting advertising of prescription/professional-supervised devices to the general public, it aggravates that exposure.

**4. "14 days straight" — verify, don't assume**

Check this against the technical documentation before it ships: is 14 days the validated *continuous* wear time for a single patch, with no re-siting, battery change, or data gap? "Straight" is a strong uninterrupted-recording claim. If the validated figure is "up to 14 days" or depends on conditions, say so.

**5. "your heart rhythm"** is acceptable lay phrasing for single-lead ECG, but the copy nowhere says the recording is reviewed and interpreted by a healthcare professional, or that the device is not for emergency use. For a recorder, that omission is material.

## Suggested rewrite

> The X100 is a wearable patch that continuously records your heart rhythm (single-lead ECG) for up to 14 days, helping your healthcare professional detect cardiac arrhythmias. Prescribed and reviewed by a clinician. For use in adults. The X100 records for later review — it does not monitor you in real time and will not alert you or anyone else to a medical event. Not for emergency use.

Adjust "prescribed" to match your actual supply route, and confirm the 14-day figure per finding 4.

## If the newborn segment matters commercially

The route is a formal intended-purpose extension: paediatric/neonatal clinical evidence, a respiration-derived parameter with its own validation if you want any breathing claim at all, neonatal skin biocompatibility, usability for lay caregivers, and — if you add any alerting function — a reclassification assessment, since real-time patient monitoring with alarms sits above IIa. That's a regulatory programme, not a campaign. Worth telling the commercial team early so they stop building the launch around it.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict: do not publish. Two of the three sentences promote outside the assessed intended purpose.

**Critical — off-label promotion (MDR Art. 7)**

*"keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"* fails on three independent counts:

- **Wrong population.** Intended purpose is *adults*. Neonates are not covered by the clinical evaluation, the biocompatibility assessment (neonatal skin adhesion/stripping), or the notified body's Class IIa conformity assessment.
- **Wrong physiological parameter.** The device records single-lead ECG. Breathing is not an output. Art. 7(a)/(d) specifically prohibits ascribing functions and properties the device does not have.
- **Implied life-supporting function.** "Keeping an eye on breathing overnight" reads as apnea/SIDS monitoring. That is a different, higher-risk indication requiring real-time alarms and alarm-condition validation (IEC 60601-1-8). A retrospective Holter-type recorder has no alarm at all — a parent relying on this could believe absence of an alert means the baby is fine.

Promoting a materially different intended purpose can be treated as placing an unassessed device on the market, not merely as an advertising infringement.

**Critical — strips the use condition**

*"just peel, stick, and sleep"* deletes "under the supervision of a healthcare professional." The assessed intended purpose has HCP supervision as a condition of safe use; copy that frames the device as self-applied consumer wellness contradicts the IFU and the risk controls that depend on that supervision.

**High — unsubstantiated testimonial**

*"New parents love it"* is a testimonial-style efficacy claim with no substantiation on file, and it is testimonial evidence for the very use that is off-label. Several member states and the UK/TGA restrict testimonials in medical device advertising outright.

**Medium — claims to verify**

- "14 days straight" must match the validated maximum wear time and adhesive performance data, not the battery spec.
- Nothing in the copy mentions arrhythmia detection — the actual medical purpose — or the single-lead limitation. The copy reads as a lifestyle product, which compounds every issue above.

**Medium — referential ambiguity**

The copy shifts subject mid-sentence: the patch records *your* rhythm, then monitors *a newborn's* breathing. Either the patch goes on the baby (off-label) or an adult wearing it somehow monitors the baby (incoherent). Both readings are defective; ambiguity is not a defence.

## Suggested compliant rewrite

> The X100 patch records a continuous single-lead ECG for up to 14 days, helping your clinician detect cardiac arrhythmias. Prescribed and fitted under the supervision of a healthcare professional, it's discreet enough to wear through work, exercise, and sleep. For use in adults.

## Actions

1. Remove the newborn/breathing sentence entirely — it is not fixable with a disclaimer.
2. Reinstate "adults" and HCP supervision in any customer-facing asset.
3. Confirm the 14-day figure against the technical documentation before this or the rewrite goes out.
4. Check whether this copy has already been published; if so, treat it as a potential Art. 7 non-compliance and route it through your regulatory/PRRC process rather than quietly editing it.

graders.evidence:
Both anchors first, since the skill won't let me start without them.

**Anchor 2 (audience) is settled:** credentialed login, hospital procurement and clinical engineering → **Fachkreise**. HWG § 11 does not apply. That matters here: the testimonial is *not* reviewable under § 11(1) no. 11, and anyone telling you "testimonials are banned" is wrong on both counts. § 3 still applies in full.

**Anchor 1 (intended purpose) is not settled**, so per the skill:

> I can review limbs (a), (b) and (c) without the intended purpose, but (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I cannot assess it against a purpose I have not seen. Can you paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC?

Everything below is complete for (a), (b), (c) and the German overlay.

---

# Device Claims Review: gated procurement page, testimonial + adoption line

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Surgical navigation system — Class IIb (notified body involvement stated by user; certificate scope not supplied)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (gated, credentialed; procurement + clinical engineering). HWG § 11 disapplied.
**Markets:** DE stated; copy asserts DACH (AT and CH engaged)

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 verify.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

The copy contains nothing I can call misleading on the material supplied. It contains two claims that are structurally unverifiable as written — a quantified benefit with no disclosed baseline, and a geographic adoption claim spanning a non-EU market — and under UWG that structure is the expensive part, independently of whether the underlying facts are good.

## Findings

**Claim:** "It took two steps out of every registration."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A quantified reduction with no disclosed comparator. "Two steps out of" is inherently relative and the baseline is unstated — previous software version, competitor system, or manual workflow. "Every" universalises one site's experience into a device property. On Fachkreise readers, who discount a single-site anecdote, I can't call this misleading on what I have.
**Evidence needed:** The baseline workflow, named; the step count before and after; whether the reduction holds across registration modes or only the one Prof. Ellwanger uses; whether the site was running a comparable configuration.
**Also engaged:**
- MDR Art. 7(a) [verified] — if the two-step reduction is specific to one site's configuration but the copy presents it as a device property.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — "Vorteile", "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse". A benefit figure a reader cannot check from public information is cheap to attack even when true.
- UWG § 6(2) no. 2 [verified] — **if** the unstated baseline is an identifiable competitor system. § 6(1) "erkennbar" is broad; the DACH navigation market is small enough that "the old way" may identify a specific vendor. If so, the comparison must be objective and *nachprüfbar*, which an undisclosed baseline is not.
- MDR Art. 7(c) [verified] — **conditional, and the one I'd chase first.** Registration is the accuracy-critical phase of navigation. If the IFU prescribes accuracy-verification steps within the registration sequence, copy celebrating the removal of steps from that sequence needs to not read as endorsing their omission. I am not raising (c) as a breach: I have no IFU and the skill forbids inferring a likely risk from the device category. Check it against the IFU.
**Call:** Needs substantiation + rewording

**Claim:** "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Three-country adoption claim. DACH includes Switzerland, a third country for MDR purposes. "Routine use" also asserts a deployment mode, not just presence.
**Evidence needed:** Sites per country, with deployment status; confirmation that Austrian and Swiss placements are routine commercial use rather than pilots, evaluations, or clinical investigation sites; earliest go-live date; whether use has been continuous since.
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 5(2) no. 4 [verified] — "Zulassung ... der Waren". A DACH-wide routine-use claim implies the device may lawfully be placed on the market in all three. Switzerland's regime is not the CE route; whether your Swiss position supports the claim turns on Swiss law, **which this skill does not verify** — I'm flagging it as an open question, not stating a rule. [verify]
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — "Verfügbarkeit"; and if pilots are counted as routine use, "wesentliche Merkmale".
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) [verified] — "Erfolge des Herstellers", if the adoption footprint is overstated.
**Call:** Needs rewording (split the geography, or narrow to what you can evidence per country)

**Claim:** "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Attribution, not a performance claim. § 11(1) no. 11 is unavailable here — Fachkreise. § 3 no. 3(b) reaches persons working or having worked for the manufacturer, so the relationship matters.
**Evidence needed:** Written consent for name, title and institution; current affiliation; correct full institutional name; disclosure of any consultancy, advisory, equity or research-funding relationship with the manufacturer. Separately — confirm "Universitätsklinikum Süd" is the institution's actual name and not an internal placeholder or anonymisation. German university hospitals are conventionally named by city; a directional name on a page that otherwise names a real professor will read as either an error or a fabrication to a procurement reader, and procurement readers check.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 3(b), UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — if the institution name, the title, or an undisclosed commercial relationship misdescribes the source of the endorsement.
**Call:** Verify

**Claim:** "since 2024"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Today is September 2026, so this reads as roughly two years of continuous use. Accurate if first go-live was 2024 and use has been continuous.
**Evidence needed:** First routine-use date; confirmation the claim will still be maintained as the page ages.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — if the earliest deployment was late 2024, or was a pilot, or lapsed.
**Call:** Verify

## Paste-ready revised copy

Placeholders in brackets are facts I don't have — fill them, don't delete the structure.

**EN:**

> Prof. [full name], [exact title], [full institution name], on the [product] [version] registration workflow: "Compared with our previous [named baseline] workflow, it removed two steps from the registration sequence." Single-site user experience, not a controlled study. Registration accuracy must still be verified in accordance with the instructions for use.
>
> In routine clinical use at [N] hospitals in Germany and Austria since [month] 2024.

**DE:**

> Prof. [Name], [Titel], [Klinik], zum Registrierungs-Workflow von [Produkt] [Version]: „Gegenüber unserem bisherigen Workflow mit [Vergleichssystem] entfielen zwei Schritte in der Registrierungssequenz." Erfahrungsbericht eines Anwenders, keine kontrollierte Studie. Die Registriergenauigkeit ist weiterhin gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung zu prüfen.
>
> Seit [Monat] 2024 im klinischen Routineeinsatz an [N] Kliniken in Deutschland und Österreich.

Four changes, each tied to a finding above: the baseline is named (kills the § 6(2) no. 2 verifiability problem and the § 5(2) no. 1 exposure); "every" is dropped and the anecdote is labelled as one site's experience; Switzerland comes out of the headline claim until you can evidence it separately; and the IFU pointer goes in — **only if** the IFU in fact prescribes accuracy verification. If it doesn't, delete that sentence rather than keep it as decoration.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "two steps out of every registration" | Named baseline, before/after step count, scope across registration modes | Product management / clinical affairs |
| Registration-step removal vs. safety | Whether the IFU prescribes accuracy-verification steps in the registration sequence | Regulatory affairs (IFU) |
| "DACH" | Per-country deployment status; Swiss market-access position | Regulatory affairs + sales ops |
| "routine use" | Routine vs. pilot/evaluation/investigation classification per site | Sales ops |
| "since 2024" | First go-live date; continuity | Sales ops |
| Prof. Ellwanger attribution | Consent, current title/affiliation, correct institution name, relationship disclosure | Legal / medical affairs |
| Limb (d) — unassessed | Intended purpose as it appears in the DoC / technical documentation | Regulatory affairs |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 — `references/hwg.md` [verified] — **considered and disapplied**, audience is Fachkreise
- UWG § 5(2) nos. 1 and 4 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]
- Swiss market-access requirements — **not verified by this skill** [verify]

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

Two things I'd want back from you: the **intended purpose from the DoC**, so I can close limb (d), and whether the **IFU prescribes verification steps inside registration** — that single fact decides whether the "two steps" line is a clean efficiency claim or an Art. 7(c) problem.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: gated procurement page (2-sentence testimonial block)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Surgical navigation system — **Class IIb** (as stated; not verified against a certificate)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed**
**Audience:** **Fachkreise** — credentialed login, hospital procurement and clinical engineering. HWG § 11 does **not** apply. HWG § 3 does. [verified — `references/hwg.md`]
**Markets:** DE (page target); copy asserts use in **DACH**, which includes Switzerland — outside EU/DE and outside this review's scope

## Before the claim pass — the missing anchor

> I can review limbs (a), (b) and (c) without the intended purpose, but (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I cannot assess it against a purpose I have not seen. Can you paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC?

This matters more than usual here, because the entire quote is about **removing steps from registration**, and registration workflow is normally part of the procedure the conformity assessment covered. Whether "two steps out" describes the device's design or a site's own deviation from the IFU workflow is the whole question, and I can't resolve it from two sentences.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 0 substantiate (on the material supplied), 2 verify. **No breach identified on what you've given me** — but three of the four claims rest on facts I haven't seen, and one of them (Switzerland) sits outside what this skill verifies.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

## Findings

**Claim:** "It took two steps out of every registration."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** The quote is ambiguous between two readings — (i) the device's design removes two steps from the IFU registration procedure, and (ii) this site has stopped performing two steps it previously performed. Reading (ii) is a workflow deviation, and publishing it as a selling point suggests that use pattern to every other reader. On the material supplied I cannot tell which reading is true, so this is a drafting defect, not a proven breach. Note also "**every** registration" — an absolute, and absolutes are the shape limb (a) catches.
**Evidence needed:** Which registration workflow the quote refers to; whether the two steps are absent from the IFU procedure or were dropped locally; whether any of the two is an accuracy-verification or check step; the comparator baseline ("two fewer than what?").
**Also engaged:**
- MDR Art. 7(a) [verified] — if the two-step reduction holds only for one registration mode, one imaging input, or one anatomy, and not "every registration"
- MDR Art. 7(d) [verified] — if the streamlined workflow is not the procedure the conformity assessment covered; **this one cannot be cured by evidence**, only by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" [verified] — a single-centre experience presented without qualification as the expected result
- UWG § 6(2) nos. 1–2 [verified] — if the unstated baseline is a competitor's system and the market can tell which one, this is comparative advertising and the step count must be objective and **nachprüfbar** by the reader
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** see the paste-ready block below

---

**Claim:** "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Not misleading on its face, but it bundles three separate assertions — a geography, a usage mode, and a start date — each of which fails differently. "Routine use" carries a specific meaning against investigational, evaluation, or loan use. "DACH" includes Switzerland.
**Evidence needed:** Site count per country (DE / AT / CH) with go-live dates; confirmation that no counted site was operating under a clinical investigation, evaluation loan, or trial installation; the earliest routine go-live date, to support "since 2024".
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — if pilots, evaluations or demo installations are counted as "routine use", or if the 2024 date is the first install rather than first routine use
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) "Erfolge des Herstellers" [verified] — a track-record claim; overstating installed base lands here
- UWG § 5(2) no. 4 "Zulassung ... der Waren" [verified] — **if the device is not lawfully placed on the Swiss market**, then advertising routine Swiss use is a claim about authorisation status independent of whether the step count is accurate
**Call:** Needs rewording — split the countries, or drop "DACH" and name DE/AT only

> The Swiss limb turns on Swiss MedDO/Swissmedik requirements (CH-REP, conformity route), which this skill does not verify. I'm flagging it as an open question rather than stating the rule. [verify]

---

**Claim:** Attribution — "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A named-clinician testimonial to a Fachkreise audience is not prohibited. Two things need checking, though. First, "Universitätsklinikum Süd" does not read like an actual German university hospital name — German Universitätskliniken are named for their city. If this is an anonymised or placeholder name presented as a real institution, the reader is given an attribution they cannot check while being led to believe they can. Second, if Prof. Ellwanger has a financial relationship with the manufacturer (consultancy, advisory board, equity, speaker fees), presenting the quote as independent user experience is the misleading-attribution shape.
**Evidence needed:** Written consent for use of name, title and institution; the institution's own approval for use of its name; disclosure status of any financial relationship; confirmation the institution name as printed is the real one.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) [verified] — "Angaben ... über die Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung ... der für sie tätigen oder tätig gewesenen Personen", if there is an undisclosed relationship
- UWG § 5(1) and § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — an undisclosed paid endorsement to a procurement audience is capable of causing a purchasing decision that would not otherwise have been made
**Call:** Verify

Two false positives to expect from other reviewers, so you can push back:
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 2** (advertising with recommendations from professionals) does **not** apply to devices at all — § 11(1) closing sentence limits devices to nos. 7–9, 11 and 12. [verified — `references/hwg.md`]
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 11** (third-party testimonials, and only where missbräuchlich/abstoßend/irreführend) doesn't reach this page either, because § 11 applies only outside Fachkreise. It **would** apply if this block ever leaves the gate.

---

**Claim:** The asset as a whole — benefit-only, no limitation, no IFU pointer
**Breach:** none raised

> The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU.

Concretely: the one thing this copy advertises is the *removal of steps from registration*. If the IFU records registration accuracy verification as a required step or names a likely risk from inaccurate registration, then copy that celebrates fewer registration steps with no accuracy caveat is where MDR Art. 7(c) [verified] would bite. I'm not asserting that risk exists — I haven't seen the IFU. Check that specific entry, not the general question.

## The gating assumption

Your Fachkreise classification holds only as long as the gate does. Confirm:

- credentials are issued to individuals, not shared per-hospital;
- the block isn't reproduced in an ungated PDF, a trade-show panel, a press release, or a syndicated partner page.

If any of those happen, HWG § 11 switches on for that copy and nos. 7, 9 and 11 become live — including no. 11 on the testimonial. That's a distribution control, not a copy change.

## Paste-ready revised copy

The asset is under 50 words, so here is actual replacement text. Fill the brackets from the technical file; if a bracket can't be filled, cut that sentence rather than softening it.

**English:**

> Prof. [full name], [department], Universitätsklinikum [city]: "With [Product], two manual steps have been removed from our standard registration workflow. All accuracy-verification steps specified in the instructions for use remain in place."
>
> Single-centre user experience; not a controlled study. [Product] has been in routine clinical use at [n] sites in Germany and [n] in Austria since [month] 2024. Prof. [name] [is / is not] a paid advisor to [Manufacturer]. Please refer to the instructions for use for the full registration procedure, accuracy specifications and contraindications.

**German**, if the page is served in German — and if the quote was originally spoken in German, use that original wording rather than a re-translation, with the speaker's sign-off:

> Prof. [Name], [Abteilung], Universitätsklinikum [Stadt]: „Mit [Produkt] entfallen in unserem Standard-Registrierungsablauf zwei manuelle Schritte. Alle in der Gebrauchsanweisung vorgesehenen Schritte zur Genauigkeitsprüfung bleiben unverändert bestehen."
>
> Erfahrungsbericht eines einzelnen Zentrums, keine kontrollierte Studie. [Produkt] ist seit [Monat] 2024 an [n] Standorten in Deutschland und [n] in Österreich im klinischen Routineeinsatz. Prof. [Name] [ist / ist nicht] als Berater für [Hersteller] tätig. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung mit dem vollständigen Registrierungsablauf, den Genauigkeitsangaben und den Gegenanzeigen.

What the rewrite does: replaces "every registration" with a named workflow at a named site, makes explicit that no verification step was dropped (which defuses the (c) and (d) exposure at once), states the single-centre basis so the reader doesn't take it as a general expected result, splits DACH so Switzerland isn't claimed unless you want to claim it, and puts the relationship disclosure on the page.

If Switzerland genuinely is in routine use and lawfully supplied, add it back as a third named country — but say "Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz", not "DACH". Naming the countries is verifiable; a regional acronym isn't.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "two steps out of every registration" | The IFU registration procedure vs. the site's actual workflow; whether either removed step is a verification/check step; the comparator baseline | Regulatory / Clinical Affairs |
| "every registration" (the absolute) | Whether the reduction holds for all registration modes, imaging inputs and anatomies covered by the intended purpose | Product Management |
| Intended purpose as assessed | Verbatim text from the technical documentation / DoC, plus certificate scope and notified body | Regulatory Affairs |
| Likely risk for Art. 7(c) | The IFU entries on registration accuracy, verification requirements, limitations, contraindications | Regulatory Affairs |
| "routine use ... since 2024" | Per-country site list with go-live dates; exclusion of pilots, evaluations, loans and investigational use | Sales Ops / Commercial |
| Switzerland | Swiss market status — CH-REP, conformity route, lawful supply | Regulatory Affairs (outside this review) |
| "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd" | Written consent from the individual and the institution; correct institution name; financial-relationship disclosure | Legal / Medical Affairs |
| Gate integrity | Credentialing model; confirmation the block is not syndicated ungated | Digital / Marketing Ops |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d)** — Regulation (EU) 2017/745 [verified — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md`]
- **HWG § 1(1) no. 1a** — devices in scope [verified — `references/hwg.md`]
- **HWG § 3 no. 3(b)** — claims about persons, credentials, track record [verified — `references/hwg.md`]
- **HWG § 11(1)** closing sentence — devices limited to nos. 7–9, 11, 12; § 11 inapplicable to Fachkreise [verified — `references/hwg.md`]

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Surgical navigation system — Class IIb
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (credentialed gate: procurement + clinical engineering) — HWG § 11 out of scope

- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "Tests"** `[verified]` — if "since 2024" spans a hardware/software configuration whose conformity assessment has since changed, the continuity implied by "since" overstates what the current certified device has in the field.

**Evidence needed:** Per-country list of sites in routine clinical use with go-live dates; CH market-access status; confirmation the 2024 date refers to routine clinical use of the currently certified configuration, not first install or first pilot.

## Verdict

Two sentences, roughly six compliance problems. Nothing here is unfixable, but I would not publish it as written — the gating buys you less than it looks like it does, and the biggest exposure isn't regulatory at all, it's the named physician.

---

## What gating does and doesn't buy you

Credentialed access to hospital procurement and clinical engineering staff plausibly makes this **Fachkreiswerbung** under § 2 HWG (staff of institutions serving human health, and persons who apply the device). That switches off the § 11 Abs. 1 restrictions — notably Nr. 2 (fachliche Empfehlungen/Zeugnisse) and Nr. 11 (Äußerungen Dritter). A testimonial is therefore *permissible in principle*. That is the whole of what gating gets you.

Still fully in force regardless of audience:

- **§ 3 HWG** (irreführende Werbung) — no audience exemption
- **§ 6 HWG** — if the quote is used as a fachliche Empfehlung, you must state the author's name, profession and place, and the date it was given
- **MDR Art. 7** — claims may not mislead as to performance or ascribe functions the device doesn't have; claims must match the intended purpose and be backed by the clinical evaluation
- **§§ 5, 5a UWG**

Two practical gating conditions: the credential check must actually verify professional status (self-declared checkbox has been held insufficient), and the page must be excluded from indexing — a crawlable meta description or cached snippet re-opens it as Publikumswerbung.

---

## Blocking issues

**1. "Universitätsklinikum Süd" does not exist.** There is no German university hospital by that name. Either it's a placeholder that survived into review copy, or it's a deliberate pseudonymisation. If the latter, you have a fabricated institution attached to a real named professor — that is misleading under § 3 HWG on its own, and it defeats § 6 HWG, which requires a verifiable attribution. Procurement readers in this market can check affiliations in about thirty seconds; a mismatch reads as a fabricated reference and does more commercial damage than the quote is worth. Name the real institution with its written consent, or drop the institution and the name together.

**2. Physician professional conduct — this is the sharpest risk.** § 27 Abs. 3 MBO-Ä prohibits a physician from lending their name, in connection with their professional title, to commercial promotion. A named chair endorsing a vendor product on a vendor page is squarely the fact pattern the Landesärztekammern act on. You need, in writing: the professor's consent, their institution's consent (most Universitätskliniken have a standing Werbeverbot on institutional name and logo), and the exact approved wording. Separately, if there is any compensation, consulting agreement, research funding or equipment loan in the relationship, disclose it — both for MedTech Europe Code purposes and because §§ 299a/299b StGB make undisclosed benefit-linked endorsement a criminal-adjacent question, not a marketing one.

**3. "It took two steps out of every registration" is an unsupported quantified performance claim.** "Every" is absolute, and "two steps" is numeric — together that reads as validated workflow performance, not one surgeon's impression. Under MDR Art. 7 it must be traceable to your clinical evaluation or PMCF data and consistent with the intended purpose in the IFU. It also carries an implicit comparison with no stated baseline: two steps fewer than what — your prior version, manual registration, a named competitor? If a competitor is identifiable, § 6 UWG comparative-advertising conditions attach. Either substantiate it as a general claim with data, or frame it unmistakably as a single-centre user observation.

**4. "Across the DACH region" includes Switzerland.** Since the EU–CH MRA lapsed for medical devices, Swiss placing on the market requires MedDO conformity, a Swiss authorised representative (CH-REP) and Swiss labelling. If you do not have that in place, this sentence claims lawful market presence you don't have. If you do, keep it; if Swiss use is limited or investigational, say "Deutschland und Österreich."

**5. "In routine use since 2024" needs a defined denominator.** "Routine use" implies established, non-investigational deployment at scale. Hold evidence: number of sites, first clinical use date per country, and confirmation that use was under the CE-marked intended purpose, not under a trial protocol or a custom-device/compassionate arrangement.

**6. No device identification anywhere.** The copy names no product, no manufacturer, no intended purpose, no CE status. For a Class IIb device addressed to procurement and clinical engineering — the two audiences whose actual job is to verify exactly that — its absence is both a compliance gap and a credibility gap. Clinical engineering will want the notified body number and whether the certificate is MDR or a legacy Art. 120 extension.

**7. Language.** German market, German-language page. A quote originally given in German must appear in German verbatim; if the English above is a translation, the translated version needs the professor's sign-off too.

---

## Revised copy

German, assuming you secure the consents and the substantiation:

> **[Produktname], chirurgisches Navigationssystem, Klasse IIb (CE [NB-Nummer]) — [Hersteller]**
>
> Prof. Dr. med. [Vorname] Ellwanger, [Klinik für …, Universitätsklinikum …], [Monat/Jahr]:
> „In unserem Registrierungsablauf entfielen zwei Arbeitsschritte."
>
> Einzelanwenderbericht aus einem Zentrum; die Erfahrung ist nicht ohne Weiteres auf andere Einrichtungen übertragbar. Prof. Ellwanger [erhielt keine Vergütung für diese Äußerung / steht in einem Beratungsverhältnis zu [Hersteller]].
>
> [Produktname] wird seit [Monat/Jahr] in Deutschland und Österreich klinisch eingesetzt ([n] Kliniken, Stand [Datum]). Zweckbestimmung und Anwendungshinweise siehe Gebrauchsanweisung.
>
> Nur für Fachkreise im Sinne des § 2 HWG.

The changes: the claim is now attributed and bounded rather than universal, § 6 HWG attribution elements are present, the DACH overreach is gone, "routine use" is replaced by a countable fact, and the device is identified.

---

## Evidence to have on file before launch

Signed quote attestation with original German wording and date · written consent from the professor · written consent from the institution for name use · disclosure of any financial relationship · the CER/PMCF section supporting the workflow claim, or an internal note that it is presented as anecdote only · site list and first-use dates per country · Swiss regulatory status if DACH wording is retained · screenshot of the credential-verification flow and the robots/noindex configuration.

One judgment call I made: I assumed procurement and clinical engineering staff qualify as Fachkreise. That's the better reading of § 2 HWG, but it isn't settled for non-clinical procurement staff specifically — if your legal team wants belt-and-braces, the revised version above stays defensible even if a court treated the page as Publikumswerbung, except for the testimonial itself, which would then fall under § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The gating helps a lot — it takes you out of HWG § 11's testimonial ban — but it doesn't solve the two real problems here: an unsubstantiated quantified performance claim, and a named-clinician endorsement with undocumented consent and relationship disclosure. Neither of those is cured by a login wall. There's also a factual exposure in "DACH."

## What the gate does and doesn't buy you

Hospital procurement and clinical engineering staff plausibly qualify as **Fachkreise** under HWG § 2 — a hospital is an *Einrichtung, die der Gesundheit von Menschen dient*, and clinical engineers apply medical devices in their professional activity. That exempts you from **§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2** (references to expert recommendations) and **Nr. 11** (third-party testimonials), which are Laienwerbung-only prohibitions.

But the Fachkreise defense is only as good as the gate:

- Credentials must be **verified**, not self-attested. A checkbox saying "I am a healthcare professional" has been treated as insufficient.
- `noindex` / robots exclusion, no public preview snippet, no shareable ungated URL.
- **Don't reuse this asset publicly** — the moment it appears in trade press, on LinkedIn, or on a booth screen, § 11 applies and the testimonial is prohibited.
- Document the access-control design now. That's the artifact you produce if the Wettbewerbszentrale or a competitor sends an Abmahnung.

What survives the gate regardless: **HWG § 3** (irreführende Werbung), **MDR Art. 7** (misleading claims — explicitly not audience-dependent), and **UWG §§ 5, 5a**. Those are where this copy is exposed.

## Blocking items

**1. "It took two steps out of every registration" — no baseline, no evidence cited.**

Two steps out of *what*? Your previous product generation, a named competitor, or non-navigated manual workflow? An undefined baseline is the classic UWG § 5 misleading-comparison finding, and if the implied comparator is a competitor you're additionally in **UWG § 6** territory with its stricter requirements. "Every registration" is a universal quantifier attached to one clinician's impression — that's the specific move that converts an anecdote into a product claim.

You need this in the claims substantiation file before it ships: a time-motion analysis or equivalent, with n, sites, and the baseline workflow defined.

**2. Which two steps?** This is the one I'd escalate to clinical affairs, not just regulatory. Registration verification steps in a surgical navigation system exist to catch registration error before it propagates into the procedure. If the removed steps are accuracy-verification steps, or if the "two fewer steps" workflow isn't the workflow described in your CE-marked IFU, then you're advertising off-label use of a Class IIb device — and the underlying issue is a safety one, not a copy one. If the steps are genuinely redundant UI interactions, say so specifically; the specificity is also better copy for this audience.

**3. Named clinician — three separate things to close.**

- **Written consent** from Prof. Ellwanger, and *separately* from Universitätsklinikum Süd. German university hospitals typically require distinct institutional sign-off for name use in commercial material; the individual's consent doesn't carry the institution's.
- **MBO-Ä § 27** — participating in product advertising can expose the physician to Kammer proceedings for berufswidrige Werbung. That's their risk, not yours, but you should raise it with them in writing rather than let them discover it.
- **Relationship disclosure.** Was there any consideration — consulting fee, device discount, sponsored travel, research funding, honorarium? If yes, disclose it in the copy and check it against **StGB §§ 299a/299b** and the **Kodex Medizinprodukte**. An undisclosed compensated endorsement to a purchasing audience is the fact pattern these provisions were written for. If there was no consideration, state that too.

**4. "Universitätsklinikum Süd" reads like a placeholder.** I can't match it to a real German university hospital. If it's a pseudonym for a real site, naming a real professor at a de-identified institution is the worst of both options — it looks like verification is available when it isn't. Either name both with consent, or de-identify both ("a university hospital in southern Germany"). Confirm which this is.

**5. "Across the DACH region" — Switzerland is your problem.** Switzerland is outside MDR; it runs on MedDO with Swissmedic, and requires a **CH-REP** and Swiss-conforming labeling. If you don't have a CH-REP and Swiss market placement, "across DACH" is simply false and simultaneously advertises a market-access gap to an audience that will notice. Say "Germany and Austria" unless Swiss placement is documented.

**6. "In routine use since 2024" — two checks.** *Routine* excludes use under clinical investigation, trial protocol, or compassionate/custom arrangements; if any of the 2024 installations were investigational, drop them from the count. And confirm the date maps to the **currently marketed configuration** — if 2024 use was the prior hardware or software generation, or under an MDD legacy certificate via Art. 120, the copy shouldn't let a reader attribute that installed history to what you're selling today. "Across the region" also needs a real site count behind it; two centers isn't a region.

## Missing mandatory-ish elements

The snippet names neither the device nor the manufacturer. The page also needs: intended purpose, a pointer to the IFU, and — since you're in Germany — **German-language copy**. English is widely tolerated for Fachkreise in practice, but the quote is presumably a translation of German speech, so keep the original German wording on file and have the translation signed off. Note that anything you'd call "Pflichtangaben" tracks the German version.

## Suggested rewrite

If the substantiation exists, keep the testimonial:

> **[Product name]** — Prof. [Full name], [Institution], on registration workflow:
> "In our hands, registration required two fewer steps than our previous workflow."
>
> Individual experience at a single centre; results may vary. Prof. [Name] [received no compensation for this statement / is a paid consultant to [Company]]. [Product name] has been in clinical use in Germany and Austria since [month] 2024 at [n] centres. Refer to the instructions for use for intended purpose, indications, contraindications and warnings.

If it doesn't, drop the testimonial and lead with the data — stronger for procurement anyway:

> In a time-motion analysis across [n] centres, **[Product name]** reduced patient registration from [x] to [y] operator steps (mean registration time [a] vs. [b] min; [k] procedures). Comparator: [named baseline workflow]. In clinical use in Germany and Austria since [month] 2024.

## What I need from you

1. Source and baseline for "two steps" — study, or one surgeon's impression?
2. Which two steps, and are they in the CE-marked IFU workflow?
3. Any consideration paid to Prof. Ellwanger, and is written consent on file from both them and the institution?
4. Is "Universitätsklinikum Süd" real or a placeholder?
5. Swiss market placement and CH-REP — yes or no?
6. Site count for 2024, and whether all of it was non-investigational use of the current configuration?

I'm not a lawyer and this isn't a legal sign-off — items 3 and 5 in particular should go to German regulatory counsel before publication.

## Verdict

The copy is not safe to publish as written. The gating helps — it likely puts you inside **Fachkreise** under §2 HWG, which switches off the testimonial bans in §11 HWG — but the two provisions that actually bite here (§3 HWG, MDR Art. 7) apply regardless of audience. Both claims in these two sentences are unsubstantiated as phrased.

## Findings

**1. "Two steps out of every registration" — absolute performance claim (high)**

MDR Art. 7 prohibits ascribing functions or performance the device does not have; §3 HWG and §5 UWG prohibit misleading claims to professionals as well as the public. Problems, in order:

- **"every"** is a universal quantifier resting on one clinician at one site. A single-centre anecdote cannot support a claim about all registrations.
- **No baseline.** Two steps out of *what* — your previous software version, a manual workflow, a competitor's system? The comparator has to be stated. If an unnamed competitor is identifiable from context, §6 UWG (vergleichende Werbung) also engages and the comparison must be objective and verifiable.
- **Not traceable to the clinical evaluation.** For a Class IIb device, a performance claim needs to be consistent with your technical documentation and IFU. If "fewer steps" isn't in the clinical evaluation or a documented workflow/time-motion study, it can't be advertised.
- **Safety adjacency.** In surgical navigation, registration is accuracy-critical. "Fewer steps" invites the inference that you can skip verification. MDR Art. 7(d) also prohibits failing to inform of likely risk. Pair the claim with a line that accuracy verification remains the user's responsibility per the IFU.

**2. "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024" (high)**

- **Switzerland is the real exposure.** Since the EU–CH MRA lapsed in May 2021, Swiss market access runs on MepV: you need a CH-REP, Swiss-compliant labelling, and registration. Advertising routine Swiss use asserts you are lawfully on that market. Verify before the word "DACH" stays in. If Swiss status isn't clean, name Germany and Austria only.
- **"Across the region" is a scale claim** with no number behind it. Three sites is not "across DACH." Give site count and month, or drop the geographic framing.
- **"Routine use"** implies use within the intended purpose. Any off-label use at reference sites cannot be counted toward it.

**3. Consents — two separate ones, both needed in writing (high)**

- The named individual: GDPR Art. 6(1)(a) plus personality rights (§22 KUG by analogy), covering this specific wording, this medium, and a defined term.
- **The institution.** German university hospitals are public bodies and most have press/legal policies restricting or prohibiting use of the Klinikum name in commercial advertising. Institutional permission is a distinct approval from the professor's, and is the one most often skipped.

**4. Undisclosed relationship (medium-high)**

If Prof. Ellwanger is a consultant, speaker, evaluation-site PI, or received any benefit, non-disclosure is misleading by omission under §5a UWG. It also sits near §§299a/b StGB and the MedTech Europe Code. Disclose the relationship inline; if there is genuinely none, say "unvergütet."

**5. §6 HWG citation particulars (medium)**

Where advertising to professionals uses Gutachten, Zeugnisse or references to them, the author, date and faithful reproduction are required. A named clinician endorsement is arguably a *Zeugnis*. Add the person's full title/function, the institution, and when the statement was given — cheap to do, and it removes the argument.

**6. Physician-side professional law (medium, often missed)**

MBO-Ä §27(3) restricts physicians lending their name and professional title to commercial advertising. The Landesärztekammer risk lands on the professor, but the fallout — a withdrawn quote, a public retraction — lands on you. Confirm they have cleared it, including any Nebentätigkeit approval as a public-sector employee.

**7. Language and translation (medium)**

For a German market you should publish in German. As it stands you are running a translated quote from a German speaker in English, which is exactly where "faithful reproduction" arguments start. Hold the German original on file and mark any English version as a translation.

**8. Gating hygiene (low, but cheap)**

The §11 HWG shield depends on the gate actually working. Set `noindex`, ensure no public teaser text or unauthenticated preview, and confirm credential checks are genuine and not a self-declared checkbox — a self-declaration gate is weak evidence that you reached only Fachkreise.

## Suggested rewrite

Placeholders are facts I don't have; each one has to be filled from documentation, not from memory.

> **[Produktname]** — [Zweckbestimmung in einem Satz].
>
> Anwendererfahrung, Universitätsklinikum [Ort], Klinik für [Fach], erhoben [Monat/Jahr]:
> „Bei uns entfallen zwei Arbeitsschritte je Registrierung." — Prof. Dr. [Vorname Nachname], [Funktion]
>
> Einzelbericht eines Anwenders gegenüber [Referenzworkflow]; nicht ohne Weiteres auf andere Einrichtungen übertragbar. Grundlage: [Studien-/Workflow-Vergleich, Methode, n, Zeitraum] — Datenblatt auf Anfrage. Prof. [Name] ist [Berater für / in keiner vergüteten Beziehung zu] [Hersteller]. Wiedergabe mit Genehmigung des Universitätsklinikums [Ort].
>
> Seit [Monat] 2024 im klinischen Routineeinsatz an [n] Kliniken in Deutschland und Österreich.
>
> Die Prüfung der Registrierungsgenauigkeit verbleibt in der Verantwortung des Anwenders; siehe Gebrauchsanweisung [Ref./Rev.].

Two notes on the rewrite: keep the CE mark and notified body number on the labelling, not in the body copy as a quality argument — that reads as using the NB as an endorsement. And restore Switzerland to the geography line only once CH-REP and MepV registration are confirmed.

The single highest-value action is deciding what evidence backs "two steps." If it's a documented workflow comparison, the claim survives with a stated comparator and scope. If it's one professor's impression, it can only run as an explicitly labelled individual anecdote — never as a product performance claim.

This is a structured review against the applicable provisions, not a legal opinion; a Class IIb launch claim set should go past your regulatory affairs function and German counsel before it goes live.
