graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: consumer web page copy (headline + subline)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Class IIa home blood-pressure monitor
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum — ungated public consumer page, settled, not assumed
**Markets:** DE (EU-wide MDR Art. 7 also applies)

I can review limbs (a), (b) and (c) without the intended purpose, but (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I can't assess it against a purpose I haven't seen. Can you paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC? It matters specifically for "daily", below.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 reword (mandatory), 2 verify, 0 OK as-is.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

The endorsement is not the problem here — the fear framing is. One note before the findings, because it's the most common false positive on copy like this: **HWG § 11(1) no. 2 (professional endorsements) does not apply to medical devices.** The closing sentence of § 11(1) limits devices to nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 [verified]. A cardiologist recommendation on a device page is not prohibited per se, and any review telling you to cut it on no. 2 grounds is citing a provision that doesn't reach your product.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart — check your pressure daily."
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 [verified]; MDR Art. 7(b) [verified]
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 7 prohibits Publikumswerbung "die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** [...] beeinträchtigt [...] werden könnte" — copy suggesting health is impaired by *not* using the device. "Don't gamble with your heart" is that shape directly: it frames non-use as a wager against your cardiac health. Separately, Art. 7(b) — the device measures blood pressure; the copy leaves the impression that the act of measuring protects the heart, which is an implied clinical benefit a monitoring-only device does not deliver.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. This is a framing breach, not a substantiation gap. Even a study showing self-monitoring improves outcomes would not rescue the "don't gamble" construction under no. 7.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) [verified] — if surrounding page copy reinforces that daily checking reliably prevents cardiac events, the "Erfolg mit Sicherheit" limb comes into play
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix (paste-ready):**

> "Recommended by Prof. Dr. Schmidt, cardiologist. Track your blood pressure at home and share the readings with your doctor."

German, if the page runs auf Deutsch (translation for convenience — have a native reviewer confirm the wording before publishing):

> „Empfohlen von Prof. Dr. Schmidt, Kardiologe. Messen Sie Ihren Blutdruck zu Hause und besprechen Sie die Werte mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt."

This keeps the intent — habitual home measurement — but drops the non-use threat and routes the clinical meaning to the physician, where it belongs.

---

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Third-party statements about devices fall under § 11(1) no. 11, which prohibits them only "wenn diese in **missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender** Weise erfolgen" [verified]. A plain, accurate recommendation is none of those. On the material supplied, nothing here breaches.
**Evidence needed:** Written confirmation the recommendation was actually given for this device; that Schmidt holds the Professor title and cardiology qualification as stated; and disclosure status if there's a commercial relationship
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 11 [verified] — if the recommendation was not given, or is stated more broadly than what Schmidt actually said (irreführend). HWG § 3 no. 3(b) [verified] — "Angaben über die Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung [...] der für sie tätigen [...] Personen", if Schmidt is engaged by you and the title or specialty is overstated. UWG § 5(2) no. 3 [verified] — Befähigung/Status of persons connected to the trader, same condition.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** Keep it, but tighten the attribution so it can't drift: full title as it appears in his Approbation/chair ("Prof. Dr. med. [Name], Kardiologe, [institution]"), and hold the signed recommendation on file. A bare surname plus "cardiologist" is thin if an Abmahnung arrives asking who he is.

---

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** cannot assess — depends on the intended purpose and IFU
**Why:** A stated measurement frequency is a use instruction. If the assessed intended purpose and IFU support routine daily self-measurement by lay users, this is fine. If they frame the device for measurement on medical advice, or at a different cadence, the copy suggests a use pattern outside what the conformity assessment covered.
**Evidence needed:** Intended purpose as assessed, plus the IFU section on measurement frequency
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) [verified] and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit") — if the IFU does not support unprompted daily lay self-measurement
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** If the IFU is silent or narrower, drop the cadence: "Track your blood pressure at home" — my suggested rewrite above already avoids asserting a frequency, so adopting it resolves this item as a side effect.

## Open question on limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — for home BP monitors the usual candidates are that readings need clinical interpretation and that patients should not adjust medication on the basis of them, but I'm not going to raise (c) on a risk I inferred from the device category rather than read in your documentation. Worth checking against the IFU. If it does record something in that register, the proportionate fix on a short consumer headline is an IFU pointer near the copy, not patient-facing safety text in the headline itself.

Note that my rewrite ("share the readings with your doctor") partly covers this ground already, which is a reason to prefer it.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Recommended by Professor Schmidt" | Signed/written recommendation for this specific device; date | Marketing / KOL relationship owner |
| "Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" | Title and specialty verification; commercial-relationship disclosure status | Medical affairs |
| "daily" | Intended purpose as assessed + IFU measurement-frequency section | Regulatory affairs |
| (c) omission | IFU review for a likely risk requiring surfacing | Regulatory affairs |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(b), Art. 7(d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 11(1) no. 7, no. 11 — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a), no. 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, no. 3 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]
- HWG § 11(1) no. 2 — cited only to record that it does **not** apply to devices [verified]

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor — Class IIa (MDR)

It matters specifically for "check your pressure daily": a measurement-frequency instruction is a use pattern, and whether daily unsupervised self-measurement sits inside the assessed purpose is not something I can infer.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`
**Why:** No. 7 prohibits Werbeaussagen "die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** [...] beeinträchtigt [...] werden könnte". "Gamble with your heart" says exactly that not using the device puts your cardiac health at risk — it is the canonical fear-of-not-using shape, and the audience here is Publikum, so no. 7 is live.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. This is a framing prohibition, not a substantiation one.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]` and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") `[verified]` — the pairing of cardiac-risk framing with a monitoring device implies that measuring protects the heart. A monitor measures; it does not treat or prevent. Whether that crosses into a false impression regarding treatment depends on the assessed intended purpose.
**Call:** Cut
**Suggested fix:** delete. No conditional rewrite of this phrase survives no. 7 — any version that motivates purchase by the consequence of *not* measuring reproduces the breach.

---

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7, second limb `[verified]` — read with the preceding sentence, this asserts health "durch die **Verwendung verbessert**". Standing alone it would be a neutral instruction; in this sentence it is the payoff of the fear premise.
**Why:** The em-dash construction makes the two clauses one proposition: gamble = don't measure, safety = measure daily.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the no. 7 point. For the frequency itself: the intended purpose and IFU-recommended measurement regimen.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]` — **unassessed pending the intended purpose.** A prescribed daily self-measurement regimen is a use pattern; if the conformity assessment covers episodic or physician-directed measurement, a blanket daily instruction to consumers is intended-purpose drift. Note the cure path: if (d) bites, it is cured by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment, **not** by producing data.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** see the paste-ready copy below — route frequency to the treating physician.

---

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Worth stating plainly, because this is where device reviews most often go wrong: **HWG § 11(1) no. 2 (professional endorsements) does not apply to medical devices.** § 11(1) closes with "Für Medizinprodukte gilt Satz 1 Nr. 7 bis 9, 11 und 12 entsprechend" `[verified]`. The only endorsement hook for a device is **no. 11**, and that catches Äußerungen Dritter only "wenn diese in **missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender** Weise erfolgen". A genuine, accurate, disclosed clinician recommendation is not prohibited.
**Evidence needed:** (1) written, current consent from the named person; (2) proof of the professorship and the cardiology qualification as stated; (3) the nature of any commercial relationship — fee, equity, advisory role, research funding.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]` — if the endorsement is not genuine, is stale, is a composite/stock persona, or if a paid relationship is undisclosed, it becomes *irreführend* and the safe harbour closes.
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — "unwahre oder zur Täuschung geeignete Angaben über die Person, Vorbildung, **Befähigung** [...] der für sie tätigen [...] Personen". If "Professor" or "cardiologist" overstates the actual title or specialty, this bites independently of no. 11.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 3 `[verified]` — "Person, Eigenschaften oder Rechte des Unternehmers [...] Befähigung", if Prof. Schmidt is affiliated with or engaged by the manufacturer.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** keep, with full identification and disclosure — see below.

---

## Two cross-cutting notes

**MDR Art. 7(c) — open question, not a finding.** The copy surfaces no limitation at all. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — for a Class IIa home BP monitor the usual candidates are cuff-size dependency, irregular-heartbeat interference, and single readings not being diagnostic, but I am not flagging (c) on a risk I inferred from the device category rather than read in your material. Worth checking the copy against the IFU's warnings section. If a likely risk is recorded there, an IFU pointer is normally the proportionate fix at this length.

**The German wording is what gets assessed.** You supplied English copy for a German-market page. HWG and UWG apply to the published German text; a translation can tighten or loosen a no. 7 problem. Have the final German reviewed, not the English source.

## Paste-ready replacement

German (the version that counts):

> Blutdruckmessgerät für zu Hause. Misst systolischen und diastolischen Blutdruck sowie den Puls.
> Wie häufig Sie messen sollten, besprechen Sie bitte mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt.
> Empfohlen von Prof. Dr. [Vorname Nachname], Fachärztin/Facharzt für Kardiologie, [Klinik/Institution]. [Bezahlte Empfehlung / Mitglied des wissenschaftlichen Beirats — zutreffendes einsetzen und nicht weglassen.]

English reference:

> A home blood-pressure monitor. Measures systolic and diastolic pressure and pulse.
> How often to measure is a question for your doctor.
> Recommended by Prof. [Full Name], Consultant Cardiologist, [Institution]. [Paid endorsement / member of our scientific advisory board — insert whichever applies; do not omit.]

What the rewrite does: removes the not-using-it-harms-you premise (§ 11 no. 7), removes the implied cardiac-protection outcome (Art. 7(b) / UWG § 5(2) no. 1), hands measurement frequency to the treating clinician (closes the (d) exposure regardless of what the intended purpose turns out to say), and puts the endorsement inside the no. 11 safe harbour by making it identifiable and disclosed.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| Daily measurement | Intended purpose as assessed, verbatim from the DoC/technical documentation | RA/QA |
| Daily measurement | IFU-recommended measurement regimen | RA/QA |
| (c) omission check | IFU warnings/limitations section | RA/QA |
| Prof. Schmidt | Signed, current endorsement consent; scope and expiry | Marketing/Legal |
| Prof. Schmidt | Verification of professorship and cardiology specialty as worded | Marketing |
| Prof. Schmidt | Full disclosure of any fee, equity, advisory or research relationship | Legal/Finance |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7 and 11, and the device-scoping sentence "Für Medizinprodukte gilt Satz 1 Nr. 7 bis 9, 11 und 12 entsprechend" — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) nos. 1 and 3 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

One practical point on priority: the § 11 no. 7 breach is the expensive one. HWG is enforced privately through UWG, so this arrives as an Abmahnung from a competitor or a Wettbewerbsverband with a strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung and costs attached — no regulator has to act first, and fear-framing in consumer health copy is exactly the shape Wettbewerbsverbände watch for.

## Open question — limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation at all. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs in this copy — for home BP monitors the candidates are usually measurement-condition dependence and the need for clinical interpretation rather than self-diagnosis, but I am not going to raise (c) on a risk I inferred from the device category. Worth checking against the IFU. If the IFU does record one, the proportionate fix on a short asset is an IFU pointer, not patient-facing safety text.

## Paste-ready revised copy

German (primary, market is DE):

> **Blutdruckmessgerät für die Selbstmessung zu Hause.**
> Messen Sie so häufig, wie es Ihre Ärztin oder Ihr Arzt empfiehlt, und besprechen Sie Ihre Werte in der Praxis. Selbstmessungen ersetzen keine ärztliche Diagnose. Bitte Gebrauchsanweisung beachten.

English equivalent, if an EN version runs:

> **A blood-pressure monitor for measuring at home.**
> Measure as often as your doctor advises, and discuss your readings with them. Self-measurement does not replace a medical diagnosis. Please read the instructions for use.

With the endorsement retained, once substantiated, and only if it stays inside what he actually said:

> Empfohlen von Prof. Dr. [Vorname] Schmidt, Facharzt für Kardiologie, [Klinik/Institution]. [Disclose any paid or advisory relationship here.]

This keeps both original intents — expert credibility and regular measurement — while removing the not-using-it-harms-you framing that no. 7 prohibits and routing frequency to a clinician instead of asserting it.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "check your pressure daily" | Intended purpose as assessed; IFU frequency + interpretation sections | RA / technical documentation |
| Limb (c) omission | Whether the IFU records a likely risk for in-purpose use | RA / IFU |
| "Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" | Written consent, dated; proof of professorship and Facharzt qualification; scope of endorsement; disclosure of any payment | Marketing + the named individual |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(b), 7(d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11, and the device-scoping sentence "Für Medizinprodukte gilt Satz 1 Nr. 7 bis 9, 11 und 12 entsprechend" — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1 and 3 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

§ 6 not engaged — no comparison. § 3a not cited — it is limited to Arzneimittel.

## Enforcement note

Per `references/uwg.md`, the realistic failure mode here is a competitor or Wettbewerbsverband Abmahnung with a strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung and costs, not a regulator's letter. The headline is the exposed item, because no. 7 is decided on the wording alone and needs no factual dispute.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

Bottom line: one hard finding — the headline breaches HWG § 11(1) no. 7 and can't be fixed with evidence, only cut. The cardiologist endorsement is **not** the problem people usually assume it is; § 11(1) no. 2 doesn't reach devices, so it survives as a substantiation task. Send me the intended purpose and I'll close out limb (d) on "check your pressure daily".

graders.evidence:
No memory access in this session, so this is a fresh read. Verdict up front: **do not publish.** Both sentences have problems, and the first one is a hard blocker under German law.

## Blockers

**1. "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" — professional endorsement in lay advertising**

This is the serious one. German advertising law (HWG) bans, in advertising directed outside professional circles, statements that a product is professionally recommended, tested, or used — and HWG applies to medical devices, not just medicines (§ 1 pulls in MDR Art. 2(1) devices). Because your page is public and ungated, you're squarely in *Laienwerbung* and the § 11 prohibitions apply in full. I'd flag one caveat: the 2012 HWG reform narrowed several of the § 11 Abs. 1 items, and I'm not fully certain how the HCP-recommendation prohibition currently reads as applied to devices versus medicines. Have counsel confirm the exact subsection — but treat the substance as settled. Physician-endorsement copy for consumer device pages is standard enforcement territory for German competitors and *Wettbewerbszentrale*, which brings UWG injunction risk and cost-bearing *Abmahnungen*.

Three further problems layered on top:

- **The doctor is also exposed.** The German model professional code for physicians (MBO-Ä § 27) prohibits doctors from lending their name or professional authority to commercial product advertising. Even if you were comfortable with your own risk, Professor Schmidt is taking on a *Berufsrecht* problem, and the realistic outcome is that the endorsement gets withdrawn after you've built a campaign around it.
- **Undisclosed commercial relationship.** If any payment, honorarium, equipment, or research funding flowed, omitting that is a separate failure to disclose commercial intent under UWG § 5a.
- **It's unverifiable as written.** No institution, no first name, no scope. "Professor Schmidt" is a generic enough German name that it reads as placeholder or invented copy. If it *is* invented, this stops being a technical HWG issue and becomes straightforward deception under UWG § 5. Please confirm with the copy owner whether this is a real, consenting, documented person.

**Recommendation: delete the sentence.** Don't try to rescue it with a disclaimer or by swapping in an unnamed "cardiologists recommend." Anonymising doesn't help — the prohibition targets the appeal to professional authority, not the identifiability of the individual.

**2. "Don't gamble with your heart" — fear-based appeal plus a benefit you don't have**

Two independent defects in eight words.

HWG prohibits advertising apt to create or exploit feelings of fear (*Angstwerbung*), and this phrasing is built to do exactly that: it frames non-purchase as recklessness with your own cardiac health. That framing is what the rule exists to catch.

Separately, it fails MDR Art. 7. Your device's intended purpose is *measuring* blood pressure. "Don't gamble with your heart" implies that using it protects you from cardiac events — a preventive or protective function the device does not have, and one that sits outside the intended purpose your notified body assessed. That engages Art. 7(b) (suggesting uses beyond the intended purpose) and Art. 7(c) (false impression as to functions or properties). A monitor produces numbers; clinical benefit comes from what a clinician and patient do with those numbers.

**Recommendation: delete.** This one can't be softened into compliance, because the implied protective benefit is the whole point of the line.

## Also needs fixing

**3. "check your pressure daily" is clinical advice, and it's not the recommended protocol.** ESH guidance for home monitoring is a structured schedule — typically seven consecutive days, duplicate morning and evening readings, ahead of a treatment decision or appointment — not indefinite daily measurement by everyone. Advertising a measurement frequency does three unhelpful things: it puts dosing-style clinical instruction in promotional copy where it doesn't belong, it will very likely contradict your own IFU (promotional material must stay consistent with the IFU; MDR Annex I Ch. III 23.4), and unstructured daily self-measurement is associated with measurement anxiety and over-monitoring in exactly the worried-well audience this copy targets. Replace with a deferral to the user's clinician.

**4. Nothing here is substantiated, and required framing is absent.** For a Class IIa device, promotional claims form part of your technical documentation and need support from the clinical evaluation. As drafted there is no clinical validation claim, no intended-purpose statement, no pointer to the instructions for use, and no "does not diagnose or treat" boundary. German device advertising conventionally carries a *"Medizinprodukt. Gebrauchsanweisung beachten."* line; whether any HWG mandatory-particulars obligation binds you specifically is worth a direct check with counsel, since those provisions are written primarily around medicinal products.

**5. The copy is in English for a German market.** Beyond the obvious, this matters procedurally: HWG assessment turns on the actual German wording, so whatever you translate to needs its own review pass. Don't treat sign-off on English as sign-off on the German.

## Suggested replacement

> Know your numbers. [Brand] is a clinically validated upper-arm blood pressure monitor for use at home. Measure as often as your doctor recommends, and share your readings at your next appointment. [Brand] measures blood pressure; it does not diagnose or treat high blood pressure. Medical device — read the instructions for use.

German, for the same content:

> Kennen Sie Ihre Werte. [Marke] ist ein klinisch validiertes Oberarm-Blutdruckmessgerät für die Anwendung zu Hause. Messen Sie so häufig, wie es Ihre Ärztin oder Ihr Arzt empfiehlt, und besprechen Sie Ihre Werte beim nächsten Termin. [Marke] misst den Blutdruck; es diagnostiziert oder behandelt keinen Bluthochdruck. Medizinprodukt. Gebrauchsanweisung beachten.

This keeps the motivating idea — home measurement is worth doing — while sourcing authority from validation evidence and the user's own clinician rather than from a named professional or from fear. Use "clinically validated" only if you can point to a validation study to the relevant protocol (e.g. ISO 81060-2 / the AAMI-ESH-ISO universal standard); if you can't, cut that word rather than defend it.

Two things I'd want before this goes live: confirmation from the copy owner on whether Professor Schmidt is a real consenting person (it changes the risk category, though the fix is deletion either way), and your current IFU text on measurement frequency so the replacement copy matches it. And to be clear about what this review is: a substantive compliance read, not regulatory-affairs or legal sign-off. The HWG subsection numbering in particular should be confirmed by German counsel before you rely on it in writing.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict: do not publish as written

Both sentences have problems, and the first one is a hard prohibition, not a judgment call. Because the page is public and ungated, you are definitively **"außerhalb der Fachkreise"** under the German Heilmittelwerbegesetz (HWG) — you cannot fall back on the professional-audience exemption. HWG applies to your device via § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a (Medizinprodukte per Art. 2 Nr. 1 MDR), and § 11 Abs. 1 expressly covers "Gegenstände."

## Issue 1 — "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist"

**HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2** bans public-facing advertising with statements that a product "ärztlich, zahnärztlich, tierärztlich oder anderweitig fachlich empfohlen oder geprüft ist oder angewendet wird." A named cardiologist's recommendation is the textbook case. This one is not fixable by rewording — the *category* of claim is prohibited in consumer advertising. Delete it.

Adjacent exposure on the same line:
- **§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 1** if the recommendation is dressed up as a testimonial, certificate, or reference to a study.
- **§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 4** if accompanied by an image of the professor in a white coat or clinical setting.
- **§ 27 MBO-Ä** — German physicians may not lend their name to commercial product advertising. You would be creating professional-conduct liability for the doctor, not just regulatory risk for yourself.
- **§ 5a UWG** if there is a paid or contractual relationship that isn't disclosed.
- If "Professor Schmidt" is not a real, identifiable, verifiable person, add **§ 5 UWG / HWG § 3** deception on top.

The endorsement *could* live behind genuine HCP gating (verified professional access), since § 11 Abs. 1 only bites outside Fachkreise. That is the only lawful home for it.

## Issue 2 — "Don't gamble with your heart"

- **HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 7**: advertising statements "die geeignet sind, Angstgefühle hervorzurufen oder auszunutzen." A gambling-with-your-heart framing is a fear appeal by construction.
- It also implies health will be harmed by *not* using the device — the same provision's core concern.
- **MDR Art. 7(a) and (d)**: it ascribes a cardioprotective function the device does not have and suggests a use beyond the intended purpose. A non-invasive BP monitor measures blood pressure; it does not protect the heart or reduce cardiovascular risk. Any implied outcome benefit would need support in your clinical evaluation under Art. 61 / Annex XIV, and I doubt your CER carries a risk-reduction endpoint.

## Issue 3 — "check your pressure daily"

This is a usage instruction in marketing copy, so it must match the IFU and intended purpose. Two risks:

- **Off-label instruction** if your IFU says measurement frequency is determined by the treating physician (most home NIBP IFUs do). Marketing cannot expand the instructed regimen — MDR Art. 7(d).
- **Clinical mismatch**: ESH and Deutsche Hochdruckliga guidance for home monitoring is a structured 7-day series (duplicate morning and evening readings) around consultations, not indefinite daily self-measurement, which is associated with over-measurement and health anxiety. Pairing it with a fear appeal compounds the § 11 Nr. 7 problem.

## Issue 4 — missing safety context

**MDR Art. 7(c)** — misleading by failing to inform of a likely risk. Consumer copy promoting self-measurement with no statement that the device does not replace medical assessment, and that readings should be discussed with a physician, is a gap. Add it.

## Suggested rewrite

Objective, verifiable, within intended purpose:

> **Know your numbers at home.**
> Clinically validated blood pressure measurement to ISO 81060-2, for use at home between doctor's visits. Measure as instructed by your doctor and share your readings at your next appointment.
>
> *This device measures blood pressure and does not replace medical diagnosis or advice. Read the instructions for use before measuring.*

For German market, localize rather than translate literally — HWG assessment attaches to the German wording that actually ships.

## Two follow-ups

1. **Third-party seals as a substitute:** a Deutsche Hochdruckliga Prüfsiegel or stridebp.org listing is tempting as an endorsement replacement, but a test/certification seal may itself read as "anderweitig fachlich geprüft" under § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2. Case law treats neutral, objective test results more permissively than expert recommendations, but this is genuinely contested — get it cleared before you rely on it. A bare CE mark and the ISO 81060-2 validation statement are safe.
2. **Process:** route this and all consumer claims through your claims-substantiation matrix so each claim traces to the intended purpose and the clinical evaluation, and keep promotional material under QMS document control (ISO 13485).

I'm flagging regulatory exposure, not giving legal advice — the § 11 Nr. 2 finding in particular should be confirmed by German regulatory counsel before you rely on it, but I'd treat the endorsement line as blocked in the meantime.

graders.evidence:
I couldn't fetch the consolidated statute text (WebFetch is blocked in this session), so the citations below are from knowledge — the substance is settled German law, but **have counsel confirm the current numbering and wording of § 11 Abs. 1 HWG**, which was substantially amended in 2012 and where several prohibitions gained "missbräuchlich/abstoßend/irreführend" qualifiers. My assessment of what's prohibited doesn't turn on that detail.

## Verdict: do not publish. Two hard blockers.

Both sentences are problems, and the first is a per-se violation that no amount of substantiation fixes.

---

### 1. "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" — blocker

**§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 HWG** prohibits advertising *outside professional circles* with statements that a product is "ärztlich … oder anderweitig fachlich empfohlen oder geprüft … oder angewendet." The HWG covers MDR (EU) 2017/745 medical devices (§ 1 Abs. 1), and an un-gated public web page is by definition Publikumswerbung — outside the Fachkreise as defined in § 2 HWG.

Key point for whoever pushes back on this: **it is a per-se prohibition.** It does not matter whether Prof. Schmidt is real, whether he genuinely holds that view, whether the recommendation is accurate, or whether you disclose the relationship. The medical endorsement itself is the violation. This is the single most-litigated provision in German device advertising.

Compounding exposures:
- **§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 1 HWG** if the recommendation is presented as an expert opinion, testimonial, or scientific/professional publication ("Gutachten, Zeugnisse … sowie Hinweise darauf").
- **§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 4 HWG** if the page pairs this with a photo of him in a white coat, with a stethoscope, or in clinical surroundings.
- **Physician-side liability.** § 34 Abs. 1 MBO-Ä (and the Landesärztekammern's Berufsordnungen) bars physicians from lending their name, title, or reputation to product advertising. Prof. Schmidt is personally exposed to his Kammer, and you are exposed via **§ 3a UWG** for exploiting that breach.
- **§§ 299a/299b StGB** if the recommendation is paid for and connects to prescribing, recommending, or procurement decisions — this is criminal, not just competition law. Check what he was paid and on what basis.
- **GDPR Art. 6 + right of personality.** Naming an identifiable professor with title and specialty needs a documented legal basis and written consent covering this specific use.

**Remedy:** delete it from public copy. There is no compliant softening — "Entwickelt mit Kardiologen," "von Ärzten empfohlen," and "klinisch geprüft" are the same violation in different clothing. Expert endorsement can only live behind genuine Fachkreise gating (verified professional credentials, not a self-declaration checkbox), and even there **§ 6 HWG** requires you to name the author, cite the source, and give the date.

If "Professor Schmidt" is a placeholder in a draft, say so and I'll treat this section as advisory rather than as a live finding.

### 2. "Don't gamble with your heart" — blocker

Two independent defects.

**Fear appeal.** § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 7 HWG prohibits advertising with statements apt to arouse or exploit fear ("Angstgefühle hervorzurufen oder auszunutzen"). A gambling metaphor about your heart, immediately followed by a use imperative, is a textbook exploitation of fear of cardiac events. The German consumer-protection bodies read this provision broadly.

**Implied efficacy the device does not have.** The sentence tells the reader that using this device protects their heart. It does not. A Class IIa sphygmomanometer *measures* — it does not prevent, treat, or reduce cardiovascular risk. That crosses:
- **§ 3 Nr. 1 HWG** — attributing effects the product does not have;
- **MDR Art. 7(a) and (b)** — ascribing functions the device lacks, and creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis;
- **Nr. 18 of the Annex to § 3 Abs. 3 UWG** — the blacklisted, per-se-unfair claim that a product cures diseases or dysfunctions, if the implication is read that strongly.

Note also that a blood-pressure monitor is not a cardiac device. Conflating "pressure" with "heart" is itself a misleading-scope problem.

### 3. "check your pressure daily" — high risk

This is clinical instruction issued to an ungated general audience.

- **MDR Art. 7(d)** — must not suggest uses beyond the stated intended purpose. Check this against your IFU: if the IFU says "as directed by your physician" or specifies structured schedules, the public copy contradicts your own technical documentation. That is the kind of inconsistency a notified body and a Landesbehörde both pick up on.
- **No clinical basis as a universal instruction.** ESH/ESC guidance frames home monitoring as structured schedules tied to clinical need — commonly 7-day series around consultations — not indefinite daily measurement by everyone. Telling the untriaged general public to measure daily invites health anxiety, white-coat effects, and self-adjustment of antihypertensives.
- **Rewrite to defer:** frequency is a matter for the treating physician.

### 4. Missing, not just wrong

- **Language.** German market copy must be in German. Separately, § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 6 HWG restricts foreign-language and technical terms in public advertising unless they've entered general usage. (Note the IFU and labelling must be German under § 8 MPDG — separate obligation, but confirm it's satisfied.)
- **No device identification.** Add "Medizinprodukt" and a pointer to the Gebrauchsanweisung. Not a codified requirement for device advertising the way § 4 Abs. 3 HWG mandates the Pflichttext for medicinal products, but it's standard German market practice, costs nothing, and helps on the misleadingness analysis.
- **No diagnostic limitation.** State that a single reading is not a diagnosis and that hypertension is diagnosed by a physician.
- **No substantiation hooks.** If you later want accuracy claims, they need ISO 81060-2 validation data on file first.

### 5. Reassurance on one point

Cardiovascular disease is **not** on the § 12 HWG Anlage list of conditions for which public advertising is barred — the former Abschnitt B, which did cover organic heart disease, was repealed in 2012. So advertising a home BP monitor to consumers is permissible as a category; the problem is entirely execution. Worth confirming with counsel, but I'd expect this to hold.

---

## Suggested replacement

German, with English gloss:

> **Blutdruck messen – zu Hause, einfach und zuverlässig.**
>
> Der [Produktname] ist ein Blutdruckmessgerät für die Selbstmessung am Oberarm. Er zeigt Ihnen systolischen und diastolischen Wert sowie den Puls und speichert Ihre Messwerte, sodass Sie sie mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt besprechen können.
>
> Wie häufig und zu welchen Zeiten Sie messen sollten, besprechen Sie mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt. Ein einzelner Messwert ist keine Diagnose.
>
> Medizinprodukt. Bitte lesen Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung.

> *Measure your blood pressure — at home, simply and reliably. The [product] is an upper-arm monitor for self-measurement. It shows systolic and diastolic values and pulse, and stores your readings so you can discuss them with your doctor. Discuss how often and when to measure with your doctor. A single reading is not a diagnosis. Medical device — please read the instructions for use.*

This keeps the "regular monitoring is worthwhile" motivation but relocates the authority from a named cardiologist to the reader's own physician, which is both compliant and, in German consumer research, more persuasive.

## What I need to finalize

1. Is "Professor Schmidt" a real named individual, and is there a paid relationship? Changes this from a copy problem to a §§ 299a/b review.
2. The exact intended purpose and the measurement-frequency language from your IFU, so the public copy can be aligned to it.
3. Whether any Fachkreise-gated version of this page is planned — the endorsement content could potentially be reused there under § 6 HWG.

Given the § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 exposure and the standing of the Wettbewerbszentrale and Verbraucherzentralen to issue an Abmahnung with Unterlassungserklärung on this exact provision, plus the Ordnungswidrigkeit risk under § 15 HWG, I'd route the final copy past German regulatory counsel rather than relying on this review alone.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: CGM consumer copy (3-line asset)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Class IIa CGM (continuous glucose monitor) — MDR applies (not IVDR: measures interstitial fluid in situ, not a specimen)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change."
**Audience:** Publikum assumed — "straight to your phone" and "know your glucose" are patient-facing, not Fachkreise. Confirm if this is trade press.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **Market not supplied** — German-market findings below are held in `Also engaged:` conditional on DE distribution.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 1 to substantiate, 0 OK.**

The asset's payoff line contradicts the express carve-out in the assessed intended purpose. This is a limb (d) problem, which means **evidence cannot cure it** — no accuracy data makes "Dose with confidence" compatible with "not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions."

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d), Art. 7(b), Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:**
- **(d)** — "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out." Insulin dosing is a treatment decision. The assessed intended purpose expressly excludes replacing blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid change. The copy suggests exactly that use, unqualified.
- **(b)** — "creating a false impression regarding treatment." A monitoring-only indication is being framed as a dosing instrument.
- **(c)** — "failing to inform the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose." The risk is not inferred from the device category here — **it is named in the intended purpose you supplied**: readings may diverge during periods of rapid glucose change. Copy that actively invites dosing on those readings, while omitting the limitation, is the paradigm (c) omission.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured only by narrowing the claim, or by extending the conformity assessment to a dosing indication (a different intended purpose, and for a Class IIa device a different assessment).
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — "fälschlich der Eindruck erweckt wird, daß ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" — if the DE market is targeted, "with confidence" as an unqualified dosing assurance is a certainty-of-outcome shape. This is additive to Art. 7; there is no Art. 7 guarantee limb.
- HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]` — if DE **and** Publikum: health-improved-by-use framing.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse". This is the UWG mirror of the (d) drift and the Abmahnung route.

**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** Replace with a monitoring-framed CTA plus the confirmation step — see paste-ready copy below.

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings every 5 minutes"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]` — "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have."
**Why:** "Real-time" asserts that the reading reflects the user's current glucose. The intended purpose's own carve-out for "periods of rapid glucose change" is an admission that it does not, in the condition that matters most. I am not importing an outside physiological claim — the limitation is in the text you supplied. "Real-time" and that carve-out cannot both be true.
**Evidence needed:** Nothing substantiates "real-time" against your own carve-out. The **"every 5 minutes"** figure is separately verifiable — confirm the sampling/transmission interval in the technical documentation matches, and that it is the interval as delivered to the phone rather than the sensor's internal sampling rate.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "wesentlichen Merkmale ... Art, Ausführung" and "Tests", if DE and the interval figure is a bench/spec value not reproduced as stated.
**Call:** **Needs rewording** (+ substantiate the interval).
**Suggested fix:** Drop "real-time". "Readings every 5 minutes" is accurate, verifiable, and narrow — cheap to defend.

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`, in combination with the CTA.
**Why:** Two things compound. First, the assessed purpose is **interstitial** glucose monitoring; "your glucose" in patient-facing copy reads as blood glucose. Standing alone, "glucose" is conventional consumer shorthand and I would not flag it. But sitting immediately above "Dose with confidence", it forms a single proposition: *this number is your blood glucose, act on it*. Second, "at a glance" is the reassurance verb — it tells the reader no confirmatory step is needed, which is precisely the step the intended purpose reserves.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — a framing fix, not an evidence gap.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]` — if DE and Publikum, weakly, as part of the improved-by-use framing; the CTA carries this finding, not this line.
**Call:** **Needs rewording.**
**Suggested fix:** Point "at a glance" at **trends**, which is what a monitoring indication supports.

---

## Paste-ready revised copy

> **Know your glucose trends at a glance.** Interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. When your glucose is changing quickly, confirm with a blood glucose test before treatment decisions.

What this preserves and what it changes:

- Keeps the three-beat rhythm, the "at a glance" hook, and the phone-delivery benefit.
- "Trends" replaces the point-value dosing promise — inside a monitoring indication.
- "Interstitial" appears once, cheaply, and defuses the blood-glucose implication.
- The third line converts the (c) omission into the limitation, in your own intended purpose's words.
- If "interstitial" is unacceptable to marketing, the minimum viable version is: keep "Know your glucose trends at a glance" and keep the third sentence. **The third sentence is the one that cannot be dropped** — it is doing the Art. 7(c) work.

One drafting note beyond the statute: check whether the IFU's limitation wording is narrower or broader than "changing quickly". Marketing copy should not state the limitation more permissively than the IFU does.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "every 5 minutes" | Interval as delivered to the app, per technical documentation — not the internal sensor sampling rate | Regulatory / systems engineering |
| Confirmation-step wording | The IFU's verbatim limitation text on rapid glucose change, to align the third sentence | Regulatory affairs |
| Target market | Whether this asset runs in Germany — decides whether the HWG § 3 no. 2(a) and § 11(1) no. 7 items above become live findings | Marketing |
| Audience gating | Whether the placement is ungated consumer or trade — decides HWG § 11 applicability | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) no. 7 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (devices: only nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 apply)
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

UWG § 6 not engaged — no comparison in this copy. IVDR Art. 7 not cited — this is a device, not an IVD. HWG § 3a not cited — Arzneimittel only.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**The one thing to take away:** "Dose with confidence" is not a wording problem, it is an indication problem. Your own intended purpose carves out treatment decisions during rapid change, and the copy's payoff line sells exactly that use. Limb (d) breaches are cured by narrowing the claim or widening the certificate — never by better data.

# Device Claims Review: CGM headline copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Continuous glucose monitor — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change"
**Audience:** Ambiguous — **assumed Publikum**. "Straight to your phone" and the second-person register read as patient-facing. Confirm; if this is trade press or an HCP-gated page, the HWG § 11 line drops out (§ 3 still applies).
**Markets:** EU assumed. **Germany not confirmed** — HWG and UWG findings below are conditional on DE being a target market. Confirm.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.**

The copy's problem is structural, not incidental: the intended purpose contains an express carve-out for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change, and the copy's payoff line ("Dose with confidence") points straight into that carve-out. The rest of the copy removes the cues a reader would need to notice it — "real-time" denies the lag, "your glucose" elides interstitial vs. blood.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:**
- **(d)** — the assessed intended purpose is *monitoring*, and it expressly states readings "are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change". Dosing is a treatment decision. The line "suggest[s] uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out."
- **(b)** — it creates "a false impression regarding treatment" by presenting the reading as a sufficient basis for an insulin dose, unqualified.
- **(c)** — the rapid-change limitation is a likely risk named in your own intended purpose, and the copy does not surface it. This is not an inferred risk; it is in the material you supplied.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — **cannot be cured by evidence.** This is intended-purpose drift. It is cured by narrowing the claim, or by extending the conformity assessment to cover a dosing/replacement indication. Better accuracy data does not fix it while the carve-out stands in the assessed purpose.
**Also engaged (DE only):** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — "fälschlich der Eindruck erweckt wird, daß ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann"; "with confidence" is a certainty framing attached to a dosing outcome. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "Zwecktauglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse".
**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** Replace with a confirmation instruction, not a dosing promise — see revised copy below.

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings every 5 minutes"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`
**Why:** "Real-time" ascribes a property in tension with interstitial measurement, and specifically with the lag that the rapid-change carve-out exists to address. The claim is doing work here — it is what makes "Dose with confidence" feel safe two words later. The 5-minute cadence is fine; "real-time" is the overclaim.
**Evidence needed:** The 5-minute sampling interval from the technical documentation. "Real-time" is not curable by evidence in the presence of the rapid-change limitation — drop the word rather than substantiate it.
**Also engaged (DE only):** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "wesentliche Merkmale ... Art, Ausführung".
**Call:** **Needs rewording.**

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`
**Why:** The assessed purpose is **interstitial** glucose monitoring. "Your glucose", to a patient audience, reads as blood glucose. That conflation is precisely the distinction the intended-purpose restriction rests on, so it is not a pedantic point — it is the point. Ascribes a property (blood glucose measurement) the device does not have.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — a wording fix.
**Call:** **Needs rewording.**

---

**Claim:** "straight to your phone"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Delivery-mechanism statement, no clinical or performance content.
**Also engaged:** Nothing, provided the app is covered by the same CE certificate and the display of readings on a phone falls inside the assessed intended purpose. If the app is separately regulated or the certificate scope does not cover mobile display, this becomes UWG § 5(2) no. 4 `[verified]` territory.
**Call:** **Verify** (certificate scope only).

---

## Revised copy — paste-ready

> **Know your glucose trends at a glance.** Interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. When your glucose is changing quickly, confirm with a blood glucose test before dosing.

Notes on what each change buys you:

- **"trends"** and **"interstitial"** keep the claim inside the assessed purpose and cure the (a) findings.
- Dropping **"real-time"** removes the property claim without losing the cadence, which is the genuinely attractive fact.
- The confirmation sentence carries the (c) disclosure *and* neutralises (d) — it converts the dosing reference from a suggested use into a stated limitation. It also removes the HWG § 3 no. 2(a) certainty framing.
- If length is constrained, the confirmation sentence is the one that cannot be cut. Everything else is tuning.

A shorter variant, if you need the fourth sentence gone: append **"Confirm with a fingerstick before dosing."** to sentence two and drop the rest.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "every 5 minutes" | Sampling interval as stated in the technical documentation / IFU | Regulatory / R&D |
| "straight to your phone" | Confirmation that the mobile app and display of readings sit inside the CE certificate scope | Regulatory |
| Rapid-change wording | The IFU's own phrasing of the limitation — mirror it rather than paraphrasing it | Regulatory |
| Audience & market | Is this page gated to HCPs? Is DE a target market? | Marketing |

## Open questions

The IFU may record further likely risks that belong in patient-facing copy — sensor site reactions, adhesive, warm-up period, known interferents. I can't tell from what I have whether any of those rise to "likely" under Art. 7(c). Worth a pass against the IFU; the (c) finding above stands on the rapid-change limitation alone.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (DE market only)
- UWG § 5(2) nos. 1, 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]` (DE market only)

HWG § 11 raised no findings. Under the Publikum assumption I considered no. 7 (health improved by use) against "Dose with confidence" and concluded it does not fit — the copy claims reliability of a decision, not improvement of health by use. Recording that as checked-and-clear rather than as a finding.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

The one thing I'd flag for a human decision: if the product team believes the device *should* support dosing decisions, that is a conformity-assessment conversation with your notified body, not a copy conversation. No rewrite makes "Dose with confidence" safe while the assessed intended purpose contains that carve-out.

# Device Claims Review: CGM launch copy (3 lines)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Class IIa CGM (continuous glucose monitor) — MDR
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change."
**Audience:** Ambiguous — assumed **Publikum** (copy addresses the wearer, "straight to your phone"). Confirm.
**Markets:** **EU assumed; DE not confirmed.** MDR Art. 7 findings below stand either way. HWG/UWG exposure is routed as `Also engaged` with the condition named — tell me if Germany is in scope and I'll promote those.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 0 OK.**

The copy's problem is concentrated but serious: the intended purpose carves out treatment decisions during rapid glucose change, and the closing line ("Dose with confidence") suggests exactly that use, unconditionally. That is the limb (d) shape, and it is not curable by data.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d), Art. 7(b), Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:** (d) — the assessed intended purpose is *monitoring*, and it expressly states readings "are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change"; this line suggests insulin dosing off the device reading with no such limit, i.e. "uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". (b) — it creates "a false impression regarding treatment" by presenting a monitoring output as a sufficient basis for a dosing decision. (c) — the one likely risk the intended purpose itself names (mis-dosing off an unconfirmed reading during rapid change) is the exact risk this line invites, and it is nowhere surfaced.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. This is cured by narrowing the claim, or by an extended conformity assessment covering dosing.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" `[verified]` — "with confidence" as a promise of certain outcome; and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" `[verified]` — both **only if the German market is in scope**.
**Call:** **Cut**
**Suggested fix:** "Confirm with a blood glucose test before treatment decisions when your glucose is changing rapidly."

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** The device measures **interstitial** glucose; "your glucose" reads as blood glucose, and "at a glance" implies the on-screen number is self-sufficient. Together they create the impression that the reading is interchangeable with a blood glucose measurement — the precise equivalence the intended purpose declines to claim.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the equivalence framing — fix by naming the measurand. (Not an (a) overclaim; the device does display a value at a glance.)
**Call:** **Needs rewording**
**Suggested fix:** "Know your glucose trends at a glance."

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings every 5 minutes"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]` — as to "real-time" only
**Why:** "Real-time" ascribes a property the device does not have in the sense a lay reader takes it. Interstitial readings track blood glucose with a lag; the intended purpose's own carve-out for "periods of rapid glucose change" is the acknowledgment of that limitation. Advertising the output as real-time contradicts the limitation the assessed purpose records.
**Evidence needed:** For the *cadence*, the technical file's sampling/display interval (see verify item below). For "real-time", no figure rescues the word — replace it.
**Call:** **Needs rewording**
**Suggested fix:** "Readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."

---

**Claim:** "every 5 minutes"
**Breach:** **none**
**Why:** A narrow, verifiable performance spec. Not misleading on the material supplied — but I have not seen the technical file, and the number must match the assessed display/sampling interval, not a best case.
**Evidence needed:** Sampling and display interval as stated in the technical documentation / IFU.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "wesentlichen Merkmale" `[verified]` — if the interval is nominal, conditional, or differs from the assessed spec, **and** Germany is in scope.
**Call:** **Verify**

---

### Asset-level omission

Across all three lines there is no pointer to the confirmatory blood glucose test or to the IFU. The risk here is not inferred from the device category — it is written into the intended purpose you supplied, which makes this a live **Art. 7(c)** point for the asset as a whole and not just for the "Dose with confidence" line. For a three-line asset, an IFU pointer plus the confirmation sentence is the proportionate fix, not patient-facing safety text.

## Paste-ready revised copy

> Know your glucose trends at a glance. Readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. Confirm with a blood glucose test before treatment decisions when your glucose is changing rapidly. See the instructions for use.

This keeps the three beats of the original (immediacy, cadence, phone delivery) and moves "confidence" from the dosing decision to the data stream. If marketing wants the word back, "Monitor with confidence" sits inside the intended purpose; "Dose with confidence" does not.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "every 5 minutes" | Assessed sampling/display interval | Regulatory / technical file owner |
| "real-time" (if marketing pushes to keep it) | Lag characterisation vs. blood glucose; whether any assessed claim supports "real-time" | Clinical affairs |
| Asset-level (c) | Whether the IFU records further likely risks belonging in consumer copy (e.g. compression lows, warm-up, interfering substances) | IFU / risk management file |
| Dosing claim | Whether the conformity assessment scope covers treatment decisions at all — if a non-adjunctive indication was assessed, the (d) analysis changes materially | Notified body certificate scope |

That last row is the one to settle first. If the certificate is in fact non-adjunctive, "Dose with confidence" moves from **Cut** to a rewording question about the rapid-change caveat. My finding above takes the intended purpose you gave me at face value, and it reads as adjunctive.

- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (conditional on DE market)

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

"Class IIa" reads as EU MDR / UK MDR framing, so that's what I've reviewed against (I flag the FDA divergence where it matters).

## Verdict

Don't ship. One line is a hard blocker; the rest need qualification.

## Findings

**1. "Dose with confidence" — blocking.**
This is a claim to support treatment decisions, which is precisely what the intended purpose excludes. It's also the closing line, so it's the takeaway the reader leaves with. Problems:

- **Outside intended purpose.** Promotional material that ascribes a function the device isn't intended for engages MDR Art. 7(a)/(b) (misleading claims), and it undercuts your Art. 10 obligation to keep claims consistent with the technical documentation and IFU.
- **It contradicts your own limitation.** You can't caveat this one down — "dose with confidence*" with an asterisk saying "except when your glucose is changing rapidly" is the exact situation in which people dose. A footnote that reverses the headline is itself misleading.
- **Highest-harm failure mode.** Rapid change is when the interstitial-to-blood lag is largest, and it's when dosing errors stack (correction dose on a falling arrow → severe hypoglycaemia).
- **FDA note:** non-adjunctive dosing claims are only available to devices cleared as iCGM. If your US clearance is adjunctive, this line is off-label there too.

**2. "Know your glucose at a glance" — needs correcting.**
The device measures *interstitial* glucose. Unqualified "your glucose" reads as blood glucose to a lay audience, and that misreading is exactly what makes finding 1 land. Say "glucose levels" with the interstitial basis disclosed somewhere in the asset, or use "sensor glucose."

**3. "Real-time readings every 5 minutes" — qualify.**
"Real-time CGM"/rtCGM is an accepted category term, so I wouldn't strike it on its own. But paired with a dosing claim it implies the number on screen equals your blood glucose right now, and it doesn't — 5-minute sampling plus physiological lag. If you fix finding 1, this becomes acceptable; if you keep any dosing adjacency, it doesn't.

**4. "Straight to your phone" — footnote.**
Implies no preconditions. Needs the standard compatibility/connectivity qualifier: compatible smartphone required, list at [URL]; alarms depend on phone settings and Bluetooth range. Absent that, it's an omission-type misleading claim.

**5. Missing indication and limitation.**
No statement of the indicated population (adults with diabetes) and no limitation statement. For a Class IIa device this material should carry both, plus a "read the instructions for use" pointer and the CE mark treatment per your labelling SOP.

**6. "Confidence" as substantiation.**
Even reworded, subjective performance language needs to trace to clinical evidence (MARD, rate-of-change performance) in the CER. Flag to regulatory whichever version you land on.

## Suggested rewrite

> **Know your glucose levels at a glance.**
> Sensor readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone.\* See where you're heading — and act sooner.
>
> \*Compatible smartphone required; see [compatibility list]. Alarms require Bluetooth connection and enabled phone notifications.
>
> For continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes. Sensor readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change. Read the instructions for use.

The substitution that does the work: **"Dose with confidence" → "See where you're heading — and act sooner."** It keeps the emotional payload (agency, reassurance) and sells the genuine differentiator — trend visibility, which fingersticks don't give you — without claiming dosing authority. "Act" is deliberately broad: eat, retest, call someone, dose after confirming.

If marketing pushes back on losing the dosing angle, the honest version is something like "Fewer surprises between fingersticks" — it concedes fingersticks remain in the loop, which is the actual product truth.

One thing I'd check before finalising: whether the "rapid glucose change" limitation is the only carve-out in your IFU. Devices in this class often also exclude the first hours after insertion, and during sensor error/signal loss states. If so, the limitation statement above is under-inclusive and should mirror the IFU wording exactly rather than the summary you gave me.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict: don't ship. One line is off-label; the other two need qualifying.

Assuming EU MDR (Class IIa is EU nomenclature) — Article 7 prohibits claims that mislead on intended purpose, ascribe functions the device doesn't have, or create false impressions about treatment. All three sentences touch that. (If this is also going to a US market, the analysis is similar but hangs off the 510(k)/iCGM indications and FDCA misbranding rather than Art. 7 — flag jurisdiction before final sign-off.)

**1. "Dose with confidence." — Critical. Cut it.**
This is the single biggest problem. The intended purpose explicitly carves out treatment decisions during rapid glucose change; this claim asserts the opposite, unconditionally. It reads as an insulin-dosing indication the device does not hold, so it's off-label promotion and it inverts the exact limitation the notified body approved. It also creates the worst-case clinical scenario: a user dosing off a lagging reading during a fast drop. No amount of small-print qualification rescues this phrasing — the words "dose" and "confidence" together are the claim.

**2. "Real-time readings" — High. Qualify or reword.**
Interstitial glucose lags blood glucose (physiological lag plus algorithm processing). "Real-time" implies concurrency with blood glucose and quietly undercuts the rapid-change limitation. "Every 5 minutes" is fine if that's the true sampling interval — it's a factual performance claim, keep it, just don't dress it as real-time.

**3. "Know your glucose" — Medium. Conflates two measurands.**
"Your glucose" reads as blood glucose. The device measures interstitial glucose. Say "sensor glucose" or "interstitial glucose" at least once so the copy and the intended purpose describe the same thing.

**4. Missing population and limitation — Medium.**
Nothing signals *adults with diabetes*. As written this is consumer-wellness-shaped copy that would draw in non-diabetic users and, depending on channel, minors — outside the indication. Promotional material carrying performance claims should also carry the fingerstick limitation and an IFU pointer, not bury them.

## Suggested rewrite

> **Know your glucose trend at a glance.** A new sensor glucose reading every 5 minutes, straight to your phone.
>
> For adults with diabetes. Sensor readings can lag blood glucose — use a blood glucose meter for treatment decisions when your glucose is changing rapidly. Read the Instructions for Use.

Punchier variant for the third line, if marketing wants to keep a confidence beat without the dosing claim: *"See where you're heading, not just where you are."* — a trend claim is defensible if trend-arrow performance is in your clinical evidence; confirm with regulatory that it is before using it.

## What to check before sign-off
- Is the 5-minute interval the actual sampling/display rate, and is "straight to your phone" accurate (no reader required, stated OS/compatibility limits)?
- Do you hold evidence for any trend or rate-of-change claim you substitute in line 3?
- Whether your channel (paid social, packaging, HCP-facing) has its own limitation-statement placement rules — the caveat can't be a footnote if the claim is in the headline.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The third sentence is a blocker. The first two are fixable with small edits.

"Dose with confidence" is the problem: it tells the reader to use the device for insulin dosing, which is precisely the use your intended purpose carves out. Under MDR 2017/745 Art. 7 that's the textbook prohibited claim — ascribing a function to the device beyond its stated intended purpose, and creating a false impression regarding treatment. It's also off-label promotion regardless of how the sentence is qualified elsewhere on the page; a footnote won't rescue it, because the headline claim and the IFU limitation contradict each other outright.

Worth separating two things: this copy would be defensible for an FDA-cleared iCGM with a dosing indication. It is not defensible for *this* device as you've described it. If the intended purpose is what you pasted, the copy has to go. If the company believes it has dosing data, the fix is a regulatory submission, not a rewrite.

## Line by line

| Copy | Issue | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| "Know your glucose" | Device measures *interstitial* glucose, and output is an estimate with a stated MARD. "Know" asserts certainty the performance data doesn't support. | Medium |
| "at a glance" | Fine. | — |
| "Real-time readings" | Defensible as the accepted term of art (rtCGM vs. intermittently-scanned), but to a lay reader it denies the 5–15 min physiological lag — which is the exact mechanism behind your rapid-change limitation. Using it in the same breath as a dosing claim compounds the problem. | Medium |
| "every 5 minutes" | Factual — just confirm it matches the technical documentation exactly (sampling vs. display interval are often different numbers). | Low |
| "straight to your phone" | Needs substantiation: no receiver required, and a compatible-device list must be reachable. "Straight to" also implies no scan — verify that's true. | Low |
| "Dose with confidence" | Off-label. Contradicts the intended purpose. | **Blocker** |

## Suggested rewrites

Closest to the original rhythm, keeping the punch:

> "See your glucose at a glance. Readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. Confirm with a fingerstick before you dose."

If marketing won't accept an instruction as the closer:

> "See your glucose at a glance. A new reading every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. So you're never guessing where you're headed."

The second version's last line is softer but note it edges toward a clinical benefit claim — if you use it, the claim needs to be traceable to something in the clinical evaluation report, not just plausible.

## Before this ships

- Confirm the 5-minute interval against the technical file, not the marketing brief.
- The rapid-change limitation should appear in the same visual field as the readings claim, not in a footer. Font-size parity matters if this is EU-facing.
- Check whether your market requires an "always read the instructions for use" line and prescription-status disclosure — several national codes do even where MDR itself doesn't mandate it in advertising.
- If there's a companion app store listing, the same copy is almost certainly in it and gets reviewed separately. Fix both.

One caveat: I'm reasoning from the intended purpose text you gave me and general MDR principles. Sign-off should come from your regulatory affairs function, who can check the claim against the actual technical file and CER.

# Device Claims Review: comparison block

**Device:** Class I software (name not supplied)

**Audience:** Fachkreise (as stated) — HWG § 11 not applied
