## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 verify.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

The block's weak point is not disparagement — it's that every load-bearing word is unverifiable. "We catch them before" is unhedged, and "half the rework" has no stated baseline, cohort, or method. Under UWG that combination is expensive to defend even if both turn out to be true.

## Findings

**Claim:** "We catch them before."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) [verified]; HWG § 3 no. 2(a) [verified]; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified]
**Why:** Unhedged and categorical — it ascribes complete pre-submission error detection ("functions and properties which the device does not have" if the software catches a subset of error types), and stated as a certainty in direct antithesis to competitors' failure it is the "Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" shape. § 5(2) no. 1 reaches it as "Zwecktauglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse".
**Evidence needed:** The defined scope of checks the software performs, plus detection performance against that scope. Note the certainty framing is *not* cured by evidence — it needs a hedge regardless.
**Call:** Needs rewording

**Claim:** "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** No provision in the reference files reaches a pejorative characterisation of *prospects* rather than a competitor. But it is an absolute assertion ("still", i.e. always) about an alternative method, with nothing behind it.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 and no. 5 [verified] — if the phrase makes a Mitbewerber "erkennbar" under § 6(1). "Spreadsheet-and-email" names a method, not a vendor, so whether § 6 is engaged at all turns on substitutability, which is case-law territory this review does not assess. If it is engaged, the claim is not objective or verifiable (no. 2) and "crowd" carries herabsetzend risk (no. 5). Also UWG § 5(1) [verified] if the absolute reading influences a purchase decision.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — fix by dropping the absolute and the pejorative.
**Call:** Needs rewording

**Claim:** "Half the rework of what most teams use today."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) [verified]; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified]
**Why:** A quantified outcome claim with no baseline, cohort, measurement definition, or period. § 5(2) no. 1 names both "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" and "Tests ... oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von Tests" — a 50% figure whose method is not disclosed is exactly the omitted essential component.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 and no. 1 [verified] — if a Mitbewerber is erkennbar. "Half" fails *nachprüfbar* because no reader can check it from public information, and that fails no. 2 **even if the figure is accurate**. No. 1 is also live: a regulated Class I device and an unregulated spreadsheet process may not serve "dieselbe Zweckbestimmung", which fails before accuracy is reached.
**Evidence needed:** The study or customer dataset — n, period, how "rework" was defined and counted, what the comparator process was, and a public method page you can point to.
**Call:** Needs substantiation

**Claim:** "what most teams use today"
**Breach:** none
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — if the prevalence assertion is not supportable
**Why:** A market-share statement of fact. Not misleading on what I have, but it rests on data I have not seen.
**Evidence needed:** A citable industry survey, or drop "most".
**Call:** Verify

## Suggested replacement copy

Paste-ready; bracketed values must be filled before publishing, not shipped as placeholders:

> Spreadsheet-and-email workflows often surface submission errors only after filing. Our automated checks run before you submit, covering [defined scope of checks]. In [our 2025 customer study, n = X], teams recorded [X]% less post-submission rework than with their previous spreadsheet-based process — [method and data].

What each change buys: "often" removes the absolute; dropping "crowd" removes the § 6(2) no. 5 exposure; "covering [scope]" bounds the Art. 7(a) capability claim; the named cohort and linked method make the comparison *nachprüfbar* under § 6(2) no. 2.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "We catch them before" | Defined scope of automated checks; detection performance within scope | Product / technical documentation |
| "Half the rework" | Study design, n, period, definition of "rework", comparator process | Customer success / whoever ran the measurement |
| "most teams use today" | Citable prevalence source, or delete the word | Marketing |

## Open questions I could not resolve

**Intended purpose — blocking for limb (d).** I can't assess the limb device marketing trips most often against a purpose I haven't seen. Can you paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or the DoC?

It matters more than usual here. The copy sells a *regulatory-workflow* benefit — catching submission errors, reducing rework. If the assessed intended purpose is clinical or otherwise narrower, this block is suggesting a use "other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out", and that is not curable by evidence — only by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment.

**Limb (c).** The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — the obvious candidate is over-reliance where checks are not exhaustive, but I won't raise (c) on a risk I inferred from the device category rather than read in your material. Worth checking against the IFU. If the IFU says output requires review by a qualified person, that belongs in the block as a pointer.

**Audience.** You've told me Fachkreise and I've applied that. If this comparison block sits on an ungated public page, a B2B framing doesn't by itself make it Fachkreise, and HWG § 11 (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only, for devices) would come into scope. Nothing in the current wording obviously trips those five, but confirm the placement.

**Claim:** "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission."

**Claim:** "We catch them before."

**Claim:** "what most teams use today" (the embedded market-prevalence assertion)

## Verdict

Don't ship as written. Three separate problems: an unsubstantiated quantified comparative claim, a comparator that isn't defined, and a tone that insults the audience you're selling to.

---

## Findings

**1. "Half the rework of what most teams use today" — unsubstantiated quantified comparison (blocking)**

This is the biggest exposure. Two defects stacked:

- *No comparator.* "What most teams use today" is undefined. If a reader takes it as "spreadsheets and email," it's a method comparison. If they take it as "the incumbent eQMS vendors," it's an indirect competitor comparison — which pulls in § 6 UWG (comparative advertising must be objective, relevant, and verifiable on a material feature). The ambiguity is the risk: you don't get to pick the reading, the Abmahnung does.
- *No substantiation.* Under German practice the advertiser carries the burden of proof for a quantified superiority claim (§ 5 UWG). "Half" needs a defined metric, baseline, sample, and period, plus a footnote pointing to it. Without that it's indefensible on a Montag morning.

Germany has an active Abmahnung culture around exactly this — Wettbewerbszentrale and competitor-driven cease-and-desist. A quantified "50% better than the market" claim with no asterisk is close to a template case.

**2. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" — disparages your buyer, not your competitor**

A large share of your target readership *is* running Excel and Outlook today. You're opening by mocking the prospect's current state. That's a conversion problem before it's a legal one. It also reads as herabsetzend toward competitors under § 6 Abs. 2 Nr. 5 UWG if the "crowd" is heard as vendors rather than users.

Separately: it doesn't localize. Any German rendering ("Excel-und-E-Mail-Fraktion") lands harsher than the English, and this audience — RA/QA leads, Benannte-Stelle-facing consultants — reads sachlich, evidence-first copy. Snark signals you're not one of them.

**3. "We catch them before" — absolute detection claim**

Unqualified "we catch them" implies completeness. Scope it to what the product actually checks (e.g. formal completeness, traceability gaps, missing references), or it's a performance claim you can't defend.

**4. "Submission" is vague — a credibility tell for this audience**

Submission of what, to whom? Technical documentation to a Benannte Stelle? Class I self-certification (no submission at all)? A consultant will notice the imprecision immediately. Name the artifact and the recipient.

---

## One thing I need you to confirm

The brief says the *product* is a Class I software device, but the copy describes an RA/QA tooling workflow. These imply different rule sets:

- **If it is a medical device under MDR:** MDR Art. 7 applies directly (no misleading claims about function/performance), plus § 3 HWG (irreführende Werbung — HWG covers Medizinprodukte). Since the audience is Fachkreise, the § 11 HWG public-advertising restrictions largely don't bite, but Art. 7 and § 3 HWG both do — and both attach to the "half the rework" claim.
- **If it's regulatory tooling that isn't itself a device:** only UWG applies. Still blocking for finding 1, but the Art. 7 / HWG layer drops away.

I've written the rewrite to clear the stricter reading, so it's safe either way.

---

## Rewrite

**Option A — keep the quantified claim, make it defensible**

> Fehler in der technischen Dokumentation fallen oft erst beim Review durch die Benannte Stelle auf. [Produkt] prüft Vollständigkeit, Rückverfolgbarkeit und Querverweise vor der Einreichung.
>
> In einer Auswertung von [n] Einreichungen im Zeitraum [Zeitraum] sank die Zahl der Nachbesserungsschleifen um [x] % gegenüber dokumentenbasierten Prozessen ohne automatisierte Prüfung.¹
>
> ¹ [Methodik, Stichprobe, Zeitraum — verlinkt]

English equivalent:

> Errors in technical documentation often surface only during notified body review. [Product] checks completeness, traceability and cross-references before you submit.
>
> Across [n] submissions between [dates], review cycles fell by [x]% compared with document-based processes without automated checking.¹

The footnote is not optional. If you can't fill it in, use Option B.

**Option B — no comparison, no substantiation burden**

> Vollständigkeit, Rückverfolgbarkeit und Querverweise Ihrer technischen Dokumentation prüfen — vor der Einreichung, nicht danach.
>
> Automatisierte Prüfregeln, nachvollziehbare Prüfprotokolle, keine Excel-Historie.

Ships today. No comparator, no quantified claim, no burden of proof. The last line acknowledges the spreadsheet status quo as a fact rather than as a punchline about the reader.

My recommendation is B now, A later once you have the data — the quantified claim is genuinely strong with a footnote behind it and genuinely dangerous without one.

---

## Before A goes live

1. Define "rework" as one measurable unit (returned documents? review cycles? deficiency letters?) and lock it.
2. Fix the baseline in writing — what exactly was measured against, over what period, n = what.
3. Keep the substantiation dossier retrievable; the burden sits with you if challenged.
4. Have German counsel clear the final wording. I'm flagging risk patterns, not giving a legal opinion, and the § 6 UWG question in particular turns on how a specific German court reads your comparator.

## Verdict

Don't ship this. Two of the three sentences carry real legal exposure in Germany, and the tone is likely to lose the audience you're addressing.

## Findings, worst first

**1. "Half the rework of what most teams use today" — unsubstantiated quantified comparative claim**

This is the highest-risk line. It's comparative advertising against an identifiable class of alternatives, with a specific number and no basis. In Germany that engages:

- **§ 5 UWG** (misleading commercial practice) — a quantified performance claim must be provable, and for this kind of claim the burden effectively sits with you, held *at the time of publication*, not assembled later when challenged.
- **§ 5a UWG** — omitting the material information (method, sample, period, comparison baseline) is itself actionable.
- **§ 6 UWG** — comparison must rest on objectively verifiable, relevant characteristics. "Rework" is undefined here: rework hours? review cycles? findings per submission?

"Most teams use today" is a second, separate factual assertion — a market-share claim about methods — that also needs a source.

Practical note: Germany has an active *Abmahnung* culture, and § 8(3) UWG gives standing to competitors and qualified associations. A round-number claim like "half" is unusually exposed because it reads as measured while being unfalsifiable as written.

**2. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" — disparagement plus an own-goal on credibility**

Legally, this is the softer risk: it targets a method rather than a named competitor, so § 6(2) Nr. 5 UWG (*Herabsetzung/Verunglimpfung*) is less directly triggered — but the framing plus the comparative number in sentence three is exactly the combination that invites the argument.

The bigger problem is commercial. You're addressing manufacturers and regulatory consultants, and a **validated** spreadsheet is a legitimate, defensible tool under ISO 13485 §4.1.6 and MDR technical-documentation practice. Calling that population "the crowd" who "still find their errors after submission" tells your buyer they've been doing it wrong — and any consultant reading it will note that the copy misstates what the standard actually permits. In German professional B2B register (Sie-form, sachlich, nominal style) this lands as *unseriös*, which is expensive for a regulatory product where trust is the whole sale.

**3. "We catch them before" — claim scope vs. intended purpose**

If the advertised product is itself the Class I device, **MDR Art. 7** prohibits claims that ascribe functions or performance the device doesn't have. "We catch them" is an unqualified detection claim; unless your technical documentation and intended-purpose statement support detection of that error class, this is a conformity issue, not just an advertising one. **§ 3 HWG** points the same way for medical devices. Safer construction: describe what the software checks (completeness, consistency, traceability), not what it guarantees to catch.

**4. Localization**

"The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" has no German equivalent that isn't either flat or insulting. "We catch them before" is an unfinished sentence — the ellipsis works in English, but in German it needs a completion, and the fragment style reads as careless rather than punchy.

**5. It's labelled a comparison block but contains no comparison**

There are no criteria, no columns, no basis — just three assertions. A German RA audience reads for *Nachvollziehbarkeit*. Give them criteria-by-criteria rows and they'll do the favourable comparison themselves.

## Rewrite

**EN**

> Class I documentation is still largely assembled in spreadsheets and email threads. Gaps surface late there — often only at review.
>
> [Product] checks completeness, consistency and traceability as you work, so gaps surface while they are still inexpensive to close.
>
> In an internal study ([year], n = [x] files), teams using [Product] spent [X]% less time on rework than teams working from spreadsheets and email.¹
>
> ¹ Method, sample and period: [link]

**DE**

> Klasse-I-Dokumentation entsteht vielerorts noch in Tabellen und E-Mail-Verläufen. Lücken zeigen sich dort spät – häufig erst in der Prüfung.
>
> [Produkt] prüft Vollständigkeit, Konsistenz und Nachverfolgbarkeit laufend. So werden Lücken sichtbar, solange sie sich günstig schließen lassen.
>
> In einer internen Untersuchung ([Jahr], n = [x] Vorgänge) benötigten Teams mit [Produkt] [X] % weniger Zeit für Nacharbeit als Teams, die mit Tabellen und E-Mail arbeiteten.¹
>
> ¹ Methodik, Stichprobe und Zeitraum: [Link]

## Two things to settle before you fill the brackets

- **Replace "half" with the number you actually measured**, and publish the footnote. If no study exists, cut sentence three entirely rather than softening it to "up to" — hedged quantifications attract the same challenge.
- **"Submission" doesn't map cleanly to MDR Class I**, where the route is self-certification, a declaration of conformity and EUDAMED registration rather than a submission to a reviewer. I used *Prüfung* in the German, but confirm which step you mean — a regulatory audience will read "Einreichung" as a category error, and it's the kind of slip that costs you the consultants specifically.

I've flagged the statutory hooks so you know where the pressure is, but the quantified-claim substantiation and the Art. 7 alignment against your intended-purpose statement both warrant sign-off from your own counsel and RA lead before publication.

## Verdict: don't ship as-is

Three of the four claims in this block are legally exposed in Germany, and the tone works against the audience you named.

**One assumption to confirm first:** you describe the product as a Class I software device, but the copy sells regulatory-submission tooling to manufacturers and consultants. Software that checks *other people's* technical documentation usually isn't a device at all. If it genuinely carries a Class I classification, MDR Art. 7 binds this copy (see finding 3). If it doesn't, findings 3, 5 and 6 drop away and only the UWG issues remain. Everything below assumes your framing is correct.

---

### Blocking

**1. "Half the rework of what most teams use today"**
A quantified comparative claim with no comparator, no metric, and no disclosed basis. §6(2)(2) UWG requires comparisons to address objectively verifiable, relevant, representative features — "what most teams use today" is neither identifiable nor verifiable, and "rework" has no operational definition. In German practice the substantiation burden sits with you, and vagueness is construed against the advertiser. The phrase also smuggles in a second unsupported claim: that spreadsheets-and-email *are* what most teams use. That's a market-share assertion needing its own source.

**2. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd"**
Disparagement risk under §6(2)(5) UWG. It targets a working method rather than a named competitor, which softens the exposure — but the register is derisive, and it lands harder in German localization, where there's no neutral equivalent for "crowd." Commercially it's worse than the legal risk: you are mocking the current daily practice of a large share of the regulatory consultants you're selling to.

**3. "We catch them before" — MDR Art. 7**
This is a performance claim. It must be consistent with the intended purpose in your technical documentation and supported by your clinical evaluation. "Catch them" also implies completeness — all errors, reliably — which creates a false impression of performance unless your validated scope actually covers that. Hedge to the validated scope (which rule sets, which document types).

### Substantive

**4. "still find their errors after submission"** — a negative performance claim about competing approaches. Same substantiation burden as the positive claim; right now it has none.

**5. Pathway mismatch.** Class I non-sterile / non-measuring / non-reusable-surgical devices are self-certified — there is no authority submission to fail. If "submission" means your *customers'* filings for their own devices, the copy needs to say so; as written it misdescribes the regulatory gate.

**6. HWG §3** prohibits misleading medical-device advertising even to Fachkreise. Most §11 restrictions don't apply to a professional audience, but §3 does. And if you add any figure sourced from a study, §6 HWG requires the source be identified and quoted accurately — so the fix in finding 1 has to name its methodology, not just footnote "internal data."

**7. Register.** The fragment ("We catch them before.") and the idiom won't survive translation. German RA/QM buyers convert on specificity — rule counts, standards referenced, named integrations — not swagger.

---

### Rewrite A — if you have the data

> **DE:** Fehler finden, bevor eingereicht wird. In einer kontrollierten Untersuchung mit [n] Konformitätsbewertungsverfahren senkte [Produkt] den Nachbearbeitungsaufwand gegenüber der Bearbeitung mit Tabellenkalkulation und E-Mail um [x] % (Median, [Zeitraum]; Methodik: [Link]).

Requires: a defined comparator (spreadsheet+email workflow, described), a defined metric (e.g. deficiency findings per dossier, or hours to close them), sample size, timeframe, and a public methodology page.

### Rewrite B — if you don't

> **DE:** Prüfen Sie Ihre technische Dokumentation auf Vollständigkeit und Konsistenz, bevor Sie einreichen — mit [n] automatisierten Prüfregeln, abgeleitet aus MDR Anhang II und III.

Drops the comparison entirely, which removes the §6 UWG exposure. Weaker hook, shippable today.

### Before either goes live

Build a claims matrix: every claim in one column, its evidence in the next, the technical-documentation or clinical-evaluation section it traces to in the third. For a device this isn't just legal hygiene — an inconsistency between marketing claims and the intended purpose in your tech docs is a findable nonconformity.

I could not verify this — WebSearch was denied in the current permission mode, and the claims-review skill I'd normally lean on carries statute text only (MDR Art. 7, HWG, UWG), with case law explicitly out of scope. So I can't hand you a verified citation right now.

I'm not going to give you a half-remembered case number as "the leading case" when you're about to put it behind published copy in an Abmahnung market. Here's what I can honestly separate:

## What I recall, flagged by confidence

**Reasonably confident** — the general German standard for health-related advertising ("Strengeprinzip"): health claims face heightened requirements of accuracy, clarity and unambiguity, and the advertiser carries the burden of showing the claim is backed by **gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis** (secured scientific knowledge). This is a reversal of the normal UWG burden — you prove it's substantiated; the claimant does not have to prove it false.

**Moderately confident** — the case I believe you're reaching for is **BGH, Urt. v. 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649), which addressed advertising with a study result and held the underlying study must satisfy the recognised rules and principles of scientific research — in practice the "Goldstandard" of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of adequate size, published so it is open to scientific scrutiny.

**Low confidence, and this is the real gap** — whether that is the leading authority *for medical devices specifically*. My recollection is that the BGH line developed on medicinal products (Arzneimittel), and that its extension to Medizinprodukte runs substantially through OLG decisions applying it by analogy. I would not assert the device-specific leading case without checking.

Treat all three as `[verify]`. Do not put any of it in a file that goes to a regulator or opposing counsel until it's been checked against a real source.

## The part that doesn't depend on the citation

Your actual question is whether n=12, unpublished, in-house carries "Heals wounds 40% faster." It does not, under any plausible formulation of the standard:

- **Unpublished** fails the scrutiny element outright — no version of this test is satisfied by evidence the scientific community cannot examine.
- **In-house** goes to independence, which is exactly what the heightened standard is aimed at.
- **n=12** will not support a quantified effect size. Even setting the case law aside, a 40% figure from twelve subjects is not a finding you can defend.
- **"40% faster" is comparative** — faster than what? Standard of care, no dressing, a named competitor? This independently engages UWG § 6(2) no. 2, which requires comparison on *verifiable* characteristics `[verified]`. A reader cannot verify against a study they cannot obtain, so the unpublished status is fatal on this limb too, separately from the efficacy standard.

That conclusion is robust whether or not I've got the case number right. The citation matters for how you *argue* it; the answer to "can we run this copy" is no either way.

## What I'd suggest

Two things I can do — tell me which:

1. **Re-run the search with permission granted**, and come back with a verified citation, the exact operative wording, and specifically whether the device line runs through the BGH or the OLGs. This is the one I'd recommend before anything goes to counsel.
2. **Run the full claims review** on the wound-dressing copy against the statute text I do have verified. For that I'd need the **intended purpose as assessed** in your technical documentation / DoC — without it I can't assess MDR Art. 7(d), which is the limb device marketing trips most often — plus whether the audience is Fachkreise or Publikum.

Either way, this needs a Fachanwalt für Wettbewerbsrecht before publication. I can get you a tight brief to walk in with; I can't clear the copy.

## What I can tell you with confidence

Here's the thing: **your claim has problems that don't depend on the case law at all.** Even if the BGH standard turned out to be generous, this copy doesn't clear the statute.

# Device Claims Review: "Heals wounds 40% faster."

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Wound dressing — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Not stated — must confirm, see below
**Markets:** DE (EU baseline also applies)

### Summary

1 claim reviewed. 1 needs rewriting; the quantified figure cannot survive in its current form.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed

### Finding

**Claim:** "Heals wounds 40% faster."
**Breach:** UWG § 5 (misleading — undefined comparator) `[verified]`; UWG § 6(2) no. 2 if a competitor is identifiable `[verified]`
**Why:** "40% faster" is a comparative performance figure with **no stated baseline**. Faster than what — no dressing, standard gauze, a named competitor, moist wound therapy generally? The reader cannot locate the reference point, which is the core § 5 defect. If the market *can* tell who is meant, § 6 engages independently and § 6(2) no. 2 requires the comparison to be on characteristics that are **verifiable** — and an unpublished in-house study is by definition not verifiable by the reader. That limb fails on the publication status alone, before anyone examines your methodology.
**Also engaged:**
- **MDR Art. 7(a)** `[verified]` — ascribing a property the device has; turns on whether n=12 supports a 40% figure at all.
- **HWG § 3 no. 1** `[verified]` — therapeutic efficacy "die sie nicht haben," same dependency.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** `[verified]` — "Erfolg mit Sicherheit." Stated as a flat indicative ("heals … faster"), the copy reads as a promise rather than an average effect. This has no MDR Art. 7 equivalent and is one of the two most commonly tripped provisions in device marketing.
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** `[verified]` — *only if the audience is Publikum*: health "durch die Verwendung verbessert." Needs the audience answer.
**Evidence needed:** A stated comparator, and data that supports the magnitude against that comparator. n=12, unpublished, in-house does not get you to a defensible quantified superiority claim — and note that the verifiability problem under § 6(2) no. 2 is **not** cured by the study being methodologically sound. It's cured by publication.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix (paste-ready):**

> **Supports faster wound healing.**

or, if you want to keep the figure and are willing to publish:

> **In einer eigenen Anwendungsbeobachtung (n=12) heilten Wunden im Mittel 40 % schneller als unter [Komparator].** — requires the comparator named and the study published or at least made available on request.

The first option drops the number and the comparison, which removes the § 6 and § 5 exposure. The second keeps them and accepts that you must name the baseline and expose the study.

### Two things I need from you

1. **The intended purpose, verbatim from the DoC or technical documentation.** This is the one that worries me most. If your assessed intended purpose is something like "management of exuding wounds" — i.e. a *barrier and exudate-management* function — then a claim about **accelerating healing** may suggest a use outside what the conformity assessment covered. That's MDR Art. 7(d), and **limb (d) cannot be cured by evidence.** No study, however large, fixes it. It's fixed by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment. For a Class IIa dressing this is a realistic risk, not a theoretical one, and I can't assess it against a purpose I haven't seen.
2. **Audience — Fachkreise or Publikum?** A public, ungated web page is Publikum even if the tone is technical. This decides HWG § 11 no. 7.

### Not assessed

I raised no MDR Art. 7(c) finding. A wound dressing plausibly has likely risks worth surfacing (maceration, sensitisation, wounds requiring clinical assessment), but I have no IFU, and inferring a risk from the device category and then flagging the copy for omitting it produces an unfalsifiable finding. Worth checking the copy against your IFU's contraindications section.

### Provisions cited

| Provision | Reference file |
|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` |
| HWG § 3 nos. 1, 2(a); § 11(1) no. 7 | `references/hwg.md` |
| UWG § 5, § 6(2) no. 2 | `references/uwg.md` |

### Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**Three questions for counsel**, which double as the answer to what you originally asked:

1. What substantiation standard do German courts apply to quantified efficacy claims for Class IIa devices, and does the Arzneimittel case law transfer?
2. Does an unpublished in-house study satisfy UWG § 6(2) no. 2 verifiability under current practice, or does the figure require publication?
3. Does our assessed intended purpose support a healing-acceleration claim, or is that Art. 7(d) drift?

So I have two options and I'm taking the honest one: I'm not going to hand you a BGH docket number and a quoted holding from memory. In this specific area the risk isn't that I draw a blank — it's that I produce something *plausible*: right-shaped case name, near-right docket, a standard paraphrased just loosely enough to be wrong. You'd then take a quantified efficacy claim to market on it. A misremembered standard is worse than no standard here.

**What I can tell you, tagged `[verify]` and not as a holding:** the doctrine you're looking for runs under *gesundheitsbezogene Werbung* and the requirement of **"gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis"**, together with the allocation of the burden of proof onto the advertiser for health-related efficacy claims. Those are the right search terms to put in front of counsel. I can't reliably attach them to a leading case and its exact wording from here — that's precisely the part I'd be guessing at.

The statutory analysis lands hard enough that the BGH standard may not be your gating question.

**Claim:** "Heals wounds 40% faster."
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — *zur Täuschung geeignete Angaben über […] von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse* and *[…] Ergebnisse […] von Tests* `[verified]`
**Why:** The figure has no comparator on the face of the copy. Faster *than what* — untreated? standard gauze? a named competitor? A bare percentage with no baseline is capable of misleading independently of how good the underlying study is. This defect is not curable by more data.
**Call:** Needs rewording **and** substantiation

**Also engaged:**

- **HWG § 3 no. 1** `[verified]` — *therapeutische Wirksamkeit oder Wirkungen […] die sie nicht haben*. A quantified healing-rate claim is squarely this provision's shape. Whether it bites depends on whether 40% survives scrutiny.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** `[verified]` — *ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann*. Stated flat and unhedged, with no population or range, the copy reads as a promise rather than a finding. Cheap to cure with hedging; note the reference file flags this as one of the two most commonly tripped provisions in device marketing, with no clean Art. 7 equivalent.
- **UWG § 6(2) no. 2** `[verified]`, *if* the market can tell what you're comparing against — § 6(1) *erkennbar* is broad and doesn't require naming anyone. The sharp edge is **nachprüfbar**: an unpublished study means the reader cannot check the claim from public information. On the reference's reading, that fails no. 2 *even if the number is accurate*. Publishing the study is the fix.

I tried to verify the citations against the original judgment text, but WebSearch/WebFetch were denied in this session. What follows is from memory, and I've flagged where the wording needs checking before you rely on it. Re-enable web access and I'll pull the actual Leitsätze.

## The honest framing first

There is no BGH decision squarely on efficacy substantiation for a **medical device**. The standard you'll be held to is the BGH's general line on health-related advertising (Heilmittelwerberecht/UWG), which reaches Class IIa devices because:

- § 1(1) no. 1a HWG expressly extends the HWG to Medizinprodukte;
- MDR Art. 7 independently bans claims that mislead as to performance/clinical benefit;
- § 5 UWG applies on top.

So the "leading case" is a pharma case that the courts apply to devices.

## Leading case

**BGH, Urteil v. 6.2.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649). This is the most-cited articulation of the substantiation standard, later refined in **BGH, Urt. v. 7.5.2015 – I ZR 29/14 – "Äquipotenzangabe in Fachinformation."**

## The standard

Three components:

**1. Strengeprinzip.** Health-related advertising is subject to "besonders strenge Anforderungen an die Richtigkeit, Eindeutigkeit und Klarheit" — stricter than ordinary advertising, because of the protected legal interest.

**2. Level of evidence.** A claim of efficacy must correspond to *gesicherter wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnis* at the time it is made. The standard formulation of what that requires:

> eine randomisierte, placebokontrollierte Doppelblindstudie mit einer adäquaten statistischen Auswertung, die durch Veröffentlichung in den Diskussionsprozess der Fachwelt einbezogen worden ist

Treat that sentence as the operative test. The last clause is not decoration — an unpublished study, by definition, has not entered the professional discussion and does not qualify.

**3. Burden of proof.** Normally the claimant proves misleadingness. In health advertising the BGH shifts it: an advertiser who makes an efficacy claim carries the burden of proving its scientific soundness, and bears the risk if the claim was scientifically unsecured *at the time of publication*. You cannot cure it by generating evidence after an Abmahnung lands.

## Applied to "Heilt Wunden 40 % schneller"

This is close to a worst-case fact pattern under that test:

- **Unpublished** → fails the Fachdiskussion prong outright.
- **n=12** → cannot support a point estimate of 40 %. A quantified claim implies a precision the confidence interval won't carry.
- **In-house** → independence problem; German courts weigh sponsor studies skeptically.
- **Not stated as randomized/blinded/controlled** → if it's an open observational study, it isn't even the right study type.
- **"Faster" than what?** No comparator is named. Separate infringement under § 5 UWG. If the market reads it as against competitor dressings, § 6 UWG (vergleichende Werbung) kicks in and requires an objectively verifiable comparison of a typical, relevant characteristic.
- **MDR Art. 7** → the claim must also be consistent with your clinical evaluation and IFU. A claim your technical documentation doesn't support is a regulatory exposure, not just a competition-law one.

The practical risk in Germany isn't a court in the first instance — it's an Abmahnung from the Wettbewerbszentrale or a competitor, then a strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung.

## What would actually clear it

To keep "40 % schneller" you need an adequately powered RCT against a named comparator, published and peer-reviewed. There is no shortcut version of that. Attributing the weak study in the ad body ("in einer Anwendungsbeobachtung mit 12 Patienten…") is *less* dangerous but not safe — the BGH has held that citing a study that isn't gesicherte Erkenntnis can itself mislead, and § 3 HWG still bites. Realistic interim copy drops the number and the comparative entirely.

Two caveats: verify the German wording of the test against the original judgment before it goes into a legal memo, and get a Fachanwalt für gewerblichen Rechtsschutz to sign off before this copy ships. I can give you the doctrine; the sign-off has to be someone with liability.

# Device Claims Review: trade-press copy (3 sentences, 27 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Continuous ECG patch — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Fachkreise — cardiology trade press. HWG § 11 does **not** apply; § 3 does.
**Markets:** DE (EU-wide MDR Art. 7 applies regardless)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword, 2 substantiate/verify, 1 OK.

This copy is disciplined. It tracks the assessed intended purpose closely, carries the supervision condition, states no performance figure it would have to defend, and makes no comparison. **No breaches identified** against the provisions this review verifies. What remains is technical-file verification plus one optional tightening.

**Ready to publish:** see the gate at the end — I can't issue that clearance.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A wear-duration spec, not a clinical claim. "Single-lead" matches the assessed purpose exactly and does not overstate lead count — the frequent (a) shape here (implying multi-lead or 12-lead-equivalent capability) is absent.
**Evidence needed:** The validated maximum wear duration from the technical documentation — adhesive performance, battery life, and signal quality all held to 14 days, not 14 days as a best case in bench conditions. "Up to" is a defensible hedge only if 14 days is achievable in the assessed use conditions.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — *wesentliche Merkmale*, *Zwecktauglichkeit* — if 14 days is not the validated ceiling, or is achievable only outside normal use conditions.
**Call:** Verify

*Drafting note (not a finding):* the assessed purpose is limited to **adults**; this sentence states no population. Silence is not "suggesting uses" under Art. 7(d) — that limb needs an affirmative suggestion, and there is none — so I am not calling it a breach. But the restriction is free to add and closes the gap before anyone argues about it in a paediatric context.

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figure is stated, so nothing is ascribed under Art. 7(a) and no expected result is asserted. The exposure is not in what is said but in what arrives when a journalist requests it.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm (1) sensitivity/specificity data exists for **this** device in **this** configuration and for the arrhythmias covered by the intended purpose; (2) the package sent on request is complete — reference standard, population, arrhythmia subtypes, confidence intervals — not a selected headline pair. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` reaches "die Ergebnisse oder **wesentlichen Bestandteile** von Tests": sending a favourable subset while omitting an essential component of the study is where a data-on-request offer becomes misleading, even though the ad itself was clean.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]` — if the fulfilment material claims performance across arrhythmias the assessment does not cover. Art. 7 covers advertising and making available generally, so the material you send is in scope, not just the printed line.
**Call:** Needs substantiation — verify the fulfilment pack, not the sentence.

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Near-verbatim to the assessed purpose. It keeps the supervision condition and stays on "detection" rather than drifting to diagnosis or treatment — so HWG § 3 no. 1 (*therapeutische Wirksamkeit... die sie nicht haben*) `[verified]` is not engaged, and neither is Art. 7(b).
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

---

### Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation. I was not given the IFU, so I can't name a likely risk from supplied material — and inferring one from "it's a single-lead patch" would produce an unfalsifiable finding, so I'm not raising (c).

Two things genuinely reduce the (c) exposure on the face of this copy: "under healthcare professional supervision" and "detection" together signal that output requires clinical interpretation. That is the substance (c) usually asks for.

**Worth checking against the IFU:** whether it records a likely risk or limitation that belongs in trade-press copy — the usual candidates for this device type being interference/artefact conditions, skin reaction, or an explicit statement that the recording does not replace diagnostic ECG. If one is recorded, the proportionate fix for trade press is an IFU pointer, not patient-facing safety text.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Validated max wear duration under assessed use conditions (adhesive, battery, signal quality) | R&D / technical documentation owner |
| "sensitivity and specificity data available on request" | The actual fulfilment pack — completeness, population, arrhythmia subtypes covered | Clinical affairs |
| (c) omission check | Whether the IFU records a likely risk/limitation warranting a pointer | RA / IFU owner |
| Population scope | Confirm whether to add "in adults" | RA |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (not engaged)
- HWG § 11 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` — **not applicable**, audience is Fachkreise
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]` — not engaged, no comparison present

Not engaged, for the record: UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4 — the copy makes no claim about class, CE scope, notified-body involvement, or company credentials. HWG § 3a applies only to Arzneimittel and does not apply to devices.

## Optional revised copy, paste-ready

> "Continuous single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days. For use in adults under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."

Two changes: "in adults" added to match the assessed population, and "continuous" added to match the assessed purpose's own wording. Both are additive precision — neither narrows what you can say.

## Before "Ready to publish"

I can say the copy has no findings I can identify against the provisions I verify — this is clean copy, and the discipline of stating no performance figure in the ad itself is doing real work for you. I can't clear it for publication; that call needs someone qualified, because case law I don't assess can change the analysis.

One-page brief for counsel:

- **Asset:** 27-word trade-press copy, cardiology press, DE market, Class IIa continuous ECG patch.
- **Claims cleared:** supervision/detection claim (tracks assessed purpose verbatim); single-lead descriptor; no performance figures asserted.
- **Provisions checked:** MDR Art. 7(a)–(d); HWG § 3; HWG § 11 (inapplicable — Fachkreise); UWG § 5, § 6.
- **Three things to ask:**
  1. Does "up to 14 days" need a qualifying condition to be defensible, given how the wear duration was validated?
  2. Does the data-on-request offer create Abmahnung exposure through the fulfilment material, and should the pack be pre-cleared?
  3. Does omitting the "in adults" restriction create any Art. 7(d) argument, or is silence safe here?

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: trade-press copy (3 sentences, 34 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Continuous ECG patch — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; HWG § 3 does `[verified]`
**Markets:** DE (EU layer also applies)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword (cheap alignment, not a breach), 2 substantiate, 1 OK.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

This is disciplined copy. It tracks the intended purpose closely, carries the supervision condition rather than dropping it, and states no performance figure it would have to defend. There are no breaches I can identify on the material supplied. The two open items are evidence questions for the technical file, not claim defects.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** The intended purpose states "continuous single-lead ECG recording" but sets no duration, so 14 days is neither confirmed nor contradicted by the anchor I have. A wear-duration spec is not an indication claim, and nothing here suggests a use outside the assessed purpose.
**Evidence needed:** The validated maximum wear duration from the technical documentation — adhesive performance, battery life, and signal quality sustained across the full 14 days, not just achievable at best case.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]` and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — "wesentliche Merkmale … Zwecktauglichkeit" `[verified]` — if the validated wear duration is shorter than 14 days, or if 14 days is a battery figure rather than a validated recording figure.
**Call:** Verify
**Note:** "up to" does real work for you here — it is a ceiling, not a typical value. Keep it. Don't let anyone upgrade it to "14-day recording" without data supporting 14 days as routine.

Two words of drift worth closing, neither a breach:

- The copy drops **"continuous"**. The assessed purpose is continuous recording; a reader could take "recording for up to 14 days" as intermittent or triggered capture. Restoring the word costs nothing and aligns the copy with the certificate.
- The copy drops **"in adults"**. Silence about the population is not a limb (d) breach — (d) prohibits *suggesting* uses beyond the assessed purpose, and omission is not suggestion `[verified]`. But the population restriction is part of what was assessed, and unrestricted copy in cardiology trade press reaches paediatric electrophysiologists. Stating it is a one-word inoculation.

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figure is stated, so there is no performance assertion to be inaccurate. An offer to supply data is not itself a claim about what the data show.
**Evidence needed:** Confirmation that sensitivity and specificity data actually exist, and that they cover **arrhythmia detection as claimed** — the indication in the intended purpose — rather than, say, R-wave detection or signal-quality benchmarking. Check what the request fulfils in practice: the dataset, the comparator, and the arrhythmias covered.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**" `[verified]` — if the data supplied on request are narrower than the claim implies, or if a favourable subgroup is sent while the full-cohort result is withheld.
**Call:** Verify
**Watch this:** The data pack you send on request is itself in scope. MDR Art. 7 covers "advertising" without limiting it to the published asset `[verified]`, so the request-fulfilment document has to clear the same four limbs the headline copy does. Whoever fulfils these requests should be sending a fixed, reviewed pack — not a deck assembled per enquiry.

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Tracks the assessed intended purpose, and keeps the supervision condition in the claim rather than relegating it to small print. "In the detection of" is also *softer* than the intended purpose's "for the detection of" — it positions the device as contributing to a clinician-led process rather than delivering the detection itself. That is the right side of MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

---

### Provisions checked and not engaged

Recording these so you can see the perimeter was walked, not to pad the list:

- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** — guaranteed success `[verified]`. No "Erfolg mit Sicherheit" shape. "Up to" and "in the detection of" are both non-committal.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(b)** — no-harmful-effects `[verified]`. No safety or tolerability claim made.
- **HWG § 3 no. 3(b)** — claims about the maker `[verified]`. None made.
- **HWG § 11** — not applicable to Fachkreise `[verified]`.
- **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4** — status and Zulassung `[verified]`. The copy claims no class, no notified body, no certificate. Nothing to misstate. If a later draft adds "Class IIa" or an NB number, re-check it against the actual certificate scope.
- **UWG § 6** — comparative advertising `[verified]`. No competitor made erkennbar, directly or indirectly.

### Open question on limb (c) — I can't close this without the IFU

MDR Art. 7(c) is an omission test: copy containing nothing false still breaches it if it fails to inform of "a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose" `[verified]`.

This copy surfaces no limitation. I'm not raising it as a breach, because I would have to invent the risk from the device category to do so, and a (c) finding built that way is unfalsifiable. **Someone should check it against the IFU**: if the IFU records a likely risk or a material limitation for use as intended, trade-press copy this short would normally discharge (c) with an IFU pointer rather than reproducing the text. Trade press is not expected to carry patient-facing safety language.

Two mitigating factors already present: the copy names the supervision requirement, which surfaces that results need clinical interpretation, and it makes no diagnostic-autonomy claim.

## Recommended copy

Paste-ready, assuming the 14-day duration verifies:

> Continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults for wear periods of up to 14 days. For use under the supervision of a healthcare professional in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data available on request.

If the validated wear duration is shorter, substitute the validated figure — do not keep 14 days behind "up to".

If the IFU check turns up a likely risk, append: `Please refer to the instructions for use.`

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Validated maximum wear/recording duration — adhesion, battery, signal quality across the full period | Regulatory affairs / technical documentation owner |
| "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" | The actual dataset: which arrhythmias, which comparator, full-cohort results; plus the fixed pack sent on request | Clinical affairs |
| Limb (c) omission | Whether the IFU records a likely risk or limitation for use as intended | Regulatory affairs / IFU owner |
| German-language version | The intended purpose **as worded in German** in the DoC / technical documentation | Regulatory affairs |

That last row matters more than it looks. If this runs in German trade press, the German copy is the advertising, and the anchor for Art. 7(d) is the assessed intended purpose in its authoritative language. Translating the English marketing copy into German independently is how drift enters — "zur Erkennung" vs. "zur Unterstützung der Erkennung" is not a stylistic choice. Have the German copy tracked against the German intended purpose directly.

## On clearing this for publication

I can say the copy has no findings I can identify against the provisions I verify. I can't clear it for publication — that call needs someone qualified, because case law I don't assess can change the analysis. Here's the one-page brief to take to counsel:

**Asset:** 34-word trade-press claim block, German cardiology trade press, Class IIa continuous ECG patch.

**Claims cleared on the material supplied:** the supervision-and-indication sentence (tracks assessed intended purpose); the offer of sensitivity/specificity data on request (no figure asserted); the 14-day wear ceiling (subject to the duration evidence above).

**Provisions checked:** MDR Art. 7(a)–(d); HWG § 3 nos. 1, 2(a), 2(b), 3(b); HWG § 11 (scoped out — Fachkreise); UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4; § 6.

**The three questions to ask counsel:**

# Device Claims Review: trade-press copy, continuous ECG patch

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Continuous single-lead ECG patch — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — HWG § 11 not applied; see note below
**Markets:** EU / DE

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword (precautionary), 2 substantiate, 1 OK.

**No breaches identified** against the provisions I verify. The copy tracks the intended purpose closely and states the supervision condition rather than burying it — that is the main thing this kind of copy usually gets wrong.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Wear duration is a performance characteristic, not a use. It does not extend the intended purpose, so limb (d) is not engaged. The copy does, however, drop the population restriction ("in adults") that the assessed intended purpose carries.
**Evidence needed:** Validated maximum wear time from the technical documentation — the 14 days must be a substantiated device specification, not a best case. Confirm whether the IFU states 14 days or something shorter.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit") — **if** the 14 days is not supported in the technical file, or if this copy runs alongside imagery, captions or case examples involving paediatric patients. Silence about the adult restriction is not itself a suggestion of paediatric use, but a cardiology readership treats both populations, and restoring one word removes the question entirely.
**Call:** Needs rewording (precautionary) + Needs substantiation

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figures are stated, so there is nothing capable of misleading on the face of it. But UWG § 5(2) no. 1 expressly reaches "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**" — an offer of performance data is a statement about test results, and it represents that such data exists and supports the arrhythmia-detection claim.
**Evidence needed:** Three things: (1) the data actually exists and can be furnished on request without delay or gating; (2) it is clinical performance data for arrhythmia detection in the intended-purpose population, not bench or algorithm-only validation presented as clinical; (3) whoever fields the requests sends the full picture, including the comparator, reference standard and the arrhythmia subtypes studied. Sending a favourable subset is where this claim turns into a § 5(2) no. 1 problem.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — if what is sent on request is narrower than what the copy implies.
**Call:** Needs substantiation

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Reproduces the assessed intended purpose, including the supervision condition and the detection (not diagnosis, not treatment) framing. No implied clinical outcome, so limb (b) is not engaged; no capability beyond the assessment, so (a) and (d) are not engaged.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

---

### Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy is benefit-framed and surfaces no limitation beyond the supervision requirement. That requirement does useful work here: it tells the reader results need clinical interpretation, which is the omission that most often bites in monitoring-device copy.

I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk that belongs in the asset. I'm not going to infer one from the device category — that would be unfalsifiable. Check the IFU's warnings and contraindications section; if a likely risk in normal use is recorded there, the proportionate fix for trade press is an IFU pointer, not patient-facing safety text.

### Suggested revised copy (paste-ready)

> Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days. For use in adults under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data available on request.

One word added. If the IFU turns up a likely risk, append: "See instructions for use for warnings and contraindications."

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Validated maximum wear time; confirm it matches the IFU | R&D / regulatory affairs |
| "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" | The dataset itself; confirm it is clinical, covers the claimed arrhythmias, and that the fulfilment process sends it complete | Clinical affairs / medical affairs |
| Limb (c) | IFU warnings and contraindications — is there a likely risk in normal use? | Regulatory affairs |

## Notes on scope

**Audience.** Cardiology trade press is Fachkreise, so HWG § 11 does not apply and I have not assessed it. If this copy is reused on an ungated website, in a booth panel open to the public, or in a patient-facing channel, § 11 (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only, for devices) comes back into play and needs a fresh pass. Nothing in the current wording looks like a no. 7 problem — there is no "improve your heart health" or fear-of-not-using framing — but the re-check should be deliberate rather than assumed.

**HWG § 3.** No guarantee of success (no. 2(a)), no absence-of-side-effects claim (no. 2(b)), no claims about the manufacturer's credentials (no. 3(b)). Not engaged.

**UWG § 6.** No comparison, express or implied. Not engaged.

**Class IIa.** The copy makes no certification, class, or notified-body claim, so UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4 are not engaged. Worth keeping that way — if a CE badge or class reference is added to the layout, it needs to match the certificate scope exactly.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a), 2(b), no. 3(b); § 11(1) (scoping only) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, nos. 3–4; § 6 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## On clearing this for publication

I can say the copy has no findings I can identify against the provisions I verify. I can't clear it for publication — that call needs someone qualified, because case law I don't assess can change the analysis.

One-page brief for counsel: **asset** — three-sentence trade-press copy, Class IIa ECG patch, DE market, Fachkreise. **Cleared on the material supplied** — the supervision/detection sentence tracks the assessed intended purpose verbatim. **Provisions checked** — MDR Art. 7 all four limbs, HWG §§ 3 and 11, UWG §§ 5 and 6. **Open questions** — the three in the evidence table. **The three things to ask:** (1) does the 14-day figure match the IFU and the validated wear time; (2) is the sensitivity/specificity dataset clinical and complete enough that furnishing it on request cannot be read as cherry-picking under UWG § 5(2) no. 1; (3) does the IFU record a likely risk that Art. 7(c) requires surfacing even in trade press.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.
