graders.evidence:
## Bottom line

Three of the four claim elements need work before this can run. The copy is directionally compliant in tone (no lay-audience overreach, no comparative or superiority claims), but it **narrows nothing and substantiates nothing**: it drops a population restriction from the intended purpose, adds a duration claim the intended purpose doesn't contain, and makes a diagnostic-accuracy claim it refuses to disclose. The last of those is the one I'd expect a competitor or a Wettbewerbszentrale complaint to hit first.

Legal cites below are pointers for your regulatory/legal sign-off, not a substitute for it.

---

## Findings

### 1. "in adults" has been dropped — HIGH

Intended purpose: *"...in adults..."*. Copy: no population limit at all. To a cardiologist reading trade press, unrestricted phrasing reads as usable across the patient mix, including paediatric and adolescent patients.

This is promotion outside the intended purpose — the classic MDR Art. 7 case (misleading as to intended purpose) and, in Germany, also an Irreführung/§5a UWG exposure for omitting material limiting information.

**Fix:** "bei Erwachsenen" is non-negotiable and must appear in the same sentence as the recording claim, not in a footnote.

### 2. "up to 14 days" is a new claim not present in the intended purpose — HIGH

The intended purpose says "continuous" with no duration. So 14 days has to come from the technical documentation, and the IFU-stated maximum wear time must be **≥ 14 days**. If the IFU says 7 or 10, this is off-label promotion outright.

Even if 14 days is the labelled maximum, a "bis zu" claim has to be achievable in normal use, not in a best-case bench run. You need, in the TD: battery life and memory capacity at 14 days, signal quality maintained across the full duration (not just day 1), adhesive/skin-tolerance data at 14 days, and ideally actual wear-time distribution from the clinical or usability data. German courts have been unfriendly to "bis zu" claims where the typical result is materially lower.

**Fix:** tie it to the IFU — "bis zu 14 Tage Tragedauer gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung" — and hold the supporting evidence in the claims matrix.

### 3. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request." — HIGH, delete or complete

This is the weakest line and I'd treat it as a blocker. Two distinct problems:

**It's an unsubstantiated teaser.** The sentence has no informational content except the implication "our accuracy figures are good." A performance claim has to be verifiable at the point where it's made. HWG § 6 treats reference to studies/expert data without naming the author, the date of publication and the exact wording relied on as misleading — "auf Anfrage" is the opposite of that. It's also poor Fachkreise practice: an accuracy claim a cardiologist cannot check is worth less to them than no claim at all.

**Sensitivity/specificity drift toward a diagnostic claim.** Your intended purpose is *detection*. Se/Sp are diagnostic-test accuracy metrics measured against a reference standard, and quoting them bare positions the patch as a diagnostic test — arguably ascribing a function the device doesn't have (MDR Art. 7(1)(b)). Whatever figures you publish must be scoped: **which arrhythmia, against which reference standard, in which population, n, with confidence intervals, and whether the figure is for the algorithm alone or for the algorithm plus professional over-read.** Those are very different numbers and the second is what the intended purpose actually describes.

**Fix:** publish the numbers with the citation, or cut the sentence. There is no compliant middle position.

### 4. "cardiac arrhythmias" unqualified, with no limitation statement — MEDIUM

Mirroring the intended purpose protects you on scope, but if your accuracy evidence covers only AF (the usual case for single-lead patches), the unqualified plural outruns the evidence the moment you attach Se/Sp to it. Separately, MDR Art. 7(1)(d) is about failing to inform of likely risk: a single-lead trace supports no ischaemia assessment, no axis or localisation, limited P-wave morphology, and — unless you have it — no real-time alerting.

**Fix:** one short limitation line. This helps you with the audience anyway; cardiologists read its absence as evasion.

### 5. No device identification, manufacturer, or IFU reference — MEDIUM

HWG § 4 Pflichtangaben are a medicines regime, so there is no statutory mandatory-text block for a device ad here. But German Fachkreise practice, and § 5a UWG, expect: product name, "Medizinprodukt", manufacturer/authorised rep, and a pointer to the Gebrauchsanweisung for risks. On CE marking: use it per MDR Art. 20 if you use it at all — don't set it decoratively, don't render the class number as part of it, and only pair the notified-body number with the marking itself.

### 6. Run it in German — MEDIUM

German market, German trade press. Beyond the audience point, the intended-purpose wording you quote should track your **German-language** labelling/IFU as closely as the sentence allows, so the claim-to-IFU traceability in your claims matrix is one-to-one rather than routed through a translation.

### 7. Watch the verb in future drafts — LOW

"Recording"/"Aufzeichnung" is correct and matches the intended purpose. Do not let this drift to "Monitoring", "Überwachung" or "Echtzeit" in later versions unless the device genuinely has that function — that's a direct Art. 7(1)(b) problem.

---

## Revised copy (DE, primary)

> **[Produktname] – kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung bei Erwachsenen**
>
> Tragedauer bis zu 14 Tage gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung. Zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal.
>
> Sensitivität [X] % (95 %-KI [–]), Spezifität [Y] % (95 %-KI [–]) für die Erkennung von [Vorhofflimmern] gegenüber [Referenzstandard], n = [–]; [Autor et al., Zeitschrift, Jahr].
>
> Einkanal-Ableitung: keine Beurteilung einer Myokardischämie, kein Ersatz für ein 12-Kanal-EKG, keine Echtzeit-Alarmierung.
>
> Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIa. Hersteller: [–]. Weitere Informationen sowie Hinweise zu Risiken und Nebenwirkungen entnehmen Sie der Gebrauchsanweisung.

**English mirror, for internal review:**

> [Product] — continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults. Wear time up to 14 days per the instructions for use. For the detection of cardiac arrhythmias under the supervision of a healthcare professional. Sensitivity [X]% (95% CI [–]), specificity [Y]% (95% CI [–]) for the detection of [AF] versus [reference standard], n = [–]; [citation]. Single-lead recording: no assessment of myocardial ischaemia, not a substitute for a 12-lead ECG, no real-time alerting.

**If you cannot publish the figures yet**, cut the accuracy sentence entirely and lead on what you can substantiate:

> Kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung bei Erwachsenen, bis zu 14 Tage gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung, zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal. Klinische Bewertung und Leistungsdaten: [Studienname/Register, Publikationsstatus].

Naming the study and its status is defensible. "Available on request" is not.

---

## What I need confirmed before sign-off

1. **IFU maximum wear time** — the single fastest way this becomes an off-label problem. Must be ≥ 14 days.
2. **Source of the Se/Sp figures** — peer-reviewed publication, or CER-internal only? Internal-only figures can still be published, but the claim must state the source and you must be able to hand over the report unchanged on request.
3. **Scope of those figures** — arrhythmia(s), reference standard, population (does it match "adults"?), algorithm-alone vs. with over-read.
4. **Does the device alert in real time?** Determines whether my "keine Echtzeit-Alarmierung" line is correct or is itself a misstatement.
5. **German IFU wording for the intended purpose** — so the headline quotes it rather than paraphrasing a translation.

One process note: every claim above should sit in a claims-substantiation matrix mapping the claim text to the specific TD evidence (CER section, verification report, test report ID) and to the IFU wording it derives from. That matrix is what makes a Fachkreise ad defensible on a competitor challenge, and "available on request" is exactly the kind of line that exists when the matrix hasn't been built yet.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The copy is close but not shippable as-is. Two changes are required, one is a substantiation gate, and one is a distribution safeguard. Nothing here is misleading in the strong sense (no superiority, no diagnostic overreach) — the problems are omission and vagueness.

Framework in play: MDR Art. 7 (claims), §3 and §6 HWG (HWG applies to devices via §1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a), §5/§5a UWG. §4 HWG Pflichtangaben does not apply — that's medicines only.

## Must fix

**1. "in adults" has been dropped.** Your intended purpose is population-restricted; the copy is not. Cardiology trade press includes readers who treat adolescents, and an unrestricted "detection of cardiac arrhythmias" invites pediatric use the CE certificate doesn't cover. This is misleading by omission under MDR Art. 7(d) and the cleanest thing for a competitor or a Landgericht to point at. Add *bei Erwachsenen*.

**2. "up to 14 days" must match the IFU verbatim.** This number is not in the intended purpose you gave me, so I can't verify it. If the IFU says 14 days maximum wear per patch, fine. If it says 7 days with an optional second patch, "up to 14 days" is an off-label claim — the aggregate of two wear periods is not a 14-day device specification. Confirm against the IFU and the technical documentation, not against engineering's bench data.

## Should fix

**3. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" is the weakest line in the copy.** Three problems, in order of seriousness:

- Sensitivity and specificity are *per arrhythmia type*. An unqualified plural implies uniform accuracy across all arrhythmias in scope. AF detection performance is typically much better than, say, non-sustained VT; a blanket claim overstates the weaker endpoints.
- §6 HWG: where advertising invokes scientific findings, the source must be identified. "Available on request" arguably invokes without identifying. Defensible, but it's free to fix.
- It's bad Fachkreise copy. Cardiologists discount withheld numbers. Naming figures with a reference standard is more persuasive than a gate.

Give the numbers for the primary endpoint with n and comparator, and keep "full data on request" for the rest.

**4. "continuous" was dropped.** Your intended purpose says continuous; the copy says only "recording." No legal exposure, but consistency between ad and IFU wording is what makes an Art. 7 defence easy. Restore it.

**5. Copy is in English for a German market.** For Fachkreise this is generally tolerated, and cardiology trade press often runs English. But the intended-purpose sentence specifically should mirror the German IFU wording — divergence between the German IFU and an English paraphrase in advertising is the exact seam a §3 HWG challenge opens.

## Distribution safeguard

If this runs anywhere reachable by lay readers (publisher website, LinkedIn, congress microsite rather than print only), gate it to Fachkreise. §11 HWG restrictions on Publikumswerbung do reach medical devices, and specialist-register performance claims presented to laypersons are a separate exposure from anything above.

## Revised copy

German, IFU-aligned:

> Kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung über bis zu 14 Tage. Zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen bei Erwachsenen unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal. Sensitivität [x %] / Spezifität [y %] für [Vorhofflimmern], [Studienkürzel], n = [n], Referenzstandard [12-Kanal-EKG / Holter]. Vollständige Leistungsdaten auf Anfrage.
>
> Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIa. CE-Kennzeichnung gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745.

English equivalent if the placement is English-language:

> Continuous single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days. For the detection of cardiac arrhythmias in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional. Sensitivity [x %] / specificity [y %] for [atrial fibrillation], [study], n = [n], reference standard [12-lead ECG / Holter]. Full performance data on request.

## Substantiation checklist before release

- IFU maximum wear duration equals 14 days as a single period
- CE certificate scope covers the adult indication and the arrhythmia classes implied
- Sensitivity/specificity figures traceable to a clinical evaluation in the technical documentation, with the population matching "adults"
- Reference standard stated and defensible
- Claims log updated so the ad text is reviewable against Art. 7 later

The last item matters more than it looks — Art. 7 defensibility is mostly about being able to show the claim was derived from the technical documentation at the time it was made.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not ready to run. Three blocking issues, all traceable to the same root cause: the copy silently *narrows* the intended purpose in one place and *widens* it in two others. Under MDR Art. 7 and § 3 HWG the safe pattern for Fachkreiswerbung is that every element of the intended purpose survives into the ad, and nothing is added that isn't in the CE-approved technical documentation.

One caveat: web access was denied this session, so I could not re-verify the statutory cites below. They're from memory and I'm confident on MDR Art. 7 and §§ 3, 6, 11 HWG — have legal confirm the paragraph numbers before you rely on them in a written sign-off.

## Blocking

**1. "in adults" has been dropped.** Your intended purpose is restricted to adults; the copy carries no population limit. To a cardiology readership — a large share of whom see paediatric or adolescent patients — an unqualified "single-lead ECG recording" reads as unrestricted. That is promotion outside the intended purpose (MDR Art. 7(a), § 3 Nr. 1 HWG). Non-negotiable fix: `bei Erwachsenen`.

**2. "up to 14 days" is not in the intended purpose.** It may still be fine, but only if the maximum wear time is stated in the IFU and supported in the technical documentation (adhesive validation, battery, signal quality over the full period). If the IFU says 7 days, or says 14 days only under stated conditions, the ad exceeds the CE-approved claim. Separately, "bis zu" claims are judged under § 5 UWG against what a non-trivial share of real users actually achieve, not a best-case bench figure — so carry the IFU's own qualifier across rather than the bare number.

**3. "Sensitivity and specificity" may claim a function the device doesn't have.** Your intended purpose is *recording* ECG *for the detection of* arrhythmias by a supervising HCP. Sensitivity and specificity are diagnostic-accuracy metrics, and offering them invites the reader to infer the device itself detects and classifies arrhythmias. Two possibilities:

- If the figures come from an **automated detection/classification algorithm**, that function is absent from your stated intended purpose. That's MDR Art. 7(a) — ascribing a function the device does not have — and it also raises a classification question you'd want closed before publishing, since an arrhythmia-detection algorithm engages Rule 11.
- If the figures are **system-level** (patch plus HCP over-read), the number is meaningless in the ad without its comparator and reference standard.

Which one it is determines whether this line can run at all. I'd resolve this before touching the wording.

## Should fix

**4. "Data available on request" is the weak form of this claim.** You make an implicit accuracy claim and withhold the substantiation — the classic shape for a § 3 HWG / § 5a UWG challenge, and a routine Abmahnung target for competitors and the Wettbewerbszentrale. Note also § 6 Nr. 3 HWG: where advertising refers to scientific publications, it must name author, date and source. Cite the study inline. For Fachkreise a real citation is more persuasive than a teaser anyway.

**5. "Continuous" was dropped.** It's in your Zweckbestimmung. Reusing the intended purpose's own vocabulary verbatim is the cheapest defence you have; there's no upside to paraphrasing it away.

**6. No limitation statement.** Single-lead is not a 12-lead diagnostic ECG. MDR Art. 7(c) prohibits creating a false impression regarding diagnosis. Your readership knows the difference, but one clause costs nothing.

**7. Language.** The copy is in English for a German market. The intended-purpose sentence must be the verbatim German from the CE-approved IFU, not a fresh translation — a translation drift here recreates issues 1–3 by accident.

**8. Housekeeping.** No manufacturer identification, device name, CE mark or "Gebrauchsanweisung beachten" pointer. The Arzneimittel-style Pflichtangaben regime in § 4 HWG doesn't apply to devices, but German trade publishers generally expect these, and without a device name the claim isn't traceable to a specific CE-certified configuration.

## Suggested revision

Assuming issue 3 resolves in favour of a validated algorithm and the IFU supports 14 days:

> **[Produktname]** – kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung bei Erwachsenen über bis zu 14 Tage.\*
> Zur Anwendung unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen. Einkanal-Ableitung; die Befundung erfolgt durch medizinisches Fachpersonal.
> Sensitivität XX %, Spezifität XX % gegenüber [Referenzstandard] ([Autor] et al., [Jahr], [Zeitschrift]; n = XXX).
>
> \*Maximale Tragedauer gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung.
> [Hersteller, Anschrift] · CE [NB-Nr.] · Bitte Gebrauchsanweisung beachten.

## What the copy gets right

Worth keeping as-is: no comparative or superiority claim, no "Goldstandard"-type language, the HCP supervision condition is retained, and it stops short of claiming diagnosis. It's an under-claimed ad with scope errors, not an over-claimed one — the fixes are additive.

## Open questions for you

1. What does the IFU state as maximum wear time, and under what conditions?
2. Do the sens/spec figures describe an algorithm or a system including human over-read? What was the reference standard and the study population?
3. Is automated arrhythmia detection inside the CE-certified intended purpose? The intended purpose as you've quoted it says no — if the technical file says yes, the quoted Zweckbestimmung is out of date.

## Verdict: don't publish as written

Two of the three elements are hard blockers under French law, independent of MDR.

### 1. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" — prohibited

French public-facing advertising for a medical device may not refer to a recommendation from scientists, health professionals, or people whose notoriety could encourage use (Code de la santé publique, advertising content rules at Art. R.5213-1 et seq., mirroring the medicinal-product regime). Because this page is ungated consumer-facing, it is "publicité auprès du public" and the prohibition applies squarely. There's no disclaimer that fixes it — the endorsement itself is the violation, so the line has to come out.

Two aggravating factors:
- **If Prof. Dubois is real and compensated**, you also hit the anti-gift/transparency regime (Art. L.1453-1 et seq. CSP): the benefit and the link must be declared, and paying an HCP for a public endorsement is itself exposed.
- **If Prof. Dubois is fictional or a composite**, it's an independent misleading-commercial-practice issue under Art. L.121-2 Code de la consommation.

### 2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — prohibited

DM advertising to the public may not make abusive, alarming or misleading use of fear or of references to disease. "Don't gamble with your heart" is a pure fear appeal tied to cardiac risk; it's the textbook case the rule targets. Also engages MDR Art. 7 (misleading presentation), since it implies the monitor mitigates cardiac risk — which is not its intended purpose. It diagnoses nothing and treats nothing; it measures.

### 3. "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — needs substantiation or removal

Two problems:
- **Intended purpose (MDR Art. 7(d))**: check this against your IFU and CE technical documentation. If the IFU doesn't prescribe indefinite daily measurement, the copy suggests a use outside the assessed intended purpose.
- **Clinically off-label as consumer advice**: standard home-BP protocols (ESH/ESC) specify measurement *schedules* — e.g. 7 consecutive days morning and evening around a consultation — not open-ended daily self-measurement, which is associated with over-measurement anxiety. Telling every reader to measure daily, with no medical framing, also edges toward making the medical consultation look superfluous, itself a prohibited content element.

### 4. Missing mandatory content

The copy has none of what French DM public advertising must include: device designation, intended purpose, information needed for correct use, an express invitation to read the instructions, and the mandatory medical-device mention. Get the exact current wording of the mention from your regulatory affairs team / ANSM guidance rather than from this review — the phrasing is prescribed and has been revised.

### 5. Two things to confirm with regulatory affairs

- **Reimbursement status.** If the device is LPPR-listed / reimbursable, public advertising is prohibited outright, not merely restricted.
- **Visa PM.** Prior ANSM authorisation applies to the higher-risk classes and to certain listed devices; Class IIa is normally outside it, but confirm your specific device isn't on the arrêté list.

## Suggested direction

Drop the endorsement and the fear hook entirely; sell accuracy and clinical validation instead of dread.

> « [Nom du produit] — tensiomètre électronique de bras pour la mesure de la pression artérielle à domicile. Validé cliniquement selon [protocole/norme]. Mesurez selon le rythme indiqué par votre médecin et conformément à la notice. »
> + intended purpose, correct-use information, invitation to read the notice, and the mandatory DM mention.

If you want third-party credibility to replace Prof. Dubois, the compliant route is **clinical validation** — reference the validation protocol (e.g. ISO 81060-2 / the STRIDE BP listing) as a factual, verifiable device property, rather than a named practitioner's opinion.

One note outside your stated scope, for future reuse only: this copy would fail German HWG § 11 on both the same grounds, so treat it as France-only-and-broken rather than France-only-issue.

---

### Blocker 1 — Endorsement by a named healthcare professional

"Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue."

French medical-device advertising rules prohibit public-facing ads containing any element referring to a **recommendation by scientists, health professionals, or persons whose celebrity could encourage use** of the device. This is the medical-device analogue of the long-standing medicines rule (Art. R.5122-4 CSP, from Art. 90 of Directive 2001/83/EC), which France extended to DM.

- Confidence: **high** on the prohibition itself; **medium** on the exact citation — I believe it sits in the R.5213-1 *et seq.* block (décret n° 2012-743 of 9 May 2012 on DM advertising). Confirm the subparagraph.
- ANSM's DM advertising guidance and the ARPP "produits de santé" recommendation both independently ban HCP testimonials, so even setting the statute aside you'd fail self-regulatory review.
- There's no fix by disclosure. Adding "avis personnel" or a paid-relationship disclaimer does not cure this — the prohibition is on the element's presence, not on undisclosed bias. **Delete it.**

Two knock-on exposures worth flagging to whoever commissioned the copy:

- **The physician's own exposure.** The Code de déontologie médicale bars a doctor from lending their name to commercial promotion (Art. R.4127-13 and R.4127-19-1/R.4127-20 CSP; high confidence on substance). If Prof. Dubois agreed to this, he's facing Ordre des médecins disciplinary risk, not just you. Someone should tell him before this ships.
- **Transparency.** If there's any remuneration or benefit in the relationship, it must be declared under the Sunshine/anti-cadeaux regime (Art. L.1453-1 CSP, Transparence Santé). Publishing the endorsement while the link is undeclared compounds the problem.

### Blocker 2 — Fear-based appeal

"Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur."

DM public advertising may not suggest that the user's health could be **affected by not using** the device, and may not use elements likely to cause alarm. "Don't gamble with your heart" does exactly the first and arguably the second: it frames non-use as risking cardiac harm.

- Confidence: **high** on substance (same R.5213 block; mirrors R.5122-4 for medicines). Same citation caveat.
- This also engages **MDR Art. 7** (Reg. (EU) 2017/745), which prohibits text that misleads the user regarding the device's intended purpose or that suggests uses not covered by the intended purpose. A BP monitor measures; it does not protect your heart. Art. 7 is directly applicable and travels regardless of market.

---

### Secondary issues

**"Mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — clinical instruction beyond intended purpose.** This is the subtlest problem and I'd push back on it even after the two deletions. You're issuing an unsupervised measurement protocol. French/ESH home-monitoring guidance is built around defined measurement series (typically morning-and-evening over ~3–7 consecutive days before a consultation), not indefinite daily self-measurement for the general public. Two consequences:

1. If your IFU-stated intended purpose doesn't specify a daily regimen, the copy claims a use the device isn't cleared for → MDR Art. 7 again.
2. Undirected daily measurement in normotensive users generates noise, and the copy gives no framing for interpreting it — this is the pattern that produces health anxiety and inappropriate self-management.

Replace with a pointer to the notice and to the user's physician for measurement rhythm.

**Missing mandatory mentions.** Public DM advertising must carry a minimum content set — device name, intended purpose, manufacturer where applicable, and an express invitation to read the notice/labelling carefully (R.5213-1 CSP; **medium-high** confidence). Your copy has none of these. Verify also whether the current mandatory CE/regulated-device statement applies in the form required today; I recall a required "dispositif médical réglementé portant le marquage CE" mention but can't confirm its current wording without Légifrance.

**Typo.** "coeur" → "cœur". Ligature is standard on a French-language site.

### Two gating questions before any version ships

1. **Is the device reimbursed (LPPR / prise en charge)?** If yes, public advertising is *prohibited outright* (Art. L.5213-3 CSP, subject to narrow ministerial exceptions) and no rewrite saves the page. Most home BP monitors in France are OTC and not reimbursed, so this probably clears — but confirm, because it's dispositive.
2. **Does this device need a prior ANSM advertising authorisation (visa PP)?** Certain DM require pre-clearance of public ads under Art. L.5213-4 CSP, with the list fixed by arrêté. I do **not** know whether Class IIa home BP monitors are on the current list, and I won't guess. Check with ANSM or your regulatory counsel — if a visa applies, timeline matters more than wording.

---

### Suggested compliant direction

> **Autotensiomètre [Nom du produit]**
> Mesurez votre tension artérielle à domicile et conservez un suivi de vos mesures à partager avec votre médecin.
> Votre médecin vous indiquera à quel rythme effectuer vos mesures.
>
> [Nom du fabricant]. Ceci est un dispositif médical. Lisez attentivement la notice avant utilisation.

This keeps the actual selling proposition — at-home measurement, a record you can bring to a consultation — while dropping the endorsement, the fear frame, and the unsupervised protocol. Have regulatory affairs confirm the mandatory-mention block against current text and add the CE statement in its required form.

One note on scope: you flagged France-only and not Germany, so I've stayed out of the HWG. Worth knowing that it wouldn't change the outcome — German §11(1) HWG bans HCP endorsement and fear appeals too, and MDR Art. 7 applies EU-wide. So the rewrite above is portable if the market ever expands; the France-specific parts are the mandatory mentions and the visa PP question.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict: do not publish as written

Both sentences are problems, and the France-only scoping doesn't rescue either one — they're violations *under French law specifically*, not spillover risk from Germany.

---

### 1. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" — prohibited outright

French law bans referencing a recommendation from scientists or health professionals in advertising for medical devices **directed at the public**. This is the medical-device analogue of the long-standing rule for medicines (Art. R.5122-4 CSP); for DM it comes from the advertising regime introduced by Décret n° 2012-743 (Arts. L.5213-1 et seq. / R.5213-x CSP). Verify the exact article number with your regulatory affairs team, but the substance is settled and ANSM enforces it.

There is no fix by rewording. "Recommandé par", "approuvé par", "choisi par les cardiologues", "conçu avec des cardiologues" — all fail. The endorsement has to come out entirely for public-facing copy. It is permissible in materials addressed exclusively to health professionals, which is a gated channel you don't have here.

Three collateral exposures worth flagging even if you drop the line:

- **The physician's own risk.** Code de déontologie médicale (Art. R.4127-13) bars a doctor from lending their name to commercial promotion. You'd be exposing Pr. Dubois to CNOM disciplinary action.
- **Loi anti-cadeaux** (L.1453-3 et seq. CSP): if any consideration flowed to Dubois, the arrangement needs to fit an authorised exception, with ANSM/CNOM formalities.
- **Transparency**: any link of interest must be declared on transparence.sante.gouv.fr. A published endorsement plus an undeclared payment is the combination that draws journalist attention.

### 2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — prohibited fear appeal

Public DM advertising may not suggest that the user's health could be **affected by not using** the device. "Don't gamble with your heart" is exactly that construction: implied cardiac consequence for non-use. Same regime as above, and it also runs into MDR Art. 7, which prohibits claims that mislead or exploit anxiety about health status.

The general obligation that DM advertising be objective and promote *bon usage* (L.5213-2) compounds it — the sentence is pure affect, no informational content.

### 3. "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — off-label frequency, and clinically wrong for France

Two separate defects:

- **Beyond intended purpose.** If your IFU doesn't prescribe daily measurement, promoting it violates MDR Art. 7(d) (suggesting uses other than the stated intended purpose). Check the IFU before anything else here.
- **Contradicts French practice.** HAS-endorsed automesure guidance is the *règle des 3* — three measurements morning, three evening, three consecutive days, ahead of a consultation. Not indefinite daily measurement by the general population. Recommending daily self-measurement to an ungated consumer audience promotes non-rational use, and for anxious users it's actively counterproductive.

Frequency guidance should be deferred to the prescriber, not asserted in an ad.

### 4. Missing mandatory mentions

Public advertising for a DM in France must carry specified content: device name, its intended purpose/destination, the manufacturer, an explicit indication that it is a medical device, and an invitation to read the instructions for use carefully. Your copy has none of these. Whatever the final wording, that block has to be present on the page.

### 5. Check whether you need an ANSM visa

Some DM categories require prior ANSM authorisation (*visa PP*) before public advertising, per L.5213-4 and the implementing arrêté listing concerned categories. I don't believe home BP monitors are on that list, but I'm not confident enough for you to rely on it — confirm against the current arrêté, since it's been amended.

---

## On the Germany point

The France-only scoping is the right instinct but irrelevant here. Germany's HWG §11(1) No. 2 bans HCP endorsements too, so the German position is the same, and German exposure is worse in kind (competitor and Wettbewerbszentrale actions under UWG, not just regulator action). A French-language page on a .fr domain with no DE fulfilment is a reasonable targeting defence — but it doesn't matter, because the copy is unlawful in its home market anyway.

## Suggested compliant direction

> Suivez votre tension artérielle chez vous, simplement.
> [Nom du produit] est un autotensiomètre, dispositif médical de classe IIa marqué CE, fabriqué par [Fabricant].
> Demandez à votre médecin ou à votre pharmacien à quelle fréquence mesurer votre tension.
> Lisez attentivement la notice avant utilisation.

Objective, no endorsement, no fear, frequency handed to the professional, mandatory mentions in place. If you want emotional pull, put it on ease of use and continuity of care with the doctor — not on consequences of inaction.

Minor: the original should be `cœur`, not `coeur`.

One caveat — I'm giving you the regulatory substance with high confidence but I'd have your RA function confirm the precise R.5213-x article numbers and the current visa arrêté scope before this goes into a compliance record.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: congress booth panel (24 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent — Class IIb, CE marked, notified body involved
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed**
**Audience:** Fachkreise (interventional cardiologists at a congress booth) — HWG § 11 does not apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU)

> I can review limbs (a), (b) and (c) without the intended purpose, but (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I cannot assess it against a purpose I have not seen. Can you paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC? For this asset it matters specifically for "across the full lesion", which is where I'd expect (d) to bite if it bites anywhere.

## Summary

5 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 2 OK-subject-to-verification.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "across the full lesion"
**Breach:** none identifiable on the material supplied — but this is the highest-risk phrase in the asset and I cannot close it without the intended purpose
**Why:** "Full lesion" is doing two jobs at once. Read as a *device property*, it asserts drug delivery over the entire lesion, when a DES elutes from the stented segment — geographic miss is the normal failure mode, so MDR Art. 7(a) "ascribing functions and properties which the device does not have" [verified] is in play if the release data don't support it. Read as an *indication*, "full lesion" with no length, diameter or lesion-type qualifier suggests use on any lesion, which engages Art. 7(d) [verified] if the assessed intended purpose is narrower (typical DES certificates carry a labelled length/diameter matrix and exclude lesion types).
**Evidence needed:** the assessed intended purpose and the labelled size matrix; drug-release/distribution data across the stented segment. Note the two cure paths differ — the (a) reading is curable by data, the (d) reading is **not** curable by data, only by narrowing the phrase or extending the conformity assessment.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit", if the phrase reaches lesions outside the labelled range
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "across the stented segment", plus the labelled length and diameter range. That keeps the intent (uniform elution, no gap) and removes the indication reading entirely.

---

**Claim:** "Approved and available now"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** The device is CE marked with notified-body involvement, so there is a real certificate behind the word. But "approved" is not what a CE mark is — there is no authority *Zulassung* for a device, and UWG § 5(2) no. 4 [verified] reaches "Aussagen oder Symbole, die sich auf eine **Zulassung** des Unternehmers oder der Waren oder Dienstleistungen beziehen". Naming the actual basis costs three words and removes the ambiguity. A Fachkreise audience is less likely to be misled, which is why I'm not calling this a breach — but the § 5(1) materiality filter ("geeignet, ... zu einer geschäftlichen Entscheidung zu veranlassen") is easily met at a booth where the purchasing decision is being made in the room.
**Evidence needed:** certificate scope and NB number; confirmation the certificate covers the configurations being promoted
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 [verified] — if the certificate is narrower than the range shown at the booth, or if "approved" is read as an authority approval
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "CE marked under MDR (Class IIb, NB [number])."

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A mechanistic claim, not a clinical-outcome claim — it does not promise an outcome, so HWG § 3 no. 2(a) "Erfolg mit Sicherheit" [verified] is **not** engaged, and I'm not raising it. But "sustained" is unquantified, and § 5(2) no. 1 "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" [verified] plus MDR Art. 7(a) [verified] both turn on whether the elution kinetics in the technical file support the word.
**Evidence needed:** elution/pharmacokinetic release profile from the technical documentation, with the release period
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** "Sustained sirolimus release over [X] days" — a number is both more persuasive to this audience and cheaper to defend than an adjective.

---

**Claim:** "available now" (availability limb)
**Breach:** none
**Why:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 lists **Verfügbarkeit** among the wesentliche Merkmale [verified]. Not misleading on what I have; it is a fact I cannot check.
**Evidence needed:** confirmation that all promoted sizes are orderable in Germany on the date of the congress — not launch-pending, not limited release
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "Our sirolimus-eluting stent"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Composition claim. HWG § 3 no. 3(a) [verified] covers untrue statements "über die Zusammensetzung oder Beschaffenheit". Straightforwardly fine if the drug matches the DoC.
**Evidence needed:** DoC drug identity (trivial check)
**Call:** OK

---

### On limb (c) — not raised, and here's why

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I am **not** raising Art. 7(c) on it.

> The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU.

I could guess at risks from the device category, but a (c) finding built by inference from "it's a stent" is unfalsifiable — every benefit-framed ad omits something inferable. Name the risk from the IFU and I'll assess it properly. Practically: for a 24-word booth panel aimed at Fachkreise, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix if (c) does bite, not patient-facing safety text.

### Provisions checked and not engaged

- **HWG § 11** — Fachkreise audience, does not apply. Flagging one thing: if this panel is reused on an ungated website or in social posts from the booth, the audience changes and § 11(1) no. 7 [verified] becomes live. Only nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 apply to devices.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a) / 2(b)** — no outcome guarantee, no no-side-effects claim.
- **HWG § 3a** — Arzneimittel only. Does not apply to devices; note this in case anyone reaches for it because the copy says "approved".
- **UWG § 6** — no comparison, express or implied. No competitor is erkennbar.

## Revised copy, paste-ready

> **[Brand] sirolimus-eluting coronary stent.** Sustained sirolimus release over [X] days across the stented segment. CE marked under MDR (Class IIb, NB [number]). Available now in Germany, [A–B] mm diameter / [X–Y] mm length. See Instructions for Use for indications, contraindications and warnings.

Three bracketed values to fill from the technical file.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "across the full lesion" | Intended purpose as assessed + labelled length/diameter matrix | RA / technical documentation owner |
| "across the full lesion" | Drug distribution data across the stented segment | R&D / preclinical |
| "sustained drug release" | Elution profile with release period in days | R&D / technical file |
| "Approved" | NB number and certificate scope; confirm it covers all promoted configurations | RA |
| "available now" | German commercial availability of every promoted size on the congress date | Commercial / supply |
| (c) omission | IFU section on likely risks, to decide whether a pointer is needed | RA / IFU owner |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a), no. 3(a); § 3a; § 11(1) scoping sentence for devices — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1, § 5(2) no. 4; § 6 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**The one thing to resolve first:** paste the intended purpose. "Across the full lesion" is the only phrase here that could be a breach no amount of data will fix, and I can't tell which side of the line it falls on without seeing what the notified body actually assessed.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: congress booth copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent — Class IIb, CE marked, notified body involved
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed**
**Audience:** Fachkreise (interventional cardiologists, congress booth) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; HWG § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (+ EU)

I can review limbs (a), (b) and (c) without the intended purpose, but (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I can't assess it against a purpose I haven't seen. Can you paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC? For a DES it will almost certainly carry vessel-diameter and lesion-length ranges, which bear directly on the "full lesion" claim below.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 verify.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

---

## Findings

**Claim:** "Approved and available now" — the word *approved*
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 `[verified]`; HWG § 3 sentence 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 5(2) no. 4 covers "Aussagen oder Symbole, die […] sich auf eine **Zulassung** des Unternehmers oder der Waren […] beziehen". A Class IIb device holds a CE marking based on conformity assessment with notified-body involvement — it does not hold a *Zulassung/approval*. On a German booth, "approved" reads as "zugelassen" and ascribes a regulatory status of a kind that does not exist for devices. HWG § 3 sentence 1 ("Unzulässig ist eine irreführende Werbung") catches the same impression; the enumerated cases are "insbesondere", so the general clause is available.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — not curable by evidence; cured by naming the actual status
**Note:** Do **not** let anyone cite HWG § 3a at you here — § 3a is limited to Arzneimittel and does not apply to devices.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "CE-marked under MDR (Class IIb, notified body [NB no.])"

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release **across the full lesion**"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`; HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(a) prohibits ascribing properties the device does not have. Drug release occurs along the **stented segment**, not along "the full lesion" — full-lesion coverage is a function of correct sizing and of the lengths you actually supply, not a property of the stent. Stated unconditionally, the sentence ascribes a capability that holds only under a condition the copy omits. § 5(2) no. 1 reaches the same statement as "Zwecktauglichkeit / Verwendungsmöglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse".
**Evidence needed:** Partially curable — uniform elution along the stent length is substantiable from elution data; "full lesion" is not, and should be narrowed rather than defended.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]` — if the assessed intended purpose is restricted to a lesion-length or vessel-diameter range (typical for DES), an unqualified "full lesion" suggests use beyond it. Cannot be confirmed until the intended purpose is supplied, and this route is **not** curable by evidence — only by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "sustained drug release along the full length of the stented segment"

---

**Claim:** "**sustained** drug release"
**Breach:** none
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a), UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Tests") — if the elution profile in the technical file does not support "sustained" as a Fachkreise reader would read it, or if the figure comes from bench data presented as clinical
**Why not a breach:** Not misleading on the material supplied; it rests on an elution duration I have not seen. Fachkreise will read "sustained" as a specific kinetic claim, so it is worth carrying the number.
**Evidence needed:** Release-kinetics data from the technical file; the duration and the test basis (bench vs. in vivo)
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** "sustained drug release ([X]-day elution profile; see IFU)"

---

**Claim:** "available now"
**Breach:** none
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "Verfügbarkeit" is expressly listed as a wesentliches Merkmal. If the stent is not commercially available in Germany, in the sizes shown, on the date of the congress, this becomes a § 5 finding on its own.
**Why not a breach:** Availability is a plain factual claim; I have no reason to doubt it, but I also cannot check it.
**Evidence needed:** German launch/shipping date and the size matrix actually orderable
**Call:** Verify

---

## Open question — limb (c)

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk that belongs here, and I won't infer one from the fact that it's a DES — that would make the finding unfalsifiable. Worth checking against the IFU. If it does record one (contraindications, antiplatelet-therapy requirements, sizing constraints), the proportionate fix for trade-show copy is an IFU pointer, not patient-facing safety text.

Note separately that HWG § 3 no. 2(b) (falsely implying no harmful effects on proper or prolonged use) is **not** tripped by this copy — it makes no safety representation at all. Keep it that way in the rewrite; don't add reassurance language to fill the gap.

---

## Paste-ready revised copy

**English:**

> Our sirolimus-eluting stent delivers sustained drug release along the full length of the stented segment ([X]-day elution profile; see IFU). CE-marked under MDR (Class IIb, notified body [NB no.]) and available in Germany now. For indications, vessel-diameter and lesion-length ranges, and contraindications, see the Instructions for Use.

**German** (if the panel runs in German — the point is to avoid "zugelassen"):

> Unser Sirolimus-freisetzender Stent gibt den Wirkstoff über die gesamte Länge des stentversorgten Segments kontinuierlich ab (Freisetzungsprofil über [X] Tage, siehe Gebrauchsanweisung). CE-Kennzeichnung nach MDR (Klasse IIb, Benannte Stelle [NB-Nr.]), in Deutschland ab sofort verfügbar. Indikationen, Gefäßdurchmesser- und Läsionslängenbereiche sowie Gegenanzeigen: siehe Gebrauchsanweisung.

---

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|

# Device Claims Review: congress booth copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent — Class IIb, CE marked, notified body involved
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (interventional cardiologists, congress booth) — HWG § 11 not applied
**Markets:** DE (EU)

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 verify.

**Ready to publish: With changes below.**

## Findings

**Claim:** "across the full lesion"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) [verified]; HWG § 3 no. 1 [verified]; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified]
**Why:** Art. 7(a) prohibits "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". The stent releases drug across **its own stented segment**, a fixed length; it cannot deliver drug across "the lesion", whose length is a patient variable independent of the device. Whether the lesion is fully covered depends on operator sizing, not on a property of the stent — geographic miss is the standing counter-example in this audience. Same test under HWG § 3 no. 1 (Wirkungen, die sie nicht haben), and under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 as *Zwecktauglichkeit / Verwendungsmöglichkeit*.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. This is cured by narrowing the claim to the stented segment.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) — if the assessed intended purpose specifies a lesion length range (as DES intended purposes normally do), unqualified "full lesion" suggests use across lesions longer than the assessed range. Confirm against the DoC.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "…across the stented segment."

---

**Claim:** "Approved and available now" — the word *approved*
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 [verified]
**Why:** § 5(2) no. 4 reaches "Aussagen oder Symbole, die […] sich auf eine **Zulassung** des Unternehmers oder der Waren oder Dienstleistungen beziehen". In the EU a device is not approved or authorised — it undergoes conformity assessment and bears a CE marking. "Approved", unqualified, states a regulatory status that does not exist for this device and cannot be checked against any register. The class and notified-body involvement themselves are accurate, so the defect is the word, not the underlying facts.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — replace with the actual status.
**Also engaged:** sharpens if the panel is translated — "zugelassen" for a CE-marked device is the same claim in a form the German audience reads as a medicinal-product authorisation.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "CE marked (Class IIb)" — or "CE-Kennzeichnung, Klasse IIb" in German.

Note: I am **not** citing HWG § 3a. It applies only to Arzneimittel; the sirolimus component does not pull a drug-eluting stent into it.

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Not misleading on the material supplied — elution kinetics are a characterised property of a DES. But "sustained" carries no period, so nothing here is verifiable by the reader, and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 covers *von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse*. A broad unverifiable claim is expensive to defend even when true; a stated duration is cheap.
**Evidence needed:** the elution profile from the technical documentation — release duration and the percentage released over it.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** "provides controlled drug release over [X] days".

---

**Claim:** "available now"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** *Verfügbarkeit* is named expressly in UWG § 5(2) no. 1, but I have nothing suggesting the statement is untrue. Open point, not a breach.
**Evidence needed:** confirmation that the device is orderable in Germany as of the congress date, and that the **full size matrix** is — not just part of it. If only some diameters or lengths ship, "available now" next to a lesion-coverage claim compounds into a coverage promise the stock cannot meet.
**Call:** Verify

**Limb (c) — open question, not a finding.** The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I have no IFU, so I cannot name a likely risk from supplied material, and I will not infer one from the device category — that would make the finding unfalsifiable. Worth checking whether the IFU records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose (antiplatelet regimen, contraindications) that belongs on the panel. Insert the elution duration from the technical file; drop the IFU line only if the IFU records no likely risk worth surfacing.

graders.evidence:
## Bottom line

Two of the three claims need rework before this can go on a booth panel. "Approved" is the hard stop; "across the full lesion" is the substantiation risk. Also flag: a sirolimus-eluting coronary stent is almost certainly **Class III**, not IIb — worth checking before anything else, since it changes the claims-evidence bar.

---

## Findings

**1. "Approved" — must go (high)**

Medical devices in the EU are not "approved." They undergo conformity assessment and carry a CE mark. In German, "zugelassen" is reserved for medicinal products and its use here reads as a state authorisation that doesn't exist. This falls under MDR Art. 7, which prohibits wording that creates a false impression regarding certification or the device's properties, and under § 3 HWG (irreführende Werbung — HWG applies to devices, and § 3 applies regardless of Fachkreise audience).

Use: "CE-gekennzeichnet" / "CE-marked". Not "approved", not "zugelassen", not "certified by [NB name]" as a quality signal.

**2. Notified body — do not turn it into an endorsement (high)**

The NB's four-digit number belongs next to the CE mark on labelling. Naming or logo-ing the NB in promotion implies review and endorsement of your marketing claims, which it isn't. Your NB contract almost certainly prohibits it, and it compounds the Art. 7 problem.

**3. "across the full lesion" — unsupported and scope-creeping (high)**

Two problems. First, a stent delivers drug where the struts are apposed — it cannot make claims about the lesion as an anatomical entity. Second, "full lesion" invites use in lesion lengths outside your certified size range, which is off-label promotion exposure.

Reformulate to the physical truth: "drug coating across the full stent length," plus the labelled lesion-length and vessel-diameter range.

**4. "sustained drug release" — needs a number and a source (medium)**

Vague performance adjectives are exactly what MDR Art. 7 and Annex I 23.2 push back on. Quantify from your clinical evaluation / bench elution data: "controlled sirolimus release over X days." Every claim on the panel needs a line in a claims-substantiation matrix traceable to the CE technical documentation and clinical evaluation report — build that before print, not after a competitor complaint.

**5. "available now" — verify per market (medium)**

Must be true for Germany specifically, and it must remain true through the congress. If supply is limited to certain sizes, say so. If you're still on a legacy MDD certificate under the Art. 120 transitional provisions, do not let any adjacent material imply MDR certification.

**6. Missing elements (medium)**

No trade name. No reference to the Gebrauchsanweisung. No Fachkreise marking — not strictly mandated for booth panels, but "Nur für Fachkreise" is how you evidence audience targeting if challenged. Also confirm whether the sirolimus mention is framed as device performance rather than pharmacological therapy; keep it on the device side of that line.

**7. Classification (verify first)**

Under MDR Annex VIII, an implant in direct contact with the central circulatory system, incorporating a medicinal substance with ancillary action, lands in Class III (Rules 8 and 14). If your file says IIb, that discrepancy matters far more than the copy. Confirm with RA.

---

## Suggested rework

**EN:**
> **[Trade name]** sirolimus-eluting coronary stent. Controlled sirolimus release over [X] days, with drug coating across the full stent length. CE-marked. Indicated for lesions [X–Y] mm in vessels Ø [A–B] mm. Please refer to the Instructions for Use. Available in Germany. For healthcare professionals only.

**DE:**
> **[Handelsname]** Sirolimus-freisetzender Koronarstent. Kontrollierte Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage; Wirkstoffbeschichtung über die gesamte Stentlänge. CE-gekennzeichnet. Indiziert für Läsionen von [X–Y] mm in Gefäßen mit Ø [A–B] mm. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung. In Deutschland verfügbar. Nur für Fachkreise.

English on a booth panel is generally accepted for a Fachkreise audience at an international congress; German labelling and IFU obligations are unaffected. If the congress audience is predominantly domestic, run the German version.

---

Two caveats: this is a copy review, not regulatory sign-off — your RA and legal functions own the release, and the substantiation matrix is the artefact they'll want. And I'd resolve the IIb/III question before spending time on wording.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Two of the three claims need to change before this goes on a booth panel. The word "Approved" is the hard blocker; "across the full lesion" is the substantive one.

## Findings

**1. "Approved" — highest risk. Change it.**
There is no approval for a Class IIb device in the EU. It is CE marked following conformity assessment by a notified body. In German, "zugelassen"/"Zulassung" is the term of art for medicinal-product marketing authorisation, and using it for a device creates a false impression of an authority-granted approval of safety and efficacy. That engages MDR Art. 7 (misleading claims), § 14 MPDG (Schutz vor Täuschung) and § 3 HWG (irreführende Werbung), and it's straightforwardly actionable by competitors under UWG.

Use: "CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745." Do **not** upgrade this to the notified body's name or logo as a quality seal — that reads as third-party endorsement (again Art. 7) and is usually prohibited by the NB contract anyway. The four-digit NB number belongs on the label, not in a headline.

**2. "across the full lesion" — unsubstantiated as written, and probably beyond intended purpose.**
As phrased this is a coverage/efficacy claim about *any* lesion, and it implies uniform drug delivery over the entire treated segment regardless of lesion length or sizing — i.e. it quietly promises no geographic miss. Full-lesion coverage is a function of correct sizing, lesion prep and operator technique, not a property of the stent. That's MDR Art. 7(a)/(b), and (d) if the intended purpose in your technical documentation doesn't state it.

Replace with something the size matrix actually supports: available lengths, and the lesion length they are indicated for.

**3. "sustained drug release" — keep, but qualify and cite.**
Legitimate if it matches the IFU and the release-kinetics data. "Sustained" is implicitly comparative ("longer than what?"), so either quantify it (release over X days, in-vitro or preclinical, with the data source named) or drop the comparative flavour. If you intend it comparatively against a named competitor, § 6 UWG applies and you need head-to-head data.

**4. Missing risk information.**
MDR Art. 7(c) treats failure to inform of likely risks as misleading in itself. Booth copy needs an IFU pointer — indications, contraindications, warnings, side effects — plus a Fachkreise designation.

**5. "available now" — verify, don't assume.**
True only if all referenced sizes are actually shipping in Germany on the day the panel is up. If part of the matrix is backordered or not yet CE-covered, the sentence is misleading. Cheap to fix, easy to forget when a panel stays in a crate for two years.

**6. Audience gate.**
A congress is Fachkreise (§ 2 HWG), so the § 11 and § 12 HWG public-advertising restrictions don't bite — which is why the drug name "sirolimus" is fine here. But that holds only if the material stays inside that channel: mark it "Nur für Fachkreise", and don't hand the same panel artwork to press or reuse it on the open web.

## Suggested rewrite

**DE:**
> **[Produktname] – Sirolimus-freisetzender Koronarstent**
> Kontrollierte Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage ([in-vitro-/präklinische] Daten, [Quelle]).
> Verfügbar in Durchmessern [a–b] mm und Längen bis [c] mm zur Behandlung von Läsionen bis [d] mm.
> CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745.
> Angaben zu Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweisen und Nebenwirkungen entnehmen Sie der Gebrauchsanweisung.
> *Nur für Fachkreise.*

**EN (for the source file):**
> Controlled sirolimus release over [X] days ([data type], [source]). Diameters [a–b] mm, lengths up to [c] mm for lesions up to [d] mm. CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Refer to the Instructions for Use for indications, contraindications, warnings and side effects. For healthcare professionals only.

## Before sign-off

Put every bracketed value in a claims matrix mapping each phrase to its evidence in the technical documentation — MDR expects claims traceable to it, and your notified body may ask. Have regulatory affairs and German counsel clear the final wording; the above is a compliance review, not legal advice.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Bottom line

Two of the eight words that carry claim weight are problems, and one is a near-automatic *Abmahnung* target in Germany. The copy also carries no risk balance and no IFU pointer. Nothing here is unfixable — but I would not run it as written.

Separately: the classification in your brief looks wrong, and that's not cosmetic. See finding 6.

---

## Findings

**1. "Approved" — HIGH**

Medical devices are not approved in the EU. They undergo conformity assessment and carry a CE mark. In German, *zugelassen* / *Zulassung* is a term of art for medicinal products (§ 21 AMG), and using it for a device is one of the most reliably actionable claims in the German market: it suggests a state authorisation procedure that does not exist for devices. That is misleading under § 3 HWG and § 5 UWG, and the Wettbewerbszentrale and competitors both police it actively.

"Approved" in English at a German booth is additionally ambiguous — an interventional cardiologist may read it as FDA-approved. If you only hold a CE certificate, that's a second misleading reading.

→ Use "CE marked" / "CE-gekennzeichnet", ideally with the notified body number.

**2. "across the full lesion" — HIGH**

This is the sharpest problem. It conflates the *stent* with the *lesion*. Your device elutes drug along the stented segment; whether that equals the full lesion depends entirely on operator sizing, lesion length, and whether the lesion falls inside your labelled diameter/length range. Stated unconditionally, it:

- ascribes a function the device does not have (MDR Art. 7(a)) and creates a false impression regarding treatment (Art. 7(b));
- asserts a therapeutic result as certain, which § 3 Nr. 2a HWG specifically prohibits;
- becomes straightforwardly false for any lesion longer than your longest stent.

If the underlying engineering point is uniform drug distribution with no gaps along the stent, say *that*. It's the defensible version of the same message.

**3. "sustained" — MEDIUM-HIGH**

Unquantified and implicitly comparative. Sustained relative to what, over what period? To Fachkreise this reads as a differentiating claim against other DES, which pulls in § 6 UWG (comparative advertising must be objective, verifiable, and on relevant characteristics of devices with the same intended purpose). Attach a number and a source: "controlled release over [X] days" tied to data in your technical documentation.

**4. No risk information, no IFU reference — MEDIUM**

MDR Art. 7(d) prohibits promotional material that fails to inform of a likely risk associated with intended use. A DES message with zero mention of contraindications, stent thrombosis risk, or DAPT requirements is exposed here.

Note what you do *not* need: § 4 HWG *Pflichtangaben* apply to Arzneimittel, not devices — don't over-comply by bolting on a drug-style mandatory box. The proportionate fix is a standard IFU reference line.

**5. "available now" — MEDIUM**

Purely factual, so verify it literally. It must be true in Germany, on the congress dates, for every size you display or discuss. If launch is staged or only part of the matrix is shipping, qualify it ("available in Germany in [range] sizes"). Otherwise § 5 / § 5a UWG.

**6. Classification — flag on the brief, not the copy**

Your brief says Class IIb. A sirolimus-eluting coronary stent should be **Class III**, on two independent grounds under MDR Annex VIII:

- **Rule 8** — implantable devices are IIb *unless* in direct contact with the central circulatory system. Annex VIII § 1.6 lists *arteriae coronariae* explicitly in that definition.
- **Rule 14** — devices incorporating a substance with ancillary medicinal action are Class III regardless.

If this is a typo in the brief, ignore it. If it reflects the actual certificate, stop and escalate before the congress — it changes the conformity assessment route (Annex IX, including the notified body's mandatory consultation of a medicinal products competent authority on the sirolimus component under Annex IX § 5.2).

It also matters for *this* review: as a Class III implantable you have an SSCP under MDR Art. 32. Every claim above needs to sit inside the SSCP and the CER, and the drug-release claim specifically needs to match what the notified body and the consulted medicinal authority actually assessed.

**7. Fachkreise gating — LOW, but check**

Relying on the Fachkreise carve-out requires access to actually be HCP-restricted. A badge-controlled congress hall is normally fine. It stops being fine the moment this copy is reused on an open website or in an area press can walk through — at which point the § 11 HWG lay-public restrictions engage and this text would need reworking again. Tag the asset as Fachkreise-only in your DAM so it isn't recycled.

---

## Suggested rewrite

**EN**
> [Brand] sirolimus-eluting coronary stent system — controlled sirolimus release over [X] days, uniformly along the full stent length.
> CE marked (notified body [NB number]). Available in Germany.
> For healthcare professionals only. Please consult the Instructions for Use for indications, contraindications, warnings and precautions.

**DE**
> [Marke] Sirolimus-freisetzendes Koronarstentsystem – kontrollierte Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage, gleichmäßig über die gesamte Stentlänge.
> CE-gekennzeichnet (Benannte Stelle [NB-Nummer]). In Deutschland verfügbar.
> Nur für Fachkreise. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung für Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweise und Vorsichtsmaßnahmen.

In the German version, **never** render "CE marked" as *zugelassen* — that reintroduces finding 1 in its most actionable form.

Booth copy in English is generally acceptable for Fachkreise in Germany; the German-language obligation bites on labelling and IFU, not advertising. A German version is still worth having for this audience.

---

## Before the congress

- [ ] Confirm the release-duration figure `[X]` traces to data in the technical documentation and is consistent with the SSCP and IFU.
- [ ] Confirm "uniformly along the full stent length" is substantiated by bench/PK data on file, not just an engineering assumption.
- [ ] Confirm German availability for every size on display, as of the congress dates.
- [ ] Resolve the IIb/III discrepancy.
- [ ] If you add any study data to the booth, § 6 HWG requires full citation — author, date, title — and the summary must not overstate the study.
- [ ] Brief booth staff to the same claim set. Verbal claims are advertising, and off-IFU conversations at a stand are a genuine exposure.
- [ ] If there are giveaways, run them past § 7 HWG and your MedTech Europe / BVMed code obligations.

I've kept legal references at statute level deliberately and haven't cited case law — worth a short confirmation pass with German counsel on the final German wording, since that's where the *zugelassen* trap lives.

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10
**Device:** Reusable surgical retractor — Class I (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (hospital procurement) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; § 3 does

## Summary

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword, 0 substantiate, 2 no-breach-with-conditions.

**No breaches identified** against MDR Art. 7, HWG § 3, or UWG §§ 5–6 on the material supplied. The copy makes no performance, outcome, or clinical claim, which is the structurally safest shape for device advertising. Two items need checking against facts I don't have, and there's one open question for the IFU.

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."

# Device Claims Review: headline + subhead (12 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-10

**Markets:** DE (EU rules apply cumulatively)

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 1 substantiate, 0 OK.

**No MDR Art. 7 breach identified.** The copy makes no performance, clinical or intended-purpose claim at all — which is why it clears Art. 7 and simultaneously why it is weak for procurement. The one live exposure is the collective-endorsement claim, which is a substantiation question under UWG, not an Art. 7 question.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

## Findings

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No therapeutic effect is attributed (HWG § 3 no. 1 not engaged) and no function or property is ascribed to the device (Art. 7(a) not engaged). It is an assertion about the reception of the product among a professional group — the kind of statement UWG § 5(1) reaches if it is "geeignet, den ... sonstigen Marktteilnehmer zu einer geschäftlichen Entscheidung zu veranlassen." Surgeon acceptance is a real procurement criterion, so materiality under § 5(1) is not hard to establish here. Whether it is *irreführend* depends entirely on what sits behind it.
**Evidence needed:** A user-satisfaction or handling evaluation with a stated n, sites, and question set. If the basis is three unsolicited emails, the claim cannot carry the word "surgeons" as a class.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse", "Tests") — if the claim is later supported by a survey, the way it is summarised must not cherry-pick. HWG § 11(1) no. 11 (Äußerungen Dritter, only where missbräuchlich/abstoßend/irreführend) — engaged only if this copy runs anywhere that is not genuinely Fachkreise.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** see paste-ready copy below.

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Three provisions worth ruling out explicitly, because each is a plausible over-read:
- **UWG § 6** is *not* engaged. § 6(1) requires a Mitbewerber or their goods to be made "erkennbar". "actually" swipes at the whole product category, not at an identifiable competitor, so this is not comparative advertising and the § 6(2) limbs never open.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** is *not* engaged. The provision covers the impression that "ein **Erfolg** mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" — therapeutic success. A promise of subjective enjoyment is a certainty framing about satisfaction, not about outcome.
- **Art. 7(d)** is *not* engaged. The copy suggests no user population, setting or indication, so there is nothing to drift from the assessed purpose.

The reason to change it is risk hygiene and procurement fit, not a statutory finding: it is an unfalsifiable second-person promise carrying an implied category-wide denigration, and it tells a procurement reader nothing about the device.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — a subjective promise is not curable by evidence; it is curable by making it specific.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** see below.

### Audience caveat

You have told me Fachkreise, and I have reviewed on that basis. Flagging once, because it changes the answer rather than decorating it: if this headline also runs on an ungated product page, in general-interest media, or on an unbadged trade-show panel, the audience is not automatically Fachkreise, § 11 opens, and "Surgeons love it" becomes an unattributed third-party endorsement under § 11(1) no. 11 — still only prohibited where misleading, but now with a second provision on it rather than one.

The copy surfaces no limitation, and it is 12 words long, so I would not expect it to. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs near this copy — for a **reusable** device, reprocessing constraints and any cycle limit are the usual candidates. Worth checking against the IFU. I am not raising this as a finding, because the risk would be inferred from the device category rather than from anything you supplied.

## Paste-ready revised copy

Bracketed values must come from your evaluation data. If those numbers don't exist, use the second option, which claims nothing you can't already show.

**Option A — keeps the surgeon-acceptance angle, made verifiable (DE):**

> Für die manuelle Retraktion von Gewebe zur Aufrechterhaltung der Exposition des Operationsgebiets bei offenen Eingriffen. In einer Handhabungsbewertung an [k] Kliniken bewerteten [x] von [n] chirurgisch tätigen Anwenderinnen und Anwendern Griffkomfort und einhändige Positionierung besser als beim bisher eingesetzten Retraktor. Wiederverwendbar – Aufbereitung gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung.

In a handling evaluation at [k] hospitals, [x] of [n] surgical users rated grip comfort and one-handed positioning better than the retractor they currently use.
