## Verdict

Don't run this. Both sentences are pure emotional assertion with no substantiation and no connection to the intended purpose — the two things claims control for medical devices in Germany is built to catch. Neither is fatal in concept; both are fatal as written.

---

## Issue 1 — "Surgeons love it"

**What it is legally:** an unattributed third-party endorsement claim about user preference.

- **MDR Art. 7:** claims in advertising must not mislead as to intended purpose, safety or performance. A blanket "surgeons love it" ascribes a general, unbounded acceptance property with nothing behind it. Art. 7 applies to Class I exactly as to Class III — self-certification changes nothing here.
- **§ 6 HWG:** if you *do* have the data (user survey, evaluation report, publication), you may not allude to it vaguely. Advertising with Gutachten, Zeugnisse or scientific publications requires the author's name, the date, and an exact citation. "Surgeons love it" is the textbook violation — it borrows the authority of evidence while withholding everything that would let the reader check it. § 6 applies to Fachkreis advertising too; it is not a Publikum-only rule.
- **§ 3 HWG / § 5 UWG:** misleading advertising. In Heilmittelwerbung the burden of proof sits with the advertiser and the standard is *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis* — the tolerance for "reklamehafte Übertreibung" is materially narrower than in general consumer goods advertising. "Love" reads as puffery in a sneaker ad; in front of a hospital it reads as an assertion about clinical user acceptance.
- **Channel risk:** hospital procurement *is* Fachkreise under § 2 HWG (Einrichtungen, die der Gesundheit von Menschen dienen). But that only holds if the copy genuinely reaches only Fachkreise. On an open website with no access gating, it becomes Publikumswerbung, and § 11 Abs. 1 HWG then bites hard: endorsements by health professionals and third-party statements of the "our surgeons are delighted" type are prohibited outright. Confirm the placement before you rely on the Fachkreise carve-out.

**How to make it usable:** replace the sentiment with the source.

> "In einer Anwenderbefragung (n = 42 Chirurginnen und Chirurgen, DE/AT, März 2026) bewerteten 38 Befragte die Griffergonomie mit 'gut' oder 'sehr gut'. [Autor, Titel, Datum]"

Keep the raw data and methodology on file as claim substantiation — claim control belongs in your QMS marketing-review record, not in the agency's deck.

## Issue 2 — "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using"

- **"actually" is the problem word.** It carries an implied comparison: every other retractor is unpleasant. That's unattributed comparative advertising touching an unnamed but identifiable competitor set → § 6 Abs. 2 UWG, and potentially Herabsetzung under § 4 Nr. 1 UWG. A superiority claim you can't prove is also a Spitzenstellungsbehauptung, which you would have to substantiate as a durable, clear market lead.
- **"enjoy" is untethered to the intended purpose.** Nothing in "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure" is about enjoyment. Claims should sit inside the intended purpose as declared in your technical documentation and IFU; this one floats free of it, which is precisely how Art. 7 exposure arises even for a benign product.
- **§ 3a UWG** turns any HWG or MDR breach into an unfair-competition claim. The practical consequence in Germany isn't a regulator knocking — it's an Abmahnung from a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale, with costs and a Unterlassungserklärung.

## Issue 3 — audience mismatch

Setting law aside: this copy is aimed at a surgeon's feelings and you are selling to procurement. Hospital purchasing decisions run through Einkauf, OP-Management, Hygiene and the Medizinprodukte-Beauftragte, on criteria like validated reprocessing per DIN EN ISO 17664, released reprocessing cycle count, material spec, autoclave parameters, weight, UDI/GS1 data quality, lot traceability, and cost per reprocessing cycle. "Enjoy" is not a line item in any Vergabe matrix. The copy would lose to a competitor's spec sheet even if it were fully compliant.

## Issue 4 — language

The copy is English for a German market. Advertising language isn't itself regulated (labelling and IFU must be German), but "you'll actually enjoy using" has no idiomatic German equivalent — any translation will land either flat or flippant. Write it in German from scratch rather than translating.

---

## Suggested direction

> **[Produktname] — Exposition sicher halten, Eingriff für Eingriff.**
> Wundspreizer zur manuellen Retraktion von Gewebe und zur Freihaltung des Situs bei offenen Eingriffen.
>
> - Material: [1.4021 / rostfreier Instrumentenstahl], Gewicht [xx] g
> - Aufbereitung validiert nach DIN EN ISO 17664, freigegeben für [xx] Aufbereitungszyklen
> - [Griffgeometrie/Sperrmechanismus — konkretes, prüfbares Merkmal]
> - UDI-DI [xxx], Lot-Rückverfolgbarkeit

Every line is verifiable, sits inside the intended purpose, and speaks to the actual buyer.

---

## Two things to check before sign-off

1. **Class Ir.** A reusable surgical instrument under MDR needs Notified Body involvement limited to reprocessing aspects — it is not fully self-certified. Any reprocessing claim you add must match the NB-reviewed IFU exactly. Worth confirming your certificate covers what the new copy will say.
2. **Where this runs.** Open web vs. gated Fachkreis portal changes which HWG rules apply, and the Issue 1 analysis above depends on it.

I've flagged the regulatory hooks as I read them, but this isn't legal advice — route the final wording through your Regulatory Affairs function or German competition counsel before publication.

## Verdict

Not usable as written. Two sentences, and both are problems — one legal, one audience-fit.

---

## Findings

**1. "Surgeons love it" — unsubstantiated third-party endorsement**

- **MDR Art. 7**: claims in advertising may not mislead the user regarding performance. An aggregate endorsement claim ("surgeons love it") is a performance/satisfaction assertion. For a Class I self-certified device it must be backed by something real in your technical documentation — a usability study (IEC 62366-1), a documented user survey with n, date and method. If that evidence doesn't exist, the claim is not defensible.
- **§ 3 HWG** (irreführende Werbung) applies regardless of audience — Fachkreise status gives you no shelter here.
- **§ 5 UWG**: bare claim, no attributable source, no verifiability.
- **§ 11 Abs. 1 HWG** (advertising *outside* Fachkreise — including the provision on claims that a product is recommended, tested or used by physicians) does **not** apply to a genuine Fachkreise piece. But that defence collapses if this copy sits on an open web page or an untargeted brochure. Gating matters: if it's reachable without a Fachkreis check, treat § 11 as live. Verify the current numbering with counsel before relying on a specific subsection.
- If any surgeon endorsement was compensated, add § 7 HWG (Zuwendungen) plus the MedTech Europe / FSA transparency codes and disclose the relationship.

**2. "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using" — implicit disparagement + no substance**

- "*actually*" carries the implication that comparable retractors are unpleasant to use. That's an unnamed comparative claim under **§ 6 UWG** / **§ 5 Abs. 2 UWG** — comparative advertising without an objective, verifiable, like-for-like criterion.
- "Enjoy using" has no relation to the intended purpose and nothing a procurement committee can score. It is not per se prohibited, but it's unsupported and adds regulatory exposure for zero commercial return.

**3. Audience mismatch**

Hospital procurement buys on intended purpose, reprocessing validation, cycle life, instrument-set compatibility, cost per procedure and availability. Neither sentence speaks to any of those. Also: German market, German-language audience — this needs to ship as German copy, not translated-sounding English.

**4. Not flagged**

§ 4 HWG mandatory particulars (Pflichtangaben) apply to medicinal products, not medical devices — you don't owe that block here. No safety-information gap under MDR Art. 7(c) either, since the copy makes no risk-relevant statement at all.

---

## Rewrite options

**A. Function-led (safest — pure intended purpose, no substantiation burden)**

> **Freie Sicht auf das Operationsfeld.**
> Manuelle Retraktion von Gewebe zum Offenhalten des Zugangs bei offenen Eingriffen. Wiederverwendbar, validiert aufbereitbar.

**B. Procurement-led (fill the brackets from your own documentation)**

> **Kalkulierbare Kosten pro Eingriff.**
> Wiederverwendbarer Wundspreizer zur manuellen Gewebe­retraktion bei offenen Eingriffen. Validierte Aufbereitung nach [Verfahren], freigegeben für [n] Aufbereitungszyklen.

**C. If you want to keep the user-satisfaction angle — make it a data claim**

> In einer Anwenderbefragung ([n] Chirurg:innen, [Monat/Jahr]) bewerteten [x] % die Griffergonomie mit „gut" oder „sehr gut". Methodik und Ergebnisse auf Anfrage.

Option C only works if the survey exists, the numbers are from it, and the methodology is in your file and releasable. "Data on file" that no one can request is not substantiation.

---

## If you keep any version of the original

Three things have to be true before it goes out:
1. Named, documented evidence for the satisfaction claim, held in the technical documentation and referenced in the piece.
2. The "actually" comparison either dropped or replaced with a stated, measurable criterion versus a named comparator.
3. Genuine Fachkreise gating on the channel, documented — not just a label saying "für Fachkreise".

I'm reviewing this as copy against the regulatory framework, not giving you sign-off; the endorsement claim and the channel-gating question are both worth a look from your regulatory affairs contact before release.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not usable as written. Both sentences are unsubstantiated claims, and one is an implicit knock on competitors. Neither gives a procurement audience anything to evaluate. Recommend a rewrite, not a patch.

## Issues

**1. "Surgeons love it" — collective endorsement, treated as a factual assertion**

German courts read a claim of broad professional approval as a statement of fact, not puffery, so you carry the substantiation burden — and health-related claims are held to the stricter standard (gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis / verifiable data). Relevant bases:

- **MDR Art. 7(a)/(b)** — no ascribing properties the device doesn't demonstrably have, no false impression.
- **§ 3 HWG** (irreführende Werbung; HWG applies to Medizinprodukte via § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a) and **§ 5 UWG**.
- If it rests on a user survey, omitting n, population, date and method is misleading by omission (**§ 5a UWG**). If it rests on individual statements, they need an identifiable source and must be typical.
- **Channel caveat:** § 11 Abs. 1 HWG only restricts advertising *outside* Fachkreise. Hospital procurement is Fachkreise per § 2 HWG — but an ungated website is Laienwerbung regardless of who you had in mind, which pulls in § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 11 (third-party statements, where misleading/abusive). Gate the material.

**2. "you'll actually enjoy using" — implicit comparative claim**

"Actually" only carries meaning if the reader infers that other retractors are not enjoyable. That makes it comparative advertising under **§ 6 UWG**: it must be objective and verifiable (Abs. 2 Nr. 2) and must not disparage (Nr. 5). "Enjoy" is by construction unverifiable, so it cannot be defended — you'd be arguing that it's both a comparison and unprovable.

**3. Wrong register, and no decision-relevant content**

Procurement scores against a Leistungsbeschreibung. This copy offers nothing scoreable: no material, no blade sizes, no validated reprocessing cycle count, no grip data, no lifecycle cost. Emotional framing on a surgical instrument also reads as trivializing to this audience — a commercial problem as much as a legal one.

**4. Missing intended-purpose anchor**

The copy names no function. Keep the intended purpose adjacent to the product name so nothing reads as suggesting use beyond it (**MDR Art. 7(d)**).

**5. Note on classification**

A reusable surgical instrument is Class Ir: notified body involvement covers reprocessing, cleaning, disinfection, sterilization and maintenance (**MDR Art. 52(7)(c)**). Any future claim about reprocessing or cycle life sits inside that scope — don't let marketing originate those numbers.

## Rewrites

**A — Factual baseline (always defensible)**

> Wiederverwendbarer chirurgischer Retraktor zur manuellen Retraktion von Gewebe und zum Offenhalten des Operationsgebiets bei offenen Eingriffen. [Werkstoff], validiert für [n] Wiederaufbereitungszyklen gemäß [Verfahren].

**B — Benefit-led, if you have bench data**

> Griffgeometrie für ermüdungsarmes Halten: [x] % geringere erforderliche Handkraft gegenüber [Vergleichsmodell] (Prüfbericht Nr. [...], n = [...], [Datum]).

**C — Only if a real survey exists**

> In einer Anwenderbefragung an [n] Kliniken bewerteten [x] von [n] Chirurginnen und Chirurgen die Handhabung mit „gut" oder „sehr gut" ([Quelle, Methode, Datum]).

Option C is the closest legitimate version of the original intent. Note the phrasing: "Chirurginnen und Chirurgen" — the literal translation "Chirurgen lieben ihn" also reads as dated in German Fachkreise material.

## To substantiate before publication

1. Source for "surgeons love it": survey instrument, n, sampling, date, raw results — or drop it.
2. Bench/usability data for any ergonomics claim, with report numbers, filed in the claims dossier alongside the technical documentation.
3. For any comparative statement: named comparator, objective criterion, current data (§ 6 UWG).
4. Confirm the channel is Fachkreise-gated, and log the gating mechanism.
